[Canonical image tagging + automated SBOM sync with CUDA/driver compatibility manifest and rollout gates]
description:
Problem: Our current image tagging and SBOM publishing are inconsistent across the hosted, dedicated, and private channels. This gap causes confusion during LTS rollouts, and has led to a recent on-call incident where nodes were upgraded to a CUDA driver not compatible with a pinned image (INC-2025-230). Goal: Establish a canonical image-tag lifecycle, ensure every released container image is accompanied by a versioned SBOM and a machine-readable compatibility manifest that pins CUDA/runtime driver ranges. Integrate verification into the release pipeline and implement rollout gates that block automatic promotion if compatibility checks fail.

acceptance_criteria:
All release images in the runtime-1.20 channel include a signed SBOM artifact published to artifacts.redwood-infra/storage with matching semantic tag (e.g., runtime:1.20.0+sha256:...),
A compatibility-manifest artifact is generated per image containing: image-tag, build-kernel-ABI, recommended CUDA driver versions, minimum driver version, and tested GPU SKUs
Release pipeline validates that node pools targeted for upgrade have drivers within the manifest's supported range; failing nodes prevent canary promotions
A dashboard shows image -> sbom -> compatibility manifest mapping and final gating status for each rollout
Documentation (Confluence) updated with the tag lifecycle and rollback procedures

implementation_notes:
Add a new step to the image build pipeline (images/builder) that runs syft/grype to produce SBOM and stores it alongside the image in the artifact registry
Create a small tool (compat-gen) that reads build metadata and produces the compatibility-manifest JSON; store manifest as an artifact with predictable path: artifacts/runtime/<tag>/compat-manifest.json
Extend the release orchestrator to fetch manifest and run a nodepool-driver-check before promoting from canary to general availability
Pinning strategy: images will carry both semantic version and build metadata; for pinned deployments we will add explicit driver pin labels to node pool configs
Use signed metadata (cosign) for SBOMs and manifests to prevent tampering in Private deployments

rollout_plan:
Phase 1 - Canary: Release to internal canary account with a single nodepool that we control; gate requires compat-manifest validation
Phase 2 - Extended Canary: Expand to staging customers (5% of traffic) with automated rollback TTL of 30 minutes if health checks degrade
Phase 3 - GA: After 48h of stable metrics, promote to GA; promotion pipeline enforces driver checks across target regions
Manual rollback instructions added to runbook: revert image tag via console or CLI and run nodepool-driver-rollback job

testing_plan:
Unit tests for compat-gen produced manifests with mocked build metadata
Integration test in CI that builds an image, publishes SBOM and manifest, then runs the release-orchestrator's validation step in a dry-run mode
Chaos test: simulate nodepool with out-of-range driver and assert pipeline blocks promotion
Post-release smoke: automated end-to-end generation of SBOM+manifest and verification in a pre-prod environment

risks:
False negatives: manifests missing required fields could block healthy rollouts if validation is too strict
Private/on-prem customers with locked drivers may require coordination and manual overrides; need clear doc and an approval audit trail
Performance: additional build steps increase image build time by ~3-7 minutes; we must parallelize SBOM creation
Key management: signing SBOMs requires access to KMS; need on-call ops to rotate keys safely

links:
https://confluence.redwood.com/display/RE/Canonical+Image+Tagging+and+SBOM+Policy
https://github.com/redwood-inference/images/pull/412 (compat-gen prototype)
https://github.com/redwood-inference/release-orchestrator/pull/98 (pipeline gating changes)
https://grafana.redwood-infra/internal/d/rollouts/image-sbom-mapping?orgId=1
INC-2025-230: driver-incompatibility-on-canary (postmortem link: https://confluence.redwood.com/display/INC/INC-2025-230)

comments:
2025-02-11 Aisha Kumar: Created ticket after INC-2025-230 postmortem. Initial spike complete; prototype for compat-gen in images repo.
2025-02-13 Mei Chen (SRE): Verified SBOM signing with cosign in staging. Need KMS access policy documented for private deployments.
2025-02-15 Design Review - Product: PM asked to add a fallback plan for edge customers; added manual approval gate for Private clusters.
2025-02-18 Liam O'Connor: Implemented pipeline step to fetch manifest and run driver checks; integration tests failing on gpu-sku mapping — investigating
2025-02-20 Security Review Request submitted: security/release reviewed SBOM signing approach and requested threat model for manifest endpoint

[Retire Chat V1 HTTP Endpoints and Sunset Associated Legacy Models - Migration Spec]
description:
Product requirements document for planned retirement of the legacy /v1/chat endpoints and sunsetting the associated legacy model variants (chat-v1-small, chat-v1-medium). Provides migration guidance, timelines, acceptance criteria, and operational runbook for the change.

background:
We maintain two generations of chat endpoints. The v1 endpoints are backed by older runtime paths and model variants that are more expensive to serve and lack structured output guarantees introduced in v2. Usage on v1 has been declining but a non-trivial set of customers and internal integrations still rely on it. Aligning customers to the v2 API and newer model variants will reduce maintenance burden, improve latency/cost, and unlock unified tooling. This PRD specifies how we retire v1 endpoints and related models with minimal customer disruption.

goals:
1) Decommission /v1/chat endpoints and retire chat-v1-* models with no critical incidents. 2) Provide clear, actionable migration paths and tooling for customers to move to /v2/chat and recommended model families. 3) Ensure monitoring, fallback policies, and rollback mechanisms during the rollout. 4) Reduce runtime complexity and maintenance surface by removing legacy kernel paths after deprecation window.

scope_included:
- Public API: /v1/chat endpoints and dependent model variants chat-v1-small and chat-v1-medium.
- SDK wrappers that call /v1/chat in official SDKs (Node, Python) — provide patched versions.
- Developer docs, changelog, and migration examples.
- Console routing rules and metrics that reference v1 routes.

scope_excluded:
- Private on-prem / VPC deployments where customers explicitly opt into extended support (handled via separate contract).
- Non-chat endpoints (embeddings, rerank) unless they reference v1 models directly; those will be handled by separate tickets.
- Internal experimental branches that are not productionized.

constraints:
- Must maintain SLA for existing customers during migration window.
- Cannot remove v1 from hosted control plane until SDK patches and major customers have migrated or opted into extended support.
- Public announcement at least 60 days before mandatory cutoff and individual outreach for high-usage customers.
- All acceptance tests and synthetic traffic must pass on v2-equivalent flows before removal.

timeline:
- 2026-03-15: Public notice and deprecation blog post published.
- 2026-03-22 to 2026-04-12: SDK patch releases (Node/Python) with automatic redirection helpers and migration examples.
- 2026-04-01 to 2026-04-30: Customer outreach and assisted migrations for top 25 customers.
- 2026-05-01: Grace period ends for standard customers; v1 marked read-only for new keys.
- 2026-06-01: v1 endpoints disabled for hosted API; private deployments subject to contract-based support.
- 2026-07-01: Remove legacy runtime kernel paths after post-mortem window.

migration_steps:
Publish detailed migration guide with examples: mapping v1 request fields to v2, typical prompt adjustments, and model recommendations.
Release SDKs that detect v1 usage and log guidance; provide a single-line command to convert calls to v2 when safe.
Add server-side compatibility layer: during window, allow v1 requests to auto-forward to v2 models with telemetry flagging and rate-limited warnings.
Provide a CLI audit tool for customers to scan codebases for hardcoded /v1/chat usage and highlight breakage risks.
Coordinate with Runtime to ensure chat-v2 recommended models (chat-moderate, chat-highperf) meet parity for key behaviors used by customers.
Execute a staged rollout: feature-flagged forwarding -> warning-only -> read-only -> disabled.
Offer migration assistance for top customers and a purchasable extended-support plan for private deployments.
Update Console UI, dashboards, and cost reports to reflect v2 as default and mark v1 as deprecated in the route selector.

communication_plan:
Deprecation blog post and docs page published on 2026-03-15 with timeline and FAQs.
Email campaign segmented by usage: high-impact customers contacted individually by CSM and Solutions Engineering; medium/low usage receive automated migration steps.
In-product banners for accounts making /v1 calls, linking to migration guide and SDK patch notes.
Changelog entries for SDK releases and a single migration checklist repo in GitHub with sample PR diffs.
Support playbook for CS and Support engineers with common troubleshooting steps and escalation contacts.

acceptance_criteria:
All public SDKs (Node, Python) have shipped patches that either transparently map safe v1 calls to v2 or clearly surface migration warnings.
Automated compatibility test suite demonstrates parity for top 50 sample prompts between v1 and recommended v2 models with <5% degradations in quality metrics where unavoidable.
No unresolved P0 incidents during the staged rollout. Any P1 regressions must have mitigation in place within SLA window.
Customer-facing docs and migration guide published and linked from Console and API docs.

rollout_plan:
Phase 0 - Announcement (2026-03-15): Publish docs and start outreach.
Phase 1 - SDK and tooling (2026-03-22 to 2026-04-12): Release SDKs and scanning tools; enable silent forwarding behind flag for internal testing.
Phase 2 - Warning mode (2026-04-13 to 2026-04-30): For accounts still calling v1, inject telemetry and warnings in responses and Console banners.
Phase 3 - Read-only (2026-05-01 to 2026-05-31): Reject write-style operations (if applicable) and continue providing read-only fallback where safe. New keys cannot create v1 routes.
Phase 4 - Disable (2026-06-01): Turn off /v1/chat endpoints on hosted API and archive metrics. Follow separate contract for private deployments.

monitoring_and_rollback:
Pre-rollout: Create dashboards for v1 and v2 traffic, error rates, latency and cost per token.

During rollout: Monitor customer error spikes, SDK telemetry, and support tickets; maintain hotline to engineering on-call.

Rollback options: Re-enable forwarding flag if significant regressions appear; reinstate v1 routing for specific account IDs as temporary mitigation.

Post-disable: Keep archived logs for 90 days and a read-only compatibility snapshot for debugging; any permanent rollback requires cross-org signoff.

followups:
Post-mortem within 2 weeks of disable date documenting migration success metrics and lessons learned.
Ticket to decommission legacy kernel and runtime code paths (ENG-xxxx).
Update internal KB and onboarding docs to remove references to v1.

[Modular Insights launch readiness: coordinated release notes, training, and cross-team comms]

[Safety-net routing and graceful deprecation strategy for pinned model versions]
description:
Summary: Define and implement a safety-net routing layer and deprecation workflow for user-pinned model versions that minimizes customer impact and preserves predictable SLAs. This ticket covers the policy model, runtime routing changes, telemetry/alerts, and an operational playbook for sunsetting pinned versions across regions and model variants.

Why this exists: Customers pin models to an exact version for reproducibility and compliance. When a pinned version becomes unavailable (hardware failure, security patch, or planned retirement), we must route requests in a deterministic, auditable way that: (1) avoids silent correctness regressions, (2) exposes clear signals to customers and SREs, and (3) supports gradual deprecation with per-customer grace windows.

Key constraints and non-goals:
- Non-goal: Automatic transparent model substitution without explicit rule/config (we allow opt-in policies).
- Constraint: Must interoperate with existing pin metadata and rollout APIs.
- Constraint: No user-visible latency regression >20% for P99 in failover path for Dedicated customers at P0 SLA.

Unique aspects of this design: introduce the "variant-bridge" concept (an explicit compatibility mapping between a pinned version and acceptable substitute variants), the "sunset corridor" (time-limited grace window configurable per customer/project), and a lightweight signal taxonomy (soft-failure, hard-failure, controlled-deprecate) used by routing decisions.

acceptance_criteria:
Routing policy engine supports three signals: soft-failure, hard-failure, controlled-deprecate
Per-customer pin config includes: allowed_variants (list), sunset_corridor_days (int), notify_level (none|banner|email)
Failover path executes: pinned -> allowed_variant -> regional-equivalent -> global-compatible -> fail-fast, with observable traces at each hop
SLO/latency regression measured and documented for hosted and dedicated customers; automated canary validates correctness on 5% traffic before 100% switch
Operational playbook created and linked; runbook validated in staged outage test

implementation_notes:
Runtime changes: add a routing policy evaluator that consumes pin metadata and health signals (node health, model-serving status, security flags). Implement 'variant-bridge' table stored in model registry: keys = pinned version, values = ordered acceptable substitutes with compatibility tags and degradation score.

Compatibility scoring: numeric 0-100 used to prefer higher-fidelity substitutes when multiple variants available. Routing algorithm: 1) check pinned instance health; 2) if soft-failure and allowed_variants non-empty, pick highest-score available variant in same region; 3) if none, attempt regional-equivalent (same model family, quantization diff) with degrade marker; 4) as last option use global-compatible variant and attach 'downgrade' metadata to response and traces.

Tech tasks: modify model-registry API (add allowed_variants field), extend routing engine, instrument trace tags (pin_status, chosen_variant, degrade_score), add database migration for per-customer sunset_corridor, and add console UI for per-pin policies.

Backward compatibility: if no allowed_variants set, default to strict fail-fast for pinned hosted customers and to regional fallback for Dedicated customers depending on tenant tier.

rollout_plan:
Phase 0 (Canary): Feature flag enabled in us-west-2 serving cluster only. Route 5% of traffic for internal test tenants; verify P50/P95/P99 and correctness via golden prompts.

Phase 1 (Beta): opt-in tenant UI in Console + API field; invite ~10 customers to enable variant-bridge; run for 2 weeks.

Phase 2 (Gradual): enable automatic safety-net for Dedicated customers with sunset_corridor default 14 days; 10% traffic -> 50% -> 100% over 4 weeks if no regressions. Hosted customers remain strict unless they opt into allowed_variants.

Rollforward / rollback criteria: Rollforward when golden-prompt top-k exactness delta < 2% and error rate stable. Rollback immediately if error rate increases >1.5x or P99 latency regresses >25% for 10 minutes. Manual override available via Console emergency toggle.

monitoring_alerts:
pin.failover.rate > 0.5% over 5m
downgrade.response.header present AND error_rate > 0.2%
sunset_corridor.expiring.without-notify - runbook reminder
variant_bridge.unavailable for regional pool >1m

test_plan:
Simulate soft-failure: mark node degraded; assert routing picks allowed_variant in-region and attaches degrade_score and reason in trace
Simulate hard-failure: entire region down; assert route to regional-equivalent or global-compatible and alerting triggered
Customer grace window test: create pin with sunset_corridor 7 days and verify notification schedule and auto-cutover after corridor expires
Load test: measure P99 latency on failover path for Dedicated GPU pools and ensure <20% regression

notes:
2026-02-20: scoping meeting with SRE/PM/Design — agreed on sunset_corridor and notification levels
2026-02-27: UX mocks uploaded by Design (link in design_links); Console work estimated at 3 points
2026-03-05: prototype routing evaluator merged behind flag (PR #1874)
2026-03-10: SRE ran staged outage test in us-west-2; observed 0.4% failover rate for internal tenants with no customer-visible errors

[Standby Augmentation Playbook — Holiday & Critical Capacity]
Summary:
This playbook defines the process for activating, operating, and retiring a temporary standby augmentation cohort when Redwood faces predictable holiday staffing gaps or unexpected critical capacity stress (GPU exhaustion, region-wide quota loss, or sudden tenancy storms). It describes activation criteria, roles, communication templates for status pages and customer notices, runbook actions during augmentation, and post-incident handoff and compensation steps.

Purpose and scope:
- Purpose: Ensure safe, auditable, and fast onboarding of extra responders (internal volunteers, contractors, or cross-functional engineers) to maintain SLOs and customer trust during periods when primary on-call capacity is reduced or overwhelmed.
- Scope: Applies to all Redwood-hosted inference production environments (hosted API, Dedicated control plane endpoints, Private ops where Redwood provides operational support). Does NOT replace normal incident command; it augments responder capacity and bridge coverage.

When to activate standby augmentation (activation criteria):
Primary activation triggers (any of the following):
1) Scheduled staffing shortfall: 40%+ of scheduled primary responders unavailable for a contiguous 8-hour period (e.g., major US/EMEA holiday windows).
2) Capacity emergency: Sustained GPU utilization > 92% across > 2 availability zones for 10+ minutes with queued requests growing by > 25% vs baseline.
3) SLO at-risk: Token-latency P95 > 3x baseline or error-rate (5xx) increase > 3x for 5+ minutes and automated mitigation has not stabilized.
Pre-checks before activation:
- Confirm incident classification in PagerDuty and link to the incident ID.
- Verify that primary on-call leads have attempted first-line mitigations: autoscale triggers, traffic shape, fallback routing.
- Obtain approval from the Contingency Coordinator (role defined below) if activation is out-of-band.

Roles and responsibilities:
- Contingency Coordinator (CC): Senior SRE or SRE Manager who authorizes augmentation, assigns bridge, and approves customer notices. Ownership: eng-sre.
- Bridge Operator (BO): Person running the incident bridge and status page. Primary BO remains the incident commander or an assigned bridge operator.
- Standby Cohort Lead (SCL): Triage lead for the augmentation cohort — responsible for onboarding volunteers, distributing runbook tasks, and tracking action items.
- Standby Responder (SR): Volunteer or contracted engineer who executes focused runbook tasks (cache eviction, traffic routing, autoscaler tuning).
- Customer Comms Liaison (CCL): Owns external-facing messages and coordinates with account teams for enterprise customers. Typically from customer-success/eng-ops.

Standby cohort composition and rules:
- Minimum cohort size: 3 responders per affected region for low-severity augmentations; 5+ for capacity-critical events.
- Max cohort tenure without rotation: 6 hours continuous work followed by mandatory 6-hour cool-down or handoff.
- Authorization: All SRs must have completed the Standby Safety Checklist (see below) and be on the valid escalation roster.

Standby Safety Checklist (must be completed before SR is placed on bridge):
1) Verified PagerDuty access and silence/ack privileges.
2) Confirmed read access to incident dashboards and traces.
3) Completed required runbook digest (15-minute read).
4) Communication channel test (bridge + slack + paging).
5) Agreed to cohort code of conduct and action logging.

Activation procedure (step-by-step):
1) CC confirms trigger and announces intent to activate standby in the incident channel.
2) BO creates a new cohort channel: #incident-<id>-standby and invites SCL and SRs.
3) SCL runs onboarding checklist with each SR (5–10 minutes per person).
4) BO updates the incident bridge header and status page with: "Standby augmentation active — additional responder cohort mobilized."
5) CCL drafts customer-facing short notice for status page (see templates).
6) SCL assigns clear tickets/tasks from the augmentation runbook and tracks in the incident board (Jira/linear).
7) Measure and report: SCL reports cohort headcount, primary tasks, and time on cohort start in the bridge cadence every 15 minutes.

Augmentation runbook (common tasks — assign by SCL):
- Traffic triage and routing:
  - Promote fallback model variants for best-effort customers.
  - Throttle/shape new sessions for non-paying tiers.
  - CLI: curl -X POST https://infra-api.redwood.internal/v1/traffic/route -d '{"route":"fallback","percent":30}' (example).
- Autoscaler and capacity tuning:
  - Validate autoscaler health: kubectl -n inference get hpa; check CPU/GPU metrics /cloud-metrics/hpa.
  - Temporarily bump minimum pool size according to policy (requires CC approval for >20% change).
- KV/prefix cache operations:
  - Trigger selective cache eviction for noisy tenants. Cache eviction script: /ops/scripts/evict-noisy-tenants.sh tenant-list.txt
- Burst offloading to Dedicated or alternate region:
  - Initiate cross-region failover runbook: see section "cross-region failover".
- Logging and artifact capture:
  - Ensure all SR actions are timestamped and posted to incident log: /incident/logs/<id>. Keep short notes with command outputs.

Communication templates (status page & customer-facing):
Status page short (100–180 chars):
- "Active mitigation: additional responder cohort mobilized to stabilize inference capacity in region <region>. We are managing traffic and expect improved response within 30-60 minutes. — Redwood Ops"
Status page long (for severity > P2):
- "Impact: customers in <region> may experience elevated latency or delayed responses. Action: a standby responder cohort has been activated and we are routing traffic to fallback model variants and scaling pools. ETA for stabilization: 30–60 minutes. Next update: in 15 minutes. Contact: support@redwood.ai for urgent account-specific questions."
Customer email (enterprise):
Subject: "Service notice — temporary capacity mitigation in <region>"
Body: "Hi <Name>,
We’re reaching out to let you know Redwood Ops has activated a temporary responder cohort to mitigate elevated inference latency observed in <region>. Actions in flight: fallback routing, autoscaler adjustments, and targeted cache eviction to reduce queuing. We do not anticipate data exposure; this is an operational mitigation. ETA for improvement: 30–90 minutes. If you have mission-critical requirements, reply and we’ll prioritize routing for your account.
Regards,
<CCL name> — Redwood Support"

Bridge cadence and operational reporting:
- Cadence: 00, 15, 30, 45 minute updates. SCL provides: active SR headcount, top-3 tasks, observed metrics (P95 latency, queued requests), and blockers.
- Evidence: Snap a 5-min metrics window and attach to the incident board. Use timestamped screenshots or query outputs.

De-escalation and retirement of standby cohort:
Deactivation triggers (choose earliest of):
- Sustained stabilization: token-latency P95 back within 1.2x baseline for 15 consecutive minutes and queued requests reduced to <10% above baseline.
- Capacity reclaimed: GPU utilization < 85% for 15 minutes with autoscaler settled.
- CC or incident commander signs off.
Deactivation steps:
1) SCL completes outstanding task list and updates incident board.
2) BO announces planned retirement on bridge and schedules final status page update.
3) SRs complete evidence capture and sign out in cohort channel.
4) CC authorizes cohort disband and documents duration and headcount.
5) CCL publishes deactivation note to status page and sends enterprise close note if required.

Post-incident: handoff, review, and compensation:
- Post-incident survey: All SRs must complete a 10-question quick survey describing blockers, suggested runbook changes, and readiness feedback within 48 hours.
- Postmortem owner: Assigned to the SCL within 24 hours. Postmortem must include augmentation timeline, headcount, actions performed, customer impact, and cost estimate for any burst capacity billed.
- Compensation: Volunteers receive standby credit (4 hours of paid time-off equivalent for each 6-hour augmentation shift), unless otherwise covered by contractor terms. Team leads must approve time-off credits.

Game-day checklist (pre-run rehearsal):
1) Schedule a 60-minute drill each quarter that includes standby cohort activation.
2) Validate cohort channel creation and onboarding flows.
3) Test status page templates and external email pipeline.
4) Run a simulated cache eviction and autoscaler bump (no-op mode for safety) and collect diagnostic outputs.
5) Scorecard: onboarding < 10 minutes per SR, first task assignment < 5 minutes after cohort creation, status page update within 10 minutes.

Operational metrics and KPIs to track for continuous improvement:
- Mean time to cohort activation (goal: < 12 minutes from CC authorization).
- Mean task assignment time (goal: < 10 minutes).
- Cohort effectiveness: % reduction in queued requests within 30 minutes of activation (goal: 50%+).
- Volunteer health: % of SRs reporting fatigue or inability to continue post-shift (goal: < 10%).

Governance, training, and documentation maintenance:
- Review cadence: This playbook is reviewed quarterly by eng-sre and customer-success.
- Training: All potential SRs complete a 30-minute mandatory Lightweight Incident Onboarding course and pass a short quiz.
- Documentation: SCLs and CCs are responsible for incorporating lessons into the master augmentation runbook in /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbook-library.

Appendix A — Cross-region failover quick reference:
- Preconditions: legal/data residency check, capacity in target region > 20% free, and routing policy allows cross-region failover for impacted tenants.
- Steps (high level):
  1) Authorize CC and update bridge.
  2) Add temporary routing policy via infra API: POST /v1/routing/override {"from":"us-east-1","to":"us-west-2","tenants":[...]}
  3) Monitor SLOs in target region closely for hot spots.
  4) Rollback policy within 1 hour if adverse effects observed.

Appendix B — Quick templates and commands:
- Create cohort channel: /ops/scripts/create-cohort-channel.sh <incident-id>
- Evict-noisy-tenants example: /ops/scripts/evict-noisy-tenants.sh --threshold 0.7 --region us-east-1
- Sample metrics query (PromQL): rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m]) by (le)

Document history and ownership:
- Owner: eng-sre
- Document steward: Priya N. Sharma (author)
- Last review: 2026-03-02
- Next scheduled review: 2026-06-01

Related resources:
- Incident board template: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-board-template
- Runbook library: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbook-library
- PagerDuty escalation roster: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/escalation-roster

Notes and rationale:
Standby augmentation is intentionally lightweight: the goal is rapid, auditable expansion of human capacity paired with narrowly scoped runbook tasks. This reduces blast radius compared to wholesale incident role changes while preserving accountability and evidence for post-incident review.

[Blameless Timeline and Evidence Standards for Incident Reviews]
Summary:
This page prescribes standardized, blameless requirements for incident timelines and evidence collection for all Redwood production incidents. The goal is to ensure consistent-quality post-incident reviews, preserve high-fidelity artifacts for RCA, and enable repeatable automation.

Scope:
- Applies to all incidents involving production-facing services (hosted API, dedicated model pools, and console).
- Includes incidents that meet the Incident Classification threshold (P1/P2) or that consume >25% of a relevant service's monthly error budget.
- Excludes internal non-production experiments unless they impact customer-facing metrics.

Why a timeline + evidence standard?
- Consistency: reviewers must be able to reconstruct a timeline without ad-hoc requests.
- Speed: clear evidence manifests accelerate RCA and mitigation playbooks.
- Auditability: compliance and enterprise customers require reproducible investigation artifacts.

High-level SLO alignment (examples):
- redwood-api-prod (text-generation): availability SLO = 99.95% monthly; error budget = 0.05%.
- embeddings-service-prod: p99 latency SLO = 600ms; error budget triggers when p99 > 600ms for 6 hours.
- model-routing: request-failure-rate SLO = 0.3% per week.

Incident timeline expectations (blameless):
1) Immediate (0–1h):
   - Create an incident page in Confluence using the incident template. Fill incident-start time, affected services, classification (P1/P2/etc.), and oncall roster.
   - Create/attach an evidence manifest (see below) to the page.
   - Notify SRE oncall and engineering owners via PagerDuty/Slack channel.
2) Short term (1–24h):
   - Document observed symptoms, customer impact (estimate of requests affected, error budget burn percentage), and mitigation steps taken in the incident page.
   - Attach initial logs/trace links and key metric dashboards.
3) Medium term (24–72h):
   - Draft the incident narrative and preliminary timeline (minute-level events where available).
   - Collect and preserve immutable artifacts for final review.
4) Postmortem (72h–7d):
   - Publish a full postmortem with RCA, action items, and acceptance criteria.
   - Assign owners and due dates for every action.
   - If incident impacted enterprise customers, notify Customer Success and Legal; escalate per the enterprise incident runbook.

Evidence manifest (required fields)
- incident_id: Confluence page id (or incident slug)
- incident_start_utc: ISO8601 timestamp
- affected_services: list of service names (e.g., redwood-api-prod, kv-cache, model-worker-gpu)
- observed_metrics: list of metric names and snapshot links (e.g., api.errors.rate -> https://grafana/redwood/api/errors)
- trace_links: list of trace/trace-group URLs (e.g., https://tracing.redwood/trace/abcd1234)
- logs_query: saved query or file (e.g., logging:/projects/redwood/prod/search?q=ERROR%20Rate)
- config_hashes: git commit SHAs or config snapshot links for service(s) involved
- core_dumps/archive: storage path if applicable (e.g., s3://redwood-incidents/2025-02-14/coredump.tgz)
- screenshots/dashboards: image links or attachments
- retained_artifact_ttl: retention window in days (default 365)

(Example manifest JSON fragment — include on incident page):
{
  "incident_id": "inc-2025-02-13-redwood-api-502",
  "incident_start_utc": "2025-02-13T03:42:00Z",
  "affected_services": ["redwood-api-prod", "model-cache"],
  "observed_metrics": ["grafana://dash/redwood/api/errors"],
  "trace_links": ["https://tracing.redwood/trace/abcd1234"],
  "logs_query": "logging:/projects/redwood/prod?q=service:redwood-api AND status>=500"
}

Minimum evidence checklist (attach at time of page creation):
- Snapshot of primary dashboards (PNG or dashboard link).
- At least one high-level trace that crosses the customer request path.
- Representative log slice: 5–10 contiguous minutes that show errors or latency spikes.
- Relevant config version commit SHA(s).
- Screenshot of PagerDuty/alerting trigger with timestamp.
- Error budget burn estimate (percent and absolute units).

Ownership and roles (who does what)
- Incident commander (IC): coordinates response and ensures evidence manifest is updated in 0–1h. Owner: rotating SRE oncall.
- Service owner(s): provide config SHAs and validate the timeline. Owner: service engineering manager.
- Postmortem author: drafts narrative and action items within 72h. Owner: designated author (can be IC or service owner).
- RCA reviewer(s): at least one SRE + one service owner.

Postmortem deliverables and acceptance criteria
- Complete timeline (minute-resolution if available).
- Clear causal chain linking root cause to impact (noting contributing factors).
- Action items with owners, due dates, and a test or validation step.
- Evidence manifest attached and verified (link checks succeed).
- Severity and customer impact stated with mitigation rationale.

Review cadence and meeting agenda
- Within 7 days: run a blameless review meeting (max 60 minutes):
  1) Quick recap and impact (5m)
  2) Timeline walk-through (15m)
  3) Root cause and contributing factors (15m)
  4) Action items and acceptance criteria (15m)
  5) Open questions and follow ups (10m)
- Invitees: SRE oncall, service owner, product representative, security/legal if sensitive.

Retention and compliance
- Default artifact retention = 365 days.
- For incidents involving customer data or regulated workloads, extend retention per legal guidance and mark page confidentiality = restricted.
- Audit snapshot: keep the evidence manifest and references immutable (export to S3/archive bucket) before editing the incident page for legal auditability.

Automation and tooling recommendations
- Incident creation: use the "incident-create" CLI to scaffold the page and evidence manifest. Example:
  curl -X POST https://infra-api.redwood/internal/incidents \
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer $INFRATOKEN' \
    -d '{"service":"redwood-api-prod","start":"2025-02-13T03:42:00Z","classification":"P1"}'
- Logs: prefer saved queries (logging:/...) rather than raw downloads to keep context.
- Traces: create a span-group link and attach to manifest.
- Dashboard snapshots: use grafana API to export PNGs and attach to Confluence page automatically.

Escalation matrix example (error budget driven)
- If incident causes >10% of monthly error budget to burn within 1 hour -> auto-escalate to SRE manager + product owner.
- If incident duration >4 hours and customer impact persists -> signaled page to exec SRE and CS lead.

Quality gates for closure
- All action items have owners and testable acceptance criteria.
- Evidence manifest verified and links reachable.
- CI tests (where applicable) added to prevent recurrence.
- Postmortem annotated with lessons learned and linked to related runbooks or playbooks.

Appendix A — Common queries and snippets
- Grafana snapshot (example):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $GRAFANA_TOKEN" \
       https://grafana.redwood/api/snapshots --data "{\"dashboard\":{...}}"
- Tracing quick link (example): https://tracing.redwood/trace?service=redwood-api&from=2025-02-13T03:30:00Z&to=2025-02-13T04:00:00Z

[Ten-Minute Stabilization Checklist and Customer Briefs]
Overview

Purpose: This document is a compact, prescriptive playbook for the first 10 minutes after an operational signal that materially affects customer experience. It combines a rapid-stabilization checklist, service-specific mitigations for common failure modes, a clear escalation ladder, and customer-facing status templates suitable for status.redwood.ai and enterprise communication. Use this when SLOs are at risk (see SLO section) or when an incident is declared.

Scope: Production services that impact hosted inference, Dedicated pools (redwood-dedicated-*), and Private control plane components. Not intended for minor developer-facing issues or backlog tasks.

Audience: On-call engineers, incident commanders, customer success, and on-call rotation leads.

Service ownership and SLOs

- Example services in scope:
  - redwood-serve-api (external REST/streaming gateway)
  - runtime-inference (GPU serving runtime pool)
  - kv-cache (Redis cluster used for prefix caching)
  - routing-proxy (smart-request-router)
- Key SLOs to watch (example thresholds):
  - Availability (p99 request success) target: 99.95% per region
  - Latency: p95 < 200ms, p99 < 600ms for small generation requests
  - Model Quality: less than 1% prompt-set regression alerts per deployment
  - Cost/Throughput: CPU/GPU saturation > 85% triggers scaling actions

Severity taxonomy (quick reference)

- Sev 1 (Critical): Global or multi-region outage or SLO breach > 30 minutes (customer-visible downtime). Examples: service returning 5xx for > 20% of requests for 5 minutes; routing-proxy down in all regions.
- Sev 2 (Major): Single-region outage or severe degradation affecting significant customer subsets. Examples: p99 latency spike > 2x SLO; KV cache > 90% eviction rate causing sustained latency increase.
- Sev 3 (Minor): Degradation limited to a small set of customers or graceful fallback working; local non-customer-facing incidents.

Ten-minute stabilization checklist (ordered tasks to run in the first 10 minutes)

0. Acknowledge and create the incident artifact (0:00 - 0:01)
  - Acknowledge page in PagerDuty/incident tool immediately.
  - Create a dedicated incident channel: #incident-<svc>-<YYYYMMDD>-<HHMM> (e.g. #incident-runtime-20260210-1023).
  - Start a shared document with timeline headers (minute marks).

1. Assign roles (0:00 - 0:02)
  - Incident Commander (IC): owns decisions, prioritization, and public messaging.
  - Service Owner / Primary on-call: subject-matter expert for impacted service.
  - Communications Lead: prepares status updates and liaises with CS.
  - Secondary on-call: escalated engineering support.

2. Initial triage (0:02 - 0:05) — rapid signal aggregation
  - Check global dashboards: grafana/redwood/global-slo, grafana/redwood/latency-p99, and redwood-alerts channel.
  - Query error rates and latency by region and by model (example query):
    - grafana query: sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="redwood-serve-api",status=~"5.."}[1m])) by (region)
  - Identify scope: all customers, specific customer IDs, or internal-only.
  - Check deployment activity in last 30 minutes: gitops status, CI/CD pipeline: ci/cd-runner -> last successful deploys to runtime-inference.

3. Immediate mitigation options (0:05 - 0:10) — pick the least-invasive that will restore customer experience
  - Fail open to fallback model: If routing-proxy can fall back to a smaller verified model variant (model-bundle-v1 -> model-bundle-fallback-v1), switch routing policy to fallback for impacted region.
  - Scale & restart: For GPU OOM or saturation, trigger scale-up: runbooks/commands:
    - kubectl -n production scale deployment runtime-inference --replicas=6
    - or trigger autoscaler: curl -X POST https://ops-api.redwood.internal/autoscaler/scale?pool=runtime-inference&delta=+2
  - Cache bypass: If kv-cache causing correctness or eviction storms, switch header X-Bypass-Cache: true at proxy for 10 minutes or flip feature flag: ff toggleset cache-bypass runtime-inference true
  - Traffic partition: Route a subset (10-20%) to Dedicated or a secondary region: routing-proxy route set --service runtime-inference --region eu-west-1 --weight 80 --backup us-west-2 20
  - Hot rollback: If a deploy in last 20 minutes correlates, initiate a rollback via ci/cd pipeline: ci rollback <pipeline-id>.
  - Controlled throttling: Apply rate-limits at edge to protect backend: edgectl set-rate-limit --service redwood-serve-api --qps 1000

4. Confirm stabilization (by minute 10)
  - Check that error-rate drops to below 5% of baseline or p99 latency returns to within 1.5x SLO for 5 consecutive minutes.
  - If not stabilized, IC escalates to full incident declaration and expands responders.

Service-specific quick mitigations (one-liners)

- runtime-inference (GPU OOM/saturation): restart affected pods, scale pool, reduce max sequence-length via request transform to limit tokens, switch to quantized model variant.
- kv-cache (Redis evictions / timeouts): increase read replicas, temporarily set prefix caching ttl to 30s, fail open to origin.
- redwood-serve-api (5xx from internal errors): toggle blue/green traffic to previous release, increase pod replicas, gather stack traces: kubectl logs -f deployment/redwood-serve-api -c api | grep ERROR -n 200
- routing-proxy (routing failures): restart routing-proxy instances in one AZ at a time; if config push failed, revert last config commit.

Escalation ladder and timeboxes

- 0m: acknowledge and assign roles.
- 3m: determine scope and impact (IC decision node).
- 10m: require an explicit stabilization action (see checklist). If unsuccessful, escalate to on-call rotation lead and SRE manager.
- 30m: involve Product (if customer-facing regression) and Customer Success for immediate customer outreach.
- 60m: consider executive notification if SLO breach persists or enterprise customers are severely impacted.

Customer-facing status templates (use these verbatim or adapt for tone)

- Initial acknowledgement (use within 10 minutes):
  Subject: Incident: {service} degraded in {region} — acknowledged
  Body:
  We are aware of an issue affecting {service} in {region}. Our on-call team has acknowledged the problem and is actively investigating. At this time:
  - Impact: {short statement of who/what is affected} 
  - Mitigation actions in progress: {eg. rolling restart / failover to fallback model / autoscaling}
  - Next update: within 15 minutes or sooner.

- 30-minute update (if not resolved):
  Subject: Update: {service} incident continuing — mitigation in progress
  Body:
  Status update at {time}:
  - Current impact and scope (updated)
  - Actions taken: {detailed bullet list of actions with timestamps}
  - Short-term plan: {what we will try next}
  - ETA for next update: 30 minutes

- Resolution notice (after service restored):
  Subject: Resolved: {service} incident in {region}
  Body:
  The incident affecting {service} in {region} has been resolved as of {time}. Summary:
  - Root cause (high-level): {brief RCA stub}
  - What we did to restore service: {list}
  - Next steps: full post-incident review scheduled; customers directly impacted will be contacted by Customer Success.

Internal incident timeline template (use in the incident doc)

- 00:00 — PagerDuty alert, IC acknowledged (who)
- 00:02 — First triage (who checked dashboards)
- 00:04 — Mitigation started (actions)
- 00:08 — Stabilization metrics observed (error-rate, latency)
- 00:12 — Decision: continue mitigation / expand incident

Postmortem and follow-up (post-incident checklist)

- Create postmortem within 72 hours. Must include:
  - Executive summary (2–3 sentences)
  - Chronology with minute resolution for first hour, 15-minute buckets after
  - Root cause analysis with evidence (logs, flamegraphs, kernel traces)
  - Corrective actions: short-term (within 7 days) and long-term (owner + timeline)
  - Measurement plan: how will we confirm the fix avoids regressions (synthetic tests, load tests, new alerts)
- Action ownership: assign Jira ticket(s) with clear owners and due dates.
- Postmortem review: schedule a 1-hour review with stakeholders within 7 days.

Runbook hygiene and game-day guidance

- Keep the most relevant runbook steps in the first 10 lines of the runbook (summary + 1-liner mitigations).
- Use canary test harnesses in the qa game-day environment before rolling fixes to production.
- Game-day checklist (preparation): verify shadowing oncall, ensure synthetic traffic generators are healthy, provision an observer channel for execs, prepare customer-facing snippets.

On-call rotation and handoff checklist

- Primary on-call: 7x24 coverage with 8-hour shifts is recommended for SMEs; for general SREs use 12-hour rotations depending on team capacity.
- Secondary on-call: follow-the-sun overlap windows (first 30 minutes of each shift) for knowledge transfer.
- Handoff checklist:
  - Confirm active incidents (none / list)
  - Review outstanding postmortem actions assigned to the oncall owner
  - Share sticky notes about recent deploys or planned maintenance
  - Ensure credentials and runbook links accessible

Evidence collection and runbook snippets to capture during incident

- Collect: stack traces, pprof, top-level flamegraphs, last 2000 lines of logs for affected pods, metrics snapshots (prometheus export), and PagerDuty timeline.
- Commands to run and capture output:
  - kubectl -n production get pods -o wide --selector=app=runtime-inference > pods.txt
  - kubectl -n production logs deployment/runtime-inference --since=15m > logs-15m.txt
  - redis-cli -h kv-cache.prod.internal INFO > redis-info.txt
  - perf top or pprof snapshot for heavy CPU profiles (if safe)

Special guidance for enterprise customers and private deployments

- If an incident impacts Dedicated or Private customers, Customer Success must be looped by minute 10. Use the enterprise template (append customer impact table) and enable a direct Slack or Zoom bridge with the customer success lead.
- For Private/VPC: coordinate with the Private Deployments on-call; do not access customer data without explicit authorization. Follow the Private incident response checklist (link in related pages).

Appendix: Example customer update (copy-paste friendly)

- Initial (10-minute) template:
  We are investigating elevated error rates for text generation calls in eu-west-1. Our on-call engineers are actively triaging and have initiated a controlled rollback to the last known-good runtime. We will provide an update within 15 minutes.

- 30-minute update example:
  Update at 14:32 UTC: The rollback has completed in eu-west-1. Error rates have decreased from 22% to 3% across affected endpoints. We are continuing to monitor and will follow up with a full RCA.

- Resolution example:
  The issue in eu-west-1 was caused by an inadvertent config change pushed to routing-proxy that increased request fanout. We reverted the change and scaled the runtime pool. A formal postmortem is scheduled and customers impacted are being contacted by CS.

Document ownership and maintenance

- Owner: eng-sre incident operations (document steward: Maya Patel)
- Review cadence: quarterly reviews and after every Sev 1/Sev 2 incident.

Related resources

- Incident command playbook: /confluence/eng-sre/incident-command-playbook-2024
- Bridge operator manual: /confluence/eng-sre/bridge-operator-manual-2024
- Runbook repository: /confluence/eng-sre/runbook-library

Notes and best practices

- Keep customer language factual and non-technical for external comms; internal channels should preserve technical evidence.
- Prefer incremental mitigations that are reversible over broad, irreversible changes.
- Timebox efforts: if an action is not producing measurable improvement in 10 minutes, switch strategy and escalate.

End of document

[Rapid restoration sprint guide for multi-region degradations]
Summary:
This document defines the 'Restoration Sprint' process for large-scale, multi-region degradations that impact inference availability or latency across Redwood’s hosted and dedicated customers. It combines a focused triage/runbook, a communications playset (status page + customer templates), on-call augmentation guidance, and a template for the post-incident review. The goal is to restore customer-facing service quickly, preserve customer trust, and capture concrete follow-ups to prevent recurrence.

When to use this runbook:
- Multi-region or cross-AZ impact where traffic routing or control-plane misconfiguration is suspected.
- Partial or full service degradation across >10% of requests or affecting multiple customer tiers (hosted API and Dedicated).
- Incident meets Severity 1 (S1) criteria: site-wide outage, customer SLA breach in progress, or sustained error rate >5% for 5+ minutes.

Owners and roles:
- Incident Lead (IL): oncall engineer owning the incident timeline and comms.
- Triage Lead: service-domain expert (routing/control-plane/runtime).
- Restore Teams: per-service owners: inference-gateway, router, kv-cache, runtime-pool, control-plane.
- SRE Coordinator: escalation and resource sourcing (upscaling, spinning extra pools).
- Customer Comms Owner: owns status page messages and stakeholder emails.
- Exec Liaison: product/security lead to brief executives as needed.

Severity and SLO thresholds (quick reference):
- Severity 1 (S1): service unavailable or >5% error rate global for 5+ minutes; requires immediate pager response.
- Severity 2 (S2): localized/regional impact, or performance regression causing customer-visible latency >2x P50 for 15+ minutes.
- Production availability SLO: 99.95% monthly for hosted inference endpoints. Error budget burn >50% in a 7-day window escalates to SRE Coordinator.

Fast checklist (first 10 minutes) - "Sprint kickoff":
1) Acknowledge pager and set status: create incident in our incident tracker (Jira/Incidentboard) with tag: restoration-sprint.
2) Assign Incident Lead and Triage Lead.
3) Post initial status to #incidents Slack channel (pinned template below) and open a video bridge if the incident is S1.
4) Identify blast radius using telemetry dashboards: per-region 5xx rate, p99 latency, gateway error logs, and routing metrics.
5) If traffic is split across regions, consider emergency routing to healthy region(s) (see containment).

Triage (10-25 minutes):
- Data to collect immediately:
  - Top-3 affected services (service names and teams).
  - Error-class breakdown (502/504/timeout/KV miss spikes).
  - Recent deploys or config changes in last 60 minutes (control-plane audit).
  - Cloud provider control-plane events and networking alerts.
  - Autoscaling metrics for runtime-pool (GPU utilization, queue length).
- Triage steps (ordered):
  1. Check control-plane health: /api/health (control-plane) and controller logs.
  2. Inspect router and gateway errors (example):
     ```bash
     # tail last 200 lines of router logs (k8s)
     kubectl -n infra logs deployment/router --tail=200
     # quick check for 5xx counts from metrics API
     curl -s "https://metrics.redwood.internal/api/v1/query?query=sum(rate(http_requests_total{job=router,status=~\"5..\"}[5m])) by (region)" | jq .
     ```
  3. Check KV cache health and hitrate (redis/kv-proxy):
     ```bash
     redis-cli -h kv-cache.prod PING
     redis-cli -h kv-cache.prod INFO stats | grep keyspace_hits
     ```
  4. Verify runtime-pool nodes: node readiness, GPU drivers, and queuing.
  5. Check recent route table or traffic-shift changes (control-plane audit log).

Containment options (use quickest safe option first):
- Local rollback of suspect config/deploy (control-plane flag-based rollback).
- Emergency traffic steering: route a portion of traffic to alternate region or degraded-but-stable model variant.
- Throttle non-critical background requests (batch/prefetch) to preserve runtime capacity for customer requests.
- Apply circuit-breaker: increase client-side timeouts or return graceful degradation where supported.

Example commands (routing steer to us-east region):
```bash
# control-plane CLI example (safe-scoped)
redwoodctl routing update --selector "service:inference-gateway" --region us-east-1 --weight 70
redwoodctl routing update --selector "service:inference-gateway" --region eu-west-1 --weight 30
```

Restore sequence (25-60 minutes):
1) Implement containment that minimizes customer impact.
2) Validate improvement metrics for 5–10 minutes (p50/p95 latency, 5xx rate).
3) If restored, start a controlled rollback of containment actions back to preferred topology with a canary window.
4) If not restored, escalate to SRE Coordinator to provision emergency capacity or vendor support.
5) Keep customers informed at regular cadence (see communications cadence).

On-call augmentation guidance:
- If incident expected >2 hours, request a second oncall rotation to relieve primary IL every 4 hours.
- Use 'Incident Relays' (pre-identified engineers for router, runtime, control-plane) to avoid context switching.
- For after-hours incidents affecting enterprise customers, call the named customer success lead for direct outreach (list maintained in the incident tracker).

Game-day exercise (schedule and goals):
- Objective: validate that traffic-steering, rollback, and cross-region routing work end-to-end under a simulated routing-misconfig scenario.
- Frequency: quarterly; includes control-plane dry-run and postmortem write-up.
- Key steps for exercise:
  1. Simulate misconfigured weight (intentionally set one region to 0% and observe failover).
  2. Measure detection time for alerting rules and run restoration sprint.
  3. Validate status page and customer comm cadence for clarity and timeliness.
  4. Produce an action list and track in engineering project board.

Status page and customer communications playset (templates):
- Initial public status (short):
  "title: Service degradation affecting inference requests in multiple regions
   created_at: <timestamp>
   summary: We're seeing elevated error rates and increased latency impacting inference requests across multiple regions. Our engineering teams are investigating.
   impact: Customers may see increased errors or longer response times.
   updates: We will post updates every 30 minutes or as we make decisive progress."

- 15-minute status update (example):
  "We have identified that recent routing changes to the inference router are correlated with increased 5xx errors in eu-west-1 and us-west-2. We are running a targeted traffic steering to redirect traffic to healthy regions and validating recovery metrics. Next update in 30 minutes."

- Resolution message (example):
  "Service restored: We have implemented a rollback of the routing change and validated successful request rates in affected regions. All services are reporting healthy. We will create a post-incident review with follow-ups and timeline. If you continue to see issues, please contact support@redwood.ai with request-id."

Customer email template (for enterprise customers):
Subject: Incident update — service degradation impacting inference requests
Body:
"Hello <CustomerName>,

We want to update you on an incident affecting inference requests across multiple regions. Our teams detected elevated error rates starting at <start_time>. We have identified the likely cause (routing configuration) and implemented traffic steering and a rollback to restore service. At <restore_time> we validated healthy metrics for impacted endpoints.

Next steps: we will publish a full post-incident report with timeline and mitigation actions by <date>. If this incident impacted SLA or you need a dedicated follow-up, your technical account manager <TAM> will reach out.

Apologies for the disruption — we appreciate your patience.

— Redwood Inference Support"

Internal Slack templates (post to #incidents and #oncall):
- Initial (use incident tag):
  ":rotating_light: Incident S1 — multi-region inference degradation. Incident lead: @<IL>. Triage lead: @<TL>. Video bridge: <link>. Affected services: inference-gateway, router, runtime-pool. Current action: running routing-steer containment to us-east-1. See incident board: <link>"

- Update: ":white_check_mark: Incident update — traffic steering reduced 5xx by ~70% in eu-west-1. Monitoring for 15 minutes before rollback."

Post-incident review template (to publish after resolution):
- Title: Post-incident review — restoration sprint for multi-region routing failure (YYYY-MM-DD)
- Timeline: ordered bullet points with timestamps (detection, triage, containment, restore, verification).
- Root cause analysis: short causal chain (e.g., control-plane route policy mis-evaluated due to late-deployed guardrail).
- Contributing factors: list (engineer rollout, missing canary, alert threshold too high, stale runbook step).
- Impact: quantitative metrics (requests affected, error budget burn, customer tiers impacted, estimated revenue/hour impact if known).
- Actions (owner + due date): clear actionable items, prioritized P0/P1.
- Learnings and follow-ups: scheduled validation in next game-day.

Example timeline excerpt (format to copy):
"10:03 UTC — Alerting rule fired: global 5xx rate >5% (S1)
10:04 UTC — Pager acknowledged; incident created #INC-4529
10:10 UTC — Identified recent route-weight change at 09:55 UTC
10:18 UTC — Traffic steering to healthy regions applied
10:30 UTC — 5xx rate reduced to <1%; monitoring
11:00 UTC — Rollback completed; verified p95 latency within baseline
11:15 UTC — Status page updated: resolved"

Runbook maintenance and review cadence:
- Owner: SRE team (runbook custodian specified in incident board).
- Review schedule: monthly automated review reminder; full-manual review after every S1 incident.
- Game-day validation: exercise restoration sprint annually (preferably quarterly for high-risk routes).

Appendix: quick reference commands and dashboards:
- Dashboards: Routing health dashboard, Global error tracker, Runtime pool utilization, Control-plane audit trail.
- Helpful queries:
  - Error rate by region: metrics query example (PromQL):
    sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~\"5..\", job=\"inference-gateway\"}[5m])) by (region)
  - Control-plane recent changes (last 60m):
    redwoodctl audit list --since 60m --component control-plane

Decision notes and escalation matrix (one-liners):
- If error budget burn >50% in 24 hours, call SRE Director and limit non-critical experiments.
- If incident extends >6 hours with customer SLA impact, escalate to product and sales leadership for direct outreach.

Document change history:
- 2024-10-15 — created by Maya Patel (initial draft)
- 2025-01-10 — added game-day exercise steps and expanded communication templates (review: Daniel Huang)
- 2025-02-12 — updated SLO references and example commands (review: Priya Rao)

Related pages:
- See SLO and error budget guidelines for escalation thresholds.
- Refer to rollout and canary docs for safe-deploy patterns.

If you are reading this while oncall: use the sprint checklist at the top and tag the incident with 'restoration-sprint' to surface it for postmortem prioritization.


[Incident Execution Guide, Runbooks, and Communication Templates]
Summary:
This page is an operational playbook for executing incidents from detection through postmortem and remediation. It standardizes roles, runbook structure, alert thresholds, communication templates, rotation rules, and game day exercises. Use this guide as the canonical source for incident execution across Redwood Inference services.

Scope:
- Applies to all Redwood-hosted and Dedicated/Private control-plane services that impact customer-facing inference APIs, console, or billing.
- Excludes routine CI failures and development branch problems (handled by triage owners).

Key definitions:
- Incident: any event causing customer-visible degradation or data/control plane impact for >30s or impacting >0.5% of requests in a region for >5 minutes.
- Severity levels: P0 (system down or data loss), P1 (significant customer impact), P2 (degraded performance impacting SLAs), P3 (minor or isolated issues).

Incident lifecycle (high level):
1) Detection & Alerting
   - Sources: Prometheus alerts, tracing-based anomaly detectors, Synthetics (every region), customer-reported tickets, platform health probes.
   - Automatic triage: Alerts with matching runbook tags are routed to oncall via PagerDuty with escalation policies defined below.
2) Triage (first 10 minutes)
   - Pager acknowledges, documents initial symptoms in the incident channel (Slack #inc-<service>-<region>).
   - If impact meets P1/P0 criteria, auto-page Incident Commander (IC) and notify Product/Customer Success.
3) Containment & Mitigation
   - IC assigns roles and calls for mitigation steps. Mitigation goal: stop customer impact, minimize blast radius, restore availability.
4) Restoration
   - Validate service health across regions, update status page, and begin traffic rehoming if required.
5) Post-incident review
   - Capture timeline within 48 hours; full postmortem completed in 7 business days with action items and owners.

Roles & responsibilities:
- Incident Commander (IC): Leads incident, sets priorities, owns the incident timeline, and makes rollout/fallback decisions. (Default: SRE oncall lead).
- Communications Lead: Owns customer-facing comms, status page updates, internal summaries. (Default: oncall primary until handed to PM/CS).
- Engineering Owner(s): Service-owner engineers who run remediation steps and confirm fixes.
- Support Liaison: Triage customer tickets, surfaces relevant customer impact details.
- War Room Coordinator: Creates and moderates incident Slack channel, ensures notes and recordings are captured.

On-call rotations and handoffs:
- Rotation cadence: 1 week primary oncall for SREs, 1 week secondary. Follow policy: maximum 6 consecutive weeks oncall per year per engineer.
- Handoff checklist (to run at every rotation swap):
  1. Confirm PagerDuty schedule and escalation contacts.
  2. Confirm access (kube, cloud console, logs-bucket).
  3. Review 3 most recent active runbooks and ongoing incidents.
  4. Share any planned maintenance windows.
- Handoff message example:
  "Handoff: @alice -> @bob. Primary oncall for inference-core this week. No active incidents. Known maintenance: database patch Thursday 02:00 UTC. Key dashboards: /dashboards/inference-overview. PD escalation: pd://redwood/inference-primary.

Runbook structure (required fields):
- Title (service-region-tag)
- Purpose and scope
- Owner & reviewers (team email + schedule)
- Triggers (alerts / symptoms that should cause invocation)
- Pre-flight checks (e.g., verify region, check KV cache status)
- Step-by-step mitigation (numbered, idempotent steps)
- Validation (how to confirm success)
- Rollback / fallback plan
- Post-incident tasks & references

Sample runbook (truncated):
---
Title: inference-api-high-5xx-us-east-1
Owner: inference-svc-team@redwood.com
Triggers:
- prometheus: inference_api_5xx_rate > 0.5% (5m)
- synthetic: /health returns 500 from 3 probes in 2 regions
Steps:
1) Confirm the alert: grep "5xx" /var/logs/inference/* | tail -n 200
2) Check deployment health: kubectl -n inference get pods -o wide | egrep "CrashLoop|0/"
3) If new deploy in last 30m: rollback: kubectl -n inference rollout undo deployment/inference-api --to-revision=<previous>
4) If not deploy-related: scale down suspect node pool: gcloud container clusters resize <cluster> --node-pool=<pool> --num-nodes=<reduced>
5) Purge local KV caches on affected hosts: redis-cli -h <host> FLUSHDB (only if cached keys are ephemeral)
Validation:
- requests_p95 latency returns below 400ms across 5 minutes
- 5xx rate < 0.1% for 10 consecutive minutes
---

Alert thresholds and metric guidelines (examples):
- 5xx error rate: trigger if >0.5% requests for 5m (P1), >2.0% for 2m (P0).
- Latency: p95 > 1000ms for 5m -> investigate P1. p99 > 2s for 3m -> P0.
- Queue backpressure: queued requests > 5k in a region -> P1.
- Synthetic failures: 3 region probes failing in 5m -> P1.

Escalation matrix (summary):
- Primary oncall (first 5 minutes)
- After 5 minutes with unresolved mitigation: escalate to secondary oncall + IC auto-notify
- After 15 minutes for P0 events: page Engineering Director + Head of SRE + Customer Success lead

Status page and customer comms templates:
- Use status.redwood.ai for public status. For Dedicated/Private customers also use ticketing system and account-level email templates.

Templates (copy/paste and fill placeholders)
1) Initial acknowledgement (15 minutes):
Subject: [Incident] Redwood Inference – {service} experiencing errors in {region}
Body:
Hello,
We are aware of elevated errors impacting {service} in {region}. Our oncall team is investigating.
Impact: {brief sentence on scope e.g., 20% of requests returning 5xx}
What we are doing: Establishing mitigation, routing traffic, and rolling back suspect deployments.
Next update: within 30 minutes or sooner.
Status page: https://status.redwood.ai/incident/{incident-id}
Contact: support@redwood.ai
2) Ongoing update (every 30 minutes):
Subject: [Update] Incident {incident-id}: {service} in {region}
Body:
Update at {time UTC}:
- What changed since last update: {progress summary}
- Current impact: {customers/regions affected and percent of traffic}
- Actions taken: {actions}
- Next steps & ETA: {next steps}
3) Resolution notice:
Subject: [Resolved] Incident {incident-id}: {service} in {region}
Body:
The incident impacting {service} in {region} is resolved as of {time UTC}.
Impact summary: {duration, affected customers, root cause (initial)}
Follow-up: A full post-incident review will be published when complete with action items and timelines.
Contact: support@redwood.ai

Customer status page content guidelines:
- Keep language non-technical and candid.
- Include impact, work underway, ETA (if available), and mitigation steps.
- Mark updates with timestamps and an internal incident id.
- For sensitive incidents (data loss, security), route updates through Security & Legal for approval.

Post-incident review process:
- Draft timeline (owner: IC) due within 48 hours — includes minute-level timeline, alerts, and remediation steps taken.
- Full postmortem document due within 7 business days. Postmortem must include: summary, timeline, root cause analysis (5 whys / RCA), corrective actions (owner and ETA), and verification plan.
- Postmortem review: mandatory review meeting attended by IC, owners, SRE manager, and PM.
- Action tracking: add all remediation tasks to the incident JIRA/project board with labels: incident-<id>, postmortem, blocker. Owners must provide progress updates weekly until complete.

Game day program (recommended cadence):
- Quarterly regional failover exercise (target: rotate primary traffic across regions without customer downtime).
- Monthly mini-simulations: single-service degradation with 30-minute time-boxed resolution.
- Annual full-stack P0 simulation conducted with exec observers.
Game day outputs:
- Runbook gaps report, playbook updates, training assignments.
- Scorecard: average MTTR, missed steps, communication quality (customer-facing clarity).

Runbook maintenance & governance:
- Ownership: every runbook must list an owner and two reviewers. Runbooks are reviewed quarterly.
- Retirement: deprecated runbooks archived with reason and date.
- PR process: runbook edits are submitted via docs repo PR; urgency edits allowed with follow-up review within 5 business days.

Oncall wellbeing and limits:
- Block high-stress sequences: restrict scheduled changes during primary oncall week unless emergency.
- Offer 4 hours backup time after P0 events for rest & paperwork (approved by manager).

Appendices:
- Useful CLI snippets:
  - View recent deploys: kubectl -n inference rollout history deployment/inference-api
  - Force rollback: kubectl -n inference rollout undo deployment/inference-api --to-revision=<rev>
  - Query error rate: prometheus-query 'sum(rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5..",job="inference"}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="inference"}[5m]))'

- Example incident timeline (abbreviated):
  00:00 Alert fires: 5xx rate spike detected (0.8%)
  00:02 PagerDuty acknowledged by oncall
  00:06 Triage finds suspect deploy 00:45 UTC -> rollback initiated 00:07
  00:14 Error rate begins to decline -> p95 latency improving
  00:20 Traffic normalized; status page updated to "Partial degradations being mitigated"
  01:10 Incident declared resolved; IC closes incident and assigns postmortem owner

- Postmortem template header (to copy into PRD):
  Title: {incident-id} – {short summary}
  Severity: {P0/P1/P2}
  Timeline owner: {name}
  Root cause: {summary}
  Corrective actions: - {action} (owner, ETA)

Contact matrix & escalation contacts (always keep PD entries up to date):
- SRE primary: oncall-sre-primary@redwood.ai
- Engineering director: director-eng@redwood.ai
- CS incident liaison: cs-liaison@redwood.ai

[Batching & Cache Setup Wizard — onboarding flow and safety guardrails]
description:
Design an end-to-end onboarding wizard inside Redwood Console that helps engineers and platform owners configure batching and KV/prefix caching for routes and model profiles. The wizard should: 1) quickly recommend safe defaults based on measured workload signals (median seq len, token rate, request size distribution), 2) explain trade-offs (latency vs cost vs variance) with short contextual explainers, 3) provide a simulated cost & latency preview for chosen presets and slider settings, 4) expose advanced controls in a scoped ‘expert’ panel with JSON preview and validation, and 5) enforce guardrails and warnings for settings that would violate SLOs or exceed estimated spend. This ticket covers the visual flows, microcopy, onboarding checklist, one progressive disclosure prototype in Figma, and a short pilot usability test with 6 backend engineers and 4 ML infra users.

acceptance_criteria:
Onboarding wizard screens created in Figma covering: intro, workload import, recommendation, preview, expert edits, review & apply
Recommendation engine UI communicates confidence and input signals used (e.g., median seq len, 95th percentile QPS)
Simulated preview shows per-100k token cost estimate and median/95th latency estimate for selected profile
Guardrail warnings shown for configurations that risk increased 95th pct latency or >20% cost increase vs baseline
Advanced JSON editor available with inline validation and link to documentation
Prototype tested with at least 6 users and documented usability notes and prioritized changes

design_notes:
Keep primary path under 5 steps to avoid flow drop-off for new users
Use progressive disclosure: simple presets (Conservative, Balanced, Aggressive) default to Balanced
Presets map to batching window, max batch size, KV prefix TTL, KV cache size, and fallback model variant
Preview should be conservative: show ranges and confidence bands rather than single-point estimates
Include small inline helper for each slider with threshold example (e.g., 'Batch window: 20–50ms suitable for QPS < 50')
Design must surface origin of workload signals (client-provided, recent request sample, estimated) — critical for trust

decisions:
Use a wizard rather than inline modal so users can step back to previous inputs without losing state
Expose only three high-level presets on the default path; advanced controls behind a clearly labeled 'Expert options' toggle
Simulated preview will not call the runtime but use sampled telemetry + static cost model to avoid accidental provisioning
Guardrails will be soft by default (warnings) with an explicit acknowledgment required for dangerous combinations
All telemetry-sourced inputs must show timestamp and window (e.g., 'based on last 6 hours') to avoid confusion

2025-01-29: Conducted 6 usability sessions (4 infra, 2 backend). Key pain: users misunderstood 'batch window' units. Action: add microcopy and an example visualizer. - Research
2025-01-31: Security requested explicit mention that KV TTL values are advisory for the runtime; will require follow-up with runtime team. Added ENG-2910 to dependencies. - Ava
