[Unusual session activity after employee reported suspicious phishing email (triage & containment)]
description:
Issue reported by employee via #security-helpdesk: received a targeted phishing email, clicked a link, then observed an unexpected active session for their account from a foreign IP. This ticket documents triage steps, containment actions, and next steps for forensic analysis.

impact:
Potential credential exposure for one SSO-enabled account. No confirmed lateral movement; some API keys associated with the user were briefly active before being revoked. A subset of internal console sessions were observed originating from a foreign IP (unknown device).

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Employee received email with subject 'Invoice overdue - Redwood billing' containing shortened link. 2) Employee clicked link and was presented with a fake SSO prompt that resembled our Okta page. 3) Employee reported to #security-helpdesk at 2026-03-10T09:18:00Z. 4) Security observed a new session from IP 185.66.124.241 at 2026-03-10T09:22:10Z for the same user.

logs:
auth.log lines of interest (redacted):
- 2026-03-10T09:22:10Z AUTH SUCCESS user=j.smith ip=185.66.124.241 ua='Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)' session_id=abc123
- 2026-03-10T09:23:03Z SSO TOKEN ISSUE user=j.smith client_id=redwood-console token_id=tok-45f
- 2026-03-10T09:24:12Z API KEY USE key=redact-*** resource=api.v1.generate model=gpt-redwood-light
SIEM event id: SEV-7621. Packet capture reference: pcap-20260310-09-22 (stored in secure evidence bucket).

timeline:
2026-03-10T09:18Z - Employee reports phishing to #security-helpdesk.
2026-03-10T09:20Z - Security triage starts (Aisha).
2026-03-10T09:22Z - New session seen from 185.66.124.241.
2026-03-10T09:25Z - Password reset enforced and user session revoked (Liam).
2026-03-10T09:30Z - All active API tokens for the user revoked; suspicious tokens flagged.
2026-03-10T10:00Z - Initial containment complete; forensic snapshot taken.
2026-03-11 - SOC confirmed no additional accounts observed with same IP. Forensic team awaiting results from disk image analysis.
2026-03-13 - Ticket escalated to incident review; containment stable.

investigation_notes:
Preliminary findings: the phishing email used a legitimate-looking domain (redwood-billing[.]info) with a redirect through bit.ly. The SSO prompt was a credential-capture page that POSTed to a third-party domain. The session IP (185.66.124.241) geolocated to Eastern Europe and matches a set of previous malicious indicators (threat intel tag: THRT-2026-03-EU1).
No new service principals were created. The user did not approve any OAuth grants. API key usage observed came from the legitimate CLI token; timestamps show a brief window (09:24-09:27) before revocation. We found one suspicious header: X-Forwarded-For: 10.200.45.67 (internal range) which likely indicates proxy manipulation; need infra to confirm NAT logs.
Hypothesis: credentials were phished and used immediately from a foreign IP; attacker attempted to leverage active CLI token for quick API calls. No evidence of code exfiltration or model weights access.

mitigation_actions:
- Immediate actions (2026-03-10): forced password reset for j.smith, revoked all active sessions, rotated affected API tokens, disabled legacy CLI tokens, blocked IP 185.66.124.241 at WAF and infra ACLs, created SIEM watchrule for THRT-2026-03-EU1.
- Communication: notified user, sent company-wide advisory (no compromise detected beyond single account), posted summary to #security-ops and #incidents.
- Evidence preservation: captured session logs, exported relevant pcap, saved mailbox headers and the phishing message to secure bucket.
- Longer-term: SSO provider support ticket opened to review token issuance logs and phishing-resistant MFA options (push-based or hardware for admin tier).

resolution:
Containment achieved: compromised account credentials invalidated, suspicious tokens rotated, and attacking IPs blocked. Forensics in progress (disk and memory imaging for the affected host). Postmortem scheduled; action items include improving phishing-resistant MFA rollout and updating the security awareness training to include this phishing template. Ticket remains In Progress until forensic report and postmortem are complete.

[Suspected phishing led to unusual service-account access; privilege scope review requested]
description:
Issue summary: On 2026-03-12 at ~09:18 UTC Security received an automated phishing report (security-phish-reporting@) referencing a credential-reset link sent to a small set of employees. Shortly after, Okta sign-in alerts flagged an atypical successful sign-in for the service account 'infra-deploy@redwood.ai' from an IP with a suspicious geolocation. This ticket captures the triage and containment steps for a suspected phishing-triggered service-account access attempt.

Detection: Automated phish mailbox + Okta adaptive auth alert + deployment pipeline audit spike.

Primary questions: Was the service account actually used to run deployments or access secrets? How did the phish lure map to a token/credential used by the service account? Is there lateral movement?

impact:
Potential privilege escalation affecting deployment pipelines and access to secret metadata. No confirmed production data exfiltration or destructive deployments found at time of last update, but elevated risk remains while the service account remained active.

timeline:
2026-03-12 09:12 UTC - Phish report received.
2026-03-12 09:18 UTC - Okta alert: successful sign-in for infra-deploy@ from anonymized IP (suspected foreign ASN).
2026-03-12 09:22 UTC - Deployment pipeline recorded an auth token refresh for infra-deploy@ (no deployment kicked).
2026-03-12 09:27 UTC - Security notified SRE and token rotation initiated.
2026-03-12 10:05 UTC - Service account disabled and active sessions revoked.
2026-03-12 11:30 UTC - Initial log sweep completed; no destructive actions observed.


logs:
Okta event IDs: evt-99827, evt-99828 indicating successful MFA bypass attempt then normal sign-in. Deployment auth logs show token refresh event id tok-20260312-44 with caller infra-deploy@. Secrets-manager access log shows a single metadata read (redacted) at 09:23 UTC from same token. No large secret bulk reads. Full raw logs stored in s3://sec-logs/2026-03-12/okta/ and s3://sec-logs/2026-03-12/deploy/ (access by Security/SRE only).

investigation_notes:
Hypotheses: (1) Targeted phishing link harvested credentials for a human admin who then triggered a flow that allowed service account token refresh; (2) Service account credentials were stored in an accessible place and were exposed via phishing link.

What we've checked: Okta session history for infra-deploy@, recent GitHub secrets changes, CI secret rotations, KMS audit logs, ECR push history, and S3 object access patterns. No code push or deployments occurred using that token. KMS logs show no CMK decrypts by the account outside a single small metadata read.

Open investigative tasks: full memory snapshot of runner that requested token (POC: infra-runner-18), forensics on host that triggered token refresh, correlate phishing recipient list with recent admin sessions.

actions_taken:
1) Disabled infra-deploy@ service account and revoked all its API tokens and active sessions (09:27 UTC).
2) Forced rotation of related CI secrets and rotated keys in secrets-manager.
3) Blocked the suspicious IP ranges at perimeter and added to blocklist (temporary).
4) Increased Okta adaptive MFA requirement for high-privilege roles and added an immediate MFA re-evaluation policy.
5) Notified Legal and CISO team; created a hold on potential affected artifacts for forensic preservation.


resolution:
Containment completed: service account disabled, tokens rotated, and immediate risk mitigations applied. No confirmed data theft or destructive action detected. Case remains 'Monitoring' pending deeper host forensics and confirmation of the phishing vector. Next steps include root-cause verification, full credential inventory, and an org-wide targeted phishing awareness email with recommended mitigations.

[Burst of OAuth token refreshes and service-account API calls after clicking external feedback link]
description:
Issue summary: Multiple Redwood employees reported suspicious account activity after interacting with a third-party 'Feedback Survey' link in an external vendor email. Detection systems flagged abnormal OAuth token refresh patterns and service-account enumeration attempts originating from IPs not previously seen in our org. This ticket is to track triage, containment, and investigation.

impact:
Potential exposure of session tokens for ~8 employees who clicked the link. No confirmed data exfiltration yet. Temporary disruption to a small number of CI jobs that rely on short-lived service tokens.

detection:
Automated anomaly alert from identity-monitoring: spike in /oauth/token POSTs from user agents matching common browsers but with atypical TLS SNI. Concurrently, audit log shows increased calls to IAM ListServiceAccounts from a subset of affected sessions.

timeline:
2026-03-12 08:21 UTC - First alert from identity-monitoring.
2026-03-12 08:30 UTC - SOC team initial review; identified 7 unique employee sessions.
2026-03-12 09:05 UTC - Support contacted affected users to revoke active sessions.
2026-03-12 10:12 UTC - Blocked outbound requests to suspected vendor domains via egress ACLs.
2026-03-12 12:40 UTC - Rotated OAuth client secrets for a small internal integration.
2026-03-13 15:00 UTC - Forensics on logs shows refresh pattern correlating with clicks on embedded marketing link.
2026-03-14 11:15 UTC - SRE and security running targeted hunts for lateral token use.

investigation_notes:
Hypothesis: The vendor email contained an embedded redirect that performed an OAuth token refresh via a hidden iframe or redirect with a CSRF-like pattern, capturing refresh tokens or prompting a silent token exchange. Evidence shows clustering around the survey domain and a small subset of IPs associated with ad/tracking networks. No clear signs of long-lived API keys being exfiltrated.
Partial findings:
- Affected sessions all used single-sign-on (IdP) and had previously active device sessions.
- Refresh bursts resumed for ~30s after initial click and then subsided for most users after session revocation.
- One CI job did attempt IAM ListServiceAccounts; the token used was short-lived and scoped to the user's session.
Open questions:
- Did the redirect chain include an authorization_code leak to a 3rd-party callback?
- Were any refresh tokens persisted server-side by the vendor?

actions_taken:
- Immediate: Support contacted impacted employees and forced web session sign-outs for 8 users.
- Containment: Blocked egress to identified tracking domains in prod us-east at 09:05 UTC.
- Credentials: Rotated two OAuth client secrets used by an internal integration that showed anomalous requests.
- Detection: Created a SIEM rule to alert on refresh bursts of >5 token refreshes/min per user and on ListServiceAccounts following a refresh within 60s.
- Notification: Security sent an org-wide advisory to avoid interacting with the vendor email until further notice.

next_steps:
- Forensics: Extract full redirect chains from web proxy logs for all affected users (owner: Marco Rivera, due 2026-03-15).
- Hunt: Expand search for similar patterns across eu-west and ap-south logs (owner: SRE team).
- Vendor outreach: Security to request details from vendor on the survey redirect implementation (owner: Priya Desai).
- Post-incident: Draft email template for future similar events and update phishing-runbook with this threat pattern.

- 2026-03-12T08:24:10Z user=a.khan ip=18.205.33.12 ua=Mozilla/5.0 refresh=true sni=survey-track.example.net
- 2026-03-12T08:24:15Z service=ci-runner action=ListServiceAccounts token_subject=a.khan ip=34.201.11.4
Link to raw slices: https://siem.internal.redwood/runs/abc123 (access restricted)

2026-03-12 09:10 - Support (Liam O'Neill): Contacted affected employees; 5 confirmed clicking the link and reported passwordless SSO prompt that looked unusual. Forced sign-outs executed.

2026-03-14 10:05 - SRE (Nina Patel): Found one CI runner IP making runtime calls right after a refresh; token was short-lived and appears scoped. Still investigating whether lateral use occurred.

resolution:
Mitigated — containment actions completed. Forensics in progress; no evidence of privileged key exfiltration as of last update. Recommend closing as 'Mitigated' once vendor confirms redirect behavior and forensics completes.

[Partial tenant diversion to legacy variant during staged prefetch causes tokenization divergence and elevated error rate]
description:
Issue summary:
During a staged canary prefetch for redwood-chat-7b-v1 we observed a subset of Cartwheel tenant traffic being silently routed to the legacy tokenization variant (redwood-chat-7b-v1-legacy-tokenizer). The divergence was not visible at routing policy configuration (no explicit pin change) and manifested as mixed-quality outputs, higher 5xx spike rate, and user-reported hallucination/formatting regressions.

Impact:
- ~6% of requests for Cartwheel (enterprise dedicated account) returned responses produced by the legacy-tokenizer variant over a 42 minute window.
- Customer reported elevated error rate (5xx) and malformed structured outputs in checkout assistant flows.
- Business impact: intermittent customer confusion and increased chatbot failures during a peak campaign window.

Environment:
- Prod - us-east-1, dedicated capacity pool dc-prod-7b-01 assigned to Cartwheel.
- Canary rollout for redwood-chat-7b-v1 (weight ramping 5% -> 25%) using prefetch/batched mirror strategy.

Important notes: routing rules in Console show model pin intact; no manual pin change recorded in audit log during the window. Edge proxies show a subset of sessions with legacy tokenizer header present (x-rt-tokenizer: legacy), but the header was not present on the original client request.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Create a staged prefetch canary for redwood-chat-7b-v1 with prewarm mirror enabled.
2) Target a dedicated tenant (Cartwheel) with session affinity enabled and model pin to redwood-chat-7b-v1.
3) Trigger bulk prefetch traffic via load test or real traffic ramp.
4) Observe edge logs for x-rt-tokenizer header and compare model hash returned from orchestrator.
5) Correlate timestamps with serving runtime traces and KV-cache keys for the tenant session.

observed_behavior:
Intermittent routing of some requests to redwood-chat-7b-v1-legacy-tokenizer leading to tokenization mismatch, malformed JSON outputs, and a 5xx spike (~4.8% baseline -> 12.6% during window).

expected_behavior:
All pinned sessions for Cartwheel should route exclusively to redwood-chat-7b-v1 during the promotion window; prefetch should mirror traffic without altering tokenizer headers or shifting live requests to legacy variants.

impact:
Customer-facing regressions in checkout assistant; elevated error rate and several enterprise escalation messages to CS. Estimated affected sessions: ~9k during 42-minute window. Billing not impacted but service quality degraded.

logs_and_traces:
edge-proxy logs: edge-prod-us-east-1-2026-03-13-18:12:xx - tenant=cartwheel - request_id=R-9a7c - x-rt-tokenizer: legacy
orchestrator trace: trace-id=orch-5581 - route-resolve: resolved_variant=redwood-chat-7b-v1-legacy-tokenizer - decision_path=mirror-prefetch-fanout
serving-runtime error: srv-7b-01 - 2026-03-13T18:18:05Z - KV cache miss -> fallback to local-legacy-instantiation - stacktrace: OOM-guard triggered during prewarm

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: prefetch path mutated request headers during mirror fanout causing edge to consider requests for legacy tokenizer variant.
Edge logs show x-rt-tokenizer header injected between mirror proxy and orchestrator for ~6% of mirrored requests. Header not present from client side.
Checked audit logs: no pin change; routing policy unchanged. Canary weight events: 5%->10% transition occurred at 18:05 UTC followed by prewarm burst at 18:06-18:20.
Replayed mirrored payloads against both tokenizer variants: legacy-tokenizer produced different token boundaries and occasional unclosed JSON blocks triggering downstream parser 5xx.
Orchestrator PR #2213 added a prefetch optimization that merges header contexts from mirror source; suspected to accidentally include upstream edge header set — flagged as potential root cause.

comments:
Aisha Patel (Support): Escalating to SRE and Orchestrator team. Customer impacted during promotional window — they requested immediate mitigation.
Lucas Chen (SRE): Reproduced header injection in staging with canary mirror enabled. Creating hotpatch to strip tokenizer headers on mirror path. See slack #support-cartwheel thread.
Maya Ruiz (Platform Eng): Noted PR 2213 comment about copying context for prewarm - will audit header copying logic. Assigning review to Orchestrator team.
Cartwheel CS rep (Kevin Hsu): Customer confirms mixed outputs and provided two request IDs where checkout assistant returned invalid JSON.
Lucas Chen: Temporarily paused prefetch mirror for Cartwheel tenant at 2026-03-13T19:02Z UTC — error rate reverted towards baseline within 3 minutes.
Maya Ruiz: Opened github PR to strip x-rt-tokenizer and other runtime-only headers from mirror payloads: https://github.com/redwood-inference/orchestrator/pull/2220

workaround:
Paused prefetch/mirror for Cartwheel (applied at 2026-03-13T19:02Z). Manually enforced header sanitize rule on edge for tenant Cartwheel to drop x-rt-tokenizer header for server-to-server mirror traffic. Customer routed to full-weight pinned variant until fix is deployed.

resolution:
Hotpatch applied: edge header sanitizer rule implemented (edge-proxy hotpatch 2026-03-13T19:05Z) and prefetch mirror header-copy behavior reverted. Orchestrator PR #2220 merged to ensure mirror payloads do not carry runtime-only tokenizer headers. Post-deploy monitoring shows 5xx rate returned to baseline and no further legacy-tokenizer responses observed for Cartwheel. Follow-up: permanent test added to prewarm e2e suite to validate header isolation; postmortem scheduled.

follow_up_actions:
Postmortem scheduled in Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/OPS/2026-03-13+Cartwheel+Prefetch+Partial-Divergence
Add unit/integration tests to prewarm mirror path to assert header whitelisting
Audit other tenants with prefetch enabled for similar header leakage over last 7 days

[tokenizer-rollout-mismatch-causes-silent-fallback-and-pinned-version-divergence]
description:
Issue summary: After a canary rollout that introduced a tokenizer change (progressive subword merges) for redwood-small-v2-tokenizer-v1, several FinSight requests previously pinned to the customer's explicit model version were routed silently to the legacy model variant. Impact: customer observed subtle response inconsistencies and a billing spike due to reprocessing; no explicit error returned to client, requests succeeded but used fallback model. Environment: production us-east-1; Dedicated/Enterprise tenant for FinSight. Steps to reproduce: 1) Use FinSight tenant token bound to a pinned model version for redwood-small-v2. 2) Issue identical prompt batches through the SDK client while shifting canary weight from 5% to 25% for the tokenizer-enabled variant. 3) Observe per-request token counts and routing decisions in the request traces. Observed behavior: When the tokenizer change produced different tokenization for identical prompts (differences in prefix token count and EOS placement), the runtime’s pinned-version matching (which relies on a request signature computed from canonicalized token stream) failed to find a matching affinity entry and quietly fell back to a compatible variant. Because the fallback path had trace-level backpressure suppression, no 5xx or 429 surfaced; response latency increased ~60ms on average and some outputs changed subtly (e.g., newline tokenization differences). Expected behavior: Pinned sessions should honor explicit model pins regardless of tokenizer divergence; if pin cannot be honored, system should surface an explicit warning/error to tenant and not silently route without audit. Logs/traces: see trace IDs in investigation_notes below. Postmortem risk: silent fallbacks can bypass audit trail and misattribute billing and quality regressions to pinned version.

investigation_notes:
trace: us-east-1:trace-20260310-55a1c3 - request_id=ff12ab34 sample prompt 'Analyze quarterly revenue' - tokens: variant-A=28, variant-B=31 - affinity lookup failed (no pinned entry) - routed to fallback variant
Hypothesis 1: Tokenizer microservice returns non-deterministic canonicalization across variants; affinity key generation depends on exact token stream -> small changes break pin lookup.
Hypothesis 2: Orchestrator cache contains epochal entries keyed by tokenizer version; cache invalidation race during canary weight increase caused shard to present older tokenizer version metadata.
Reproducer: Deployed two tokenizer binary builds (stable and canary) to staging and ran 10k identical prompts through pinned session harness; observed 0.7% of requests dropped pin affinity when tokenizer mismatch present.
Related config: affinity-key = sha256(<tenant_id> + <model_version> + <tokenizer_version> + <first_16_tokens>) - tokenizer_version was not included in previous pin schema; changed behavior surfaced when tokenizer changed token counts across variants.
Temporary mitigation: patched proxy to include 'x-tokenizer-version' header from tokenizer-service in routing key to make affinity lookup tolerant (shim) and surfaced audit event when mismatch occurs.
Next steps: 1) Add tokenizer_version as required field in pin-generation schema and migrate active affinities (coord with orchestrator). 2) Build rollout presubmit test to detect tokenization deltas for pinned tenants. 3) Consider fallback policy: explicit error or enroll tenant into grace-mode when pin cannot be honored.

comments:

2026-03-11 02:30 - Elena Zou (Infra Eng): Found that affinity lookup uses a hashed canonical token stream produced by the tokenizer microservice. Canary variant altered the tokenizer merges which changed canonicalization; affinity lookup missed and fallback executed. Adding reproducer and traces to ticket.

resolution:
Workaround applied: shim to include tokenizer-version in routing metadata and audit mismatches (rolled 2026-03-12). Permanent fix in progress: update affinity schema to include tokenizer_version and run migration job to recompute pinned entries for active sessions; rollout plan pending CR approval. Customer asked for final ETA; target complete by 2026-03-19. Follow-up task INT-4412 created for migration orchestration.

[Retention Settings in Console — IA, warnings, and permissions model]
description:
Goal
Design the Redwood Console “Retention Settings” experience for admins across Hosted/Dedicated/Private tenants, with clear information architecture, warning states, and a permissions model that matches security/compliance expectations.

Context / Why
Retention controls are a procurement blocker for regulated customers (Dedicated/Private). The console needs to make retention policy behavior explicit (TTL + purge semantics + exceptions like legal hold), reduce misconfiguration, and support evidence generation (downloadable exports) without turning this into a full GRC tool.

Primary personas
- Security Admin: configures retention to match policy; needs auditability and exports.
- SRE/Platform Admin: cares about operational debugging needs; wants safe defaults and guardrails.
- Auditor (read-only): views policy + change history; downloads export for evidence packet.

Scope for this ticket (Design)
1) Information architecture
- Location: Console → Settings → Security & Compliance → Retention
- Page sections (top to bottom):
  A. Summary banner (current effective policy, tier defaults, last updated, legal hold status)
  B. Data classes table (editable where supported)
  C. Advanced settings (region scope + overrides if enabled, export/download, change history)
  D. Help + docs links + “Request Compliance Report Pack” CTA (gated by role)

2) Data classes UI model
Each row represents a data class with consistent controls:
- Data class name + short description
- Storage scope indicator: Control plane / Data plane / Third-party (where relevant)
- Retention control: TTL selector (days) with min/max constraints by tier
- Status pill: “Default”, “Customized”, “Not collected”, “Locked (Legal hold)”, “Not supported in this deployment”
- “Details” drawer: purge semantics, what gets deleted, timing expectations, and known exceptions

In-scope data classes for v1 UI
- Request/response logs (where enabled)
- Prompts/completions (only if stored; reflect logging mode)
- Audit logs
- Traces
- Metrics
- Artifacts (eval datasets / uploaded artifacts) — display-only if not yet enforceable

3) Warning states + guardrails
Global warnings (top banner)
- Legal hold active: “Retention is currently overridden by an active hold. Editing is disabled for affected data classes.” Includes link to view hold details and the approval workflow note.
- Policy drift / enforcement lag: if verification signals show high TTL lag or purge failures (read-only indicator; links to dashboards).
- Deployment limitations: show when certain classes are not enforceable in a given deployment mode.

Inline warnings (per row / per field)
- Below default retention: warning copy that shortened retention may impact debugging/incident response; require confirmation.
- Below minimum TTL: hard validation error (cannot save).
- Disabled logging mode: if request logs are disabled, show “Not collected” and hide TTL control; show link to logging settings.
- Changing audit log retention: extra warning + “Recommended minimum” copy; require second confirmation.

Save flow / confirmations
- Draft changes tracked on page; “Review changes” modal lists diffs by data class.
- Confirmations:
  - Any decrease in retention requires typed confirmation (string: DELETE) for users without “Break-glass” role.
  - For “Security Admin” role: regular confirmation.
  - For “SRE Break-glass” role: additional note that change is logged and time-bounded access is required.

4) Permissions model (RBAC)
Read-only roles
- Auditor: view effective policy + change history + export current configuration.
- Support/Read-only: view only (no export if customer chooses to restrict).

Write roles
- Security Admin: edit TTL values within allowed bounds; cannot override legal hold; can download exports.
- Org Owner: same as Security Admin + can delegate permissions.

Break-glass / exception capability (separate permission)
- “Retention.Override” capability: allowed to temporarily increase retention during incident response (if configured), but cannot reduce below minimums.
- UI requirement: show “Break-glass required” chip and route to existing access request flow; all actions must generate an audit log event.

Export/report permissions
- “Retention.Export” capability: can download retention configuration export.
- “CompliancePack.Request” capability: can trigger compliance report pack generation/request flow (MVP is request ticket creation / async job; see ENG follow-up).

5) Change history + auditability (UI expectations)
- Read-only “Change history” table on the page:
  - Timestamp, actor, data classes affected, old TTL → new TTL, reason (optional field), source (Console/API/Terraform)
- Provide “Copy JSON” action for the effective policy (for security questionnaire responses).

Design deliverables
- Figma: page layout + empty/loaded/error states
- Component specs for: data class table rows, diff modal, legal hold lock state, permission-gated actions
- Copy deck: warning copy + helper text + tooltips reviewed by Security/GRC

Acceptance criteria
- IA aligns with Console nav conventions and doesn’t add new top-level sections.
- Clear, non-ambiguous labels differentiating “Not collected” vs “Retained for X days”.
- Warning states cover: disabled logging, min/max TTL validation, legal hold lock, enforcement lag indicator.
- Permissions map to capabilities; no “silent” hidden failures (users see why actions are disabled).
- Export actions are discoverable but not noisy; can be performed by Auditor/Security Admin.

Open questions (captured for Eng/PM)
- Per-region overrides: do we expose in v1 or keep as read-only indicator (ADR suggests evaluation in control plane; UI can support later)?
- Enforcement timing language: how specific can we be (“within 24h” vs “best effort”) without creating an SLA?
- Artifacts retention: do we ship as display-only row with “Coming soon” or omit entirely from v1?

Links / references
- Confluence (UX spec target): sources/confluence/product-docs/design-specs/console-retention-settings-page-spec.json
- PRD: sources/confluence/product-docs/requirements/retention-controls-prd.json
- Legal hold policy: sources/confluence/security-and-compliance/data-residency-and-retention/legal-hold-and-retention-exceptions.json
- FAQ inputs (copy alignment): sources/confluence/sales-enablement/security-faq/retention-controls-and-compliance-reporting-faq.json

Handoff notes
- Please ensure backend exposes enough metadata for the UI pills: “not collected”, “not supported”, “locked by hold”, and min/max TTL bounds.
- Console should request “effective policy” (post-evaluation) plus “configured policy” (what the admin set) to avoid confusion when defaults/overrides apply.

Follow-ups (new tickets suggested)
- Console: enforcement verification indicator wiring + dashboard deep links (ENG + SRE)
- Console: request compliance pack CTA flow (async job/request + status)
- Console: per-region override editor (Phase 2+) if product confirms requirement

2025-01-27 (Marcus Lin): +1 on conservative defaults. Also, legal hold state must fully lock editing for affected stores. We need explicit UI that the hold overrides customer TTL and is audited.

[Residency & Retention Policy Assertor with Automated Drift Resolver]
description:
Problem: We currently lack a single enforcement and remediation layer that ensures data residency and retention configurations across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments remain compliant with customer region and retention SLAs. Drift shows up as misconfigured S3/R2 bucket region tags, expired retention TTLs, or runtime overrides in Dedicated pools. Manual detection is slow and evidence collection for audits is error-prone.

Goal: Implement a Policy Assertor service (policy-as-code) that continuously validates residency and retention settings, automatically generates signed audit evidence, and triggers a Drift Resolver that can either remediate (when safe) or open a proposed change with a rollback-safe playbook. The feature must work across hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private (VPC) deployments and integrate with the Console for visibility and with the audit-log pipeline for evidence storage.

Scope:
- A policy language subset (YAML) for residency/retention rules and severity mapping.
- Continuous scanner that computes authoritative state from config stores (Terraform state, config DB), runtime metadata (instance labels, GPU pool region), and cloud resource tags.
- Deterministic drift detector with time-windowed scoring and root-cause hints.
- Automated remediation actions: 1) safe auto-fix (e.g., apply TTL migration for non-customer-facing caches), 2) patch proposal for operator approval, 3) escalation to SRE for high-risk changes.
- Evidence generator that produces signed artifacts (JSON + SHA256) containing pre/post state, remediation actions, and linked PR/Runbook IDs.
- Console UI hooks for per-customer drift timeline, and alerts integration (PagerDuty, Slack).

Non-goals: Full policy DSL or arbitrary rule eval for non-compliance domains (that is future work). This ticket focuses on residency and retention controls only.

acceptance_criteria:
CLR-1: Policy Assertor evaluates all active residency/retention rules against authoritative config weekly and flags drift with severity levels.
CLR-2: Drift Resolver can automatically remediate low-risk drifts in hosted API without human intervention; remediation must be reversible and logged.
CLR-3: Evidence generator emits signed artifacts and pushes them to the audit S3 bucket; artifacts are queryable by Console and retained per customer retention policy.
CLR-4: Console displays drift timeline and current policy compliance status per customer and per-model route.
CLR-5: PagerDuty alert is created for high-severity drifts and includes links to evidence and rollback runbook.

success_metrics:
Reduce time-to-detect residency/retention misconfigurations from ~48h to <2h for hosted customers.
Auto-remediation rate >= 70% for low-severity drifts without false positives over a 30-day window.
Audit evidence generation coverage 100% for remediated drifts and 95% for detected but not remediated drifts.
Decrease manual remediation work for SRE by 60% for residency/retention incidents in first quarter after launch.

risks_and_mitigation:
Risk: Unsafe auto-remediation could change runtime behavior for live customers. Mitigation: restrict auto-fix to explicit low-risk classes and require canary rollback tests in Dedicated pools.
Risk: Incomplete authoritative sources may yield false positives. Mitigation: implement confidence scoring combining config store, runtime tags, and customer-provided overrides; show confidence in Console.
Risk: Evidence artifacts leak PII if not sanitized. Mitigation: evidence generator must scrub payloads and only include config metadata and cryptographic hashes of any customer data references.

design_decisions:
Use a small, opinionated YAML policy subset (residency.region, retention.ttl_days, severity) rather than a full policy DSL to speed delivery.
Store canonical policies in the config DB and as a Git-backed repo for change history and code review (GitHub).
Evidence artifacts will be signed with a per-tenant key and stored in immutable S3 paths; signing service reuses existing KMS integration.

implementation_plan:
Phase 1 (2 weeks): Policy schema + Git-backed repo; scanner prototype reading config DB and tagging resources.
Phase 2 (3 weeks): Deterministic drift detector with scoring, Console flagging, and notification wiring.
Phase 3 (3 weeks): Build Drift Resolver with auto-fix handlers for low-risk classes and operator proposal flow for others.
Phase 4 (2 weeks): Evidence generator (signed artifacts), integration with audit S3, and end-to-end tests.
Phase 5 (1 week): Gradual rollout to hosted customers, monitoring, and tune thresholds; Dedicated & Private rollout afterwards.

transcript:
Meeting: Northbridge Bank - Security review: retention controls + audit logs (Dedicated/Private)
Recorded: 2025-02-06 14:03 ET
Duration: 53 min

Attendees
- Redwood Inference: Markus Klein (Solutions Engineering, host), Marcus Lin (Security Engineering), Olga Petrov (GRC), Kevin Osei (Engineering - audit exports/retention)
- Northbridge Bank: Erin Caldwell (Vendor Risk), Priyanka Shah (InfoSec/GRC), Miguel Alvarez (Cloud Platform), Hannah Wu (Security Architect), Tom Becker (Procurement)

Auto Summary (Fireflies)

Transcript
[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, cool. Thanks everyone for making time. This is Markus from Redwood. This call is focused on retention controls and audit logging, and what evidence you all need for the vendor risk package. We’ve got Marcus from Security, Olga from GRC, and Kevin who’s been working on the audit export bits.

[00:19] Erin Caldwell: Great. Thanks Markus. Just to level set, we’re early-ish but this is a blocker. We need to understand retention by data type, whether you can do shorter TTLs, and what the audit logs look like. Also we’ll need something we can attach to our SOC 2 aligned questionnaire.

[00:36] Priyanka Shah: Yeah, and we’re looking at Dedicated or Private, not the public shared thing. We have some residency requirements too.

[00:46] Markus Klein: Makes sense. We’ll cover Dedicated and Private. Quick intros? Erin you already did. Miguel, Hannah, Tom?

[00:54] Miguel Alvarez: Miguel, platform engineering. I’ll ask the “where does it run and where do logs go” questions.

[01:01] Hannah Wu: Hannah, security architect. I’m focused on audit coverage, admin actions, RBAC, SSO, that stuff.

[01:08] Tom Becker: Tom, procurement. I’ll mostly listen and then ask about deliverables and timelines.

[01:14] Markus Klein: Great. I’ll start with a quick framing then we’ll go Q&A. So, retention controls: the product direction is customer-configurable retention across key data classes: request/response logs (if enabled), audit logs, traces/metrics, and artifacts like evaluation datasets if you’re using them in the console. For Private, depending on architecture, some of that is in your VPC or on-prem, and you control storage. For Dedicated, it’s Redwood-managed infra but isolated.

[01:43] Erin Caldwell: When you say request/response logs, do you mean you store the prompt and completion?

[01:49] Marcus Lin: It depends on configuration. By default, we do not persist full prompt/completion content for Hosted API except in limited debugging modes, and those are time-bound. For Dedicated and Private, we can configure request logging levels. You can disable request/response logging entirely, or store metadata only, like route, model, latency, tokens, and error codes. If content logging is enabled, it’s treated as a separate data class with strict TTL.

[02:17] Priyanka Shah: Okay. We need an explicit answer we can paste: “can be disabled,” “metadata only,” and “retention is X.”

[02:26] Olga Petrov: We can provide that in writing. We’ve been standardizing the language for questionnaire responses so it’s consistent: what’s stored by default, what’s optional, and what controls exist.

[02:39] Hannah Wu: For audit logs, what’s the retention default? Our internal standard for some systems is 365 days for audit trails, but for app logs we often want 30 or 90.

[02:50] Kevin Osei: Audit logs have a different default than request logs. Typically we keep audit longer, and we set min/max bounds by tier. I don’t want to quote exact numbers offhand because it depends on Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private, but the pattern is: audit logs longer, request logs shorter, traces/metrics somewhere in between.

[03:11] Miguel Alvarez: That’s fine. Mechanically, how does TTL enforcement happen? Is it a database TTL, or a job, or…?

[03:18] Kevin Osei: It’s enforced with scheduled purge jobs per data store. Some stores support native TTL indexes, some are job-based deletes. The important parts: deletions are idempotent, batched to avoid DB pressure, and we emit verification metrics like “ttl lag seconds” and “rows deleted” and failures.

[03:39] Hannah Wu: I want to dig into “prove deletion.” We get asked by audit, “how do you validate records are actually removed at end of retention?”

[03:47] Marcus Lin: Great question. We do a couple things: we log the purge job execution and we track lag between record age and deletion time. Additionally, we can do periodic sampling checks, like querying for records older than retention and ensuring the count is zero or within a small tolerated window while jobs catch up. For Private deployments, you can also validate in your own logging backend since it’s your storage.

[04:15] Erin Caldwell: You said “tolerated window.” That’s a phrase that sometimes causes problems. What’s the SLA there?

[04:21] Markus Klein: Yeah, fair. The deletion is best-effort within the enforcement interval. We typically express it as “purge runs at least daily” and “maximum lag” with alerting. For regulated customers we can commit to tighter operational targets in Dedicated/Private. We should give you the exact language we use.

[04:42] Tom Becker: And will that language be in the compliance pack you’re building? Or is that separate?

[04:47] Olga Petrov: The baseline compliance reporting pack includes: retention configuration export (what TTL is set per data class), audit log coverage summary, data residency summary, RBAC/access controls report, and an evidence checklist. It won’t be a custom SLA doc by itself, but it will include the evidence that controls exist and are configured as agreed.

[05:12] Priyanka Shah: Can you show us an example of the “retention configuration export”? Like what fields are in it.

[05:18] Kevin Osei: We can send an example JSON export. It includes policy version, effective date, who changed it, and TTL per data class. It also includes exceptions like “legal hold enabled” or “logging disabled,” and it references the scope—tenant, environment, and region if applicable.

[05:41] Miguel Alvarez: Region-specific retention matters for us because we might run us-east and eu-west. Is that supported?

[05:48] Kevin Osei: The schema supports per-region overrides, yes, with guardrails so you don’t accidentally set conflicting policies. There’s a precedence model: tenant default, then environment, then region overrides. Policy changes are audited.

[06:06] Hannah Wu: Can you define the data classes? Because sometimes vendors call everything “audit log.” We separate “security audit logs” from “application request logs.”

[06:16] Marcus Lin: Same. We define “audit logs” as security/admin events: authentication events, console access, API key creation/rotation, role changes, retention policy changes, export actions, and similar. “Request logs” are request/response metadata and optionally content if enabled. “Telemetry” is traces/metrics used for performance monitoring. Artifacts are things like evaluation datasets, if you upload them.

[06:45] Erin Caldwell: Do you store customer payloads in traces?

[06:48] Markus Klein: Generally no. Traces are metadata—timings, route names, status, and request IDs. We avoid putting prompt content into trace spans. If there’s an exception, it’s documented and would be under the same logging controls.

[07:06] Priyanka Shah: We also need legal hold. If there is an investigation, can you stop deletion?

[07:12] Marcus Lin: Yes. There are two concepts: legal hold and incident hold. Legal hold is a formal process—requires approval from Security and Legal, and it’s auditable. Incident hold is short-term for production incidents, also auditable, and time-bounded. Both prevent purge for the scoped data classes and time ranges.

[07:36] Hannah Wu: Who can activate it? That’s usually the crux.

[07:40] Marcus Lin: Not an individual engineer. It’s restricted. For legal hold, it’s CISO delegate plus Legal approval, and it creates an audit event. For incident hold, it’s on-call lead plus Security approval, and it also creates an audit event and an expiration time.

[08:01] Erin Caldwell: We’ll need that in writing too.

[08:04] Olga Petrov: Understood.

[08:07] Miguel Alvarez: On Private deployment, are those purge jobs running in our environment?

[08:13] Markus Klein: For Private, yes—generally the data plane is in your network boundary. The control plane can be private as well. The purge framework runs as part of the deployment; you can monitor it and integrate with your observability. Redwood provides the job definitions, dashboards, and runbooks.

[08:32] Miguel Alvarez: Does it require specific backing services? Like Postgres vs ClickHouse.

[08:36] Kevin Osei: It depends on which stores you deploy. For audit logs and request logs, there’s a supported set. We’ll outline the prerequisites in the Private installer docs. The key is: whatever store is used must support TTL enforcement via native TTL or scheduled deletions.

[08:55] Hannah Wu: Audit event types. Can you list them? We need to know whether “role change,” “SSO config change,” “token creation,” “export performed,” are captured.

[09:05] Kevin Osei: High-level yes to those. We have a catalog of event types. Off the top: user login/logout, SSO/SAML config changes, API key create/rotate/revoke, RBAC role create/update/delete, policy changes (including retention policy), admin actions in the console, and audit export generation/download.

[09:28] Priyanka Shah: What about data plane access? Like if a Redwood SRE accesses a host.

[09:34] Marcus Lin: For Dedicated, privileged access is tightly controlled, logged, and requires ticketed approval. Some of that is captured as operational audit events. For Private, your team controls the infrastructure access, so those events are in your own IAM and host logging.

[09:55] Erin Caldwell: I’m going to be blunt: we get dinged when audit logs are “partial.” Are there known gaps?

[10:02] Kevin Osei: There are always edge cases. For example, some older admin actions weren’t emitting events historically; we’ve been closing those. Also, exporter filters sometimes omitted certain event types—there was a known issue we fixed recently. I’ll provide the current coverage list and note anything “planned” vs “GA.”

[10:27] Markus Klein: And to be clear, we’ll include that in the audit-log coverage summary in the compliance pack, so it’s explicit.

[10:35] Tom Becker: On exports: our audit team wants a time window export, like “Jan 1 to Jan 31,” and also filters by actor sometimes.

[10:43] Kevin Osei: That’s supported. The exporter can do time-windowed exports, filters by actor, event type, and tenant/environment. Output is CSV and JSON today, and we can bundle it into an evidence package.

[11:02] Hannah Wu: Evidence package: what does “bundle” mean? Like a zip file?

[11:07] Olga Petrov: Exactly. A customer-ready package that includes: retention config export, audit log export for a time window, and a README describing how it was generated, plus an evidence checklist. For some customers we also include screenshots from the console showing the retention settings page and RBAC.

[11:29] Erin Caldwell: That would help. We’re trying to avoid five different PDFs.

[11:33] Markus Klein: Yup, that’s the goal.

[11:37] Miguel Alvarez: One more: Do you have data residency reporting? We need to show “data stored in US only” for some environments.

[11:44] Markus Klein: For Dedicated, we can pin region and provide a region summary. For Private, it’s your environment, so residency is determined by where you deploy. The compliance pack includes a data residency summary section—regions configured, and which services are region-scoped.

[12:05] Priyanka Shah: Our questionnaire also asks about retention of metrics and traces, and whether logs go to third parties.

[12:12] Marcus Lin: In Hosted/Dedicated, there are sub-processors for telemetry depending on configuration, but we can provide the list and whether the data includes customer content. For regulated customers, we can route telemetry to a customer-managed sink or restrict it. For Private, again, it’s typically in your own observability stack.

[12:34] Hannah Wu: Okay. Let’s talk about defaults and guardrails. Can customers set retention to “0”?

[12:40] Kevin Osei: For some classes, yes—meaning disabled storage. For audit logs, typically we don’t allow “zero,” because you need auditability. But we can set a minimum, like 30 days or 90 days, depending on tier and requirements. For request logs, you can disable content and keep metadata only.

[13:02] Erin Caldwell: That’s acceptable. But we need it clearly stated. We’ve had vendors say “configurable” and then it’s not.

[13:10] Markus Klein: Understood. We’ll send the concrete min/max ranges we support for Dedicated and Private.

[13:17] Miguel Alvarez: Another technical: purge semantics. If I reduce retention from 365 to 30, does it back-delete older data?

[13:25] Kevin Osei: Yes, there’s a backfill behavior. When a policy becomes stricter, purge jobs will delete records older than the new threshold. It’s still batched, and we watch for backlog. When a policy becomes less strict, we obviously can’t resurrect data, but we will keep future data longer.

[13:50] Hannah Wu: And that policy change is audited?

[13:52] Kevin Osei: Yes, policy changes generate audit events and we keep a change history: who, when, what changed.

[14:03] Priyanka Shah: If an admin changes retention in the console, is that logged too? Not just via API.

[14:08] Kevin Osei: Yes. Console actions go through the same control plane and create audit events.

[14:17] Erin Caldwell: How many admins at Redwood can change retention on our behalf?

[14:22] Marcus Lin: In Dedicated, we aim for customer-managed configuration. Redwood can assist under a support workflow, but it’s controlled and auditable, and we can restrict it further contractually. In Private, Redwood doesn’t have access unless you explicitly grant it.

[14:43] Tom Becker: That’s going to come up in contracting. We’ll handle later.

[14:46] Markus Klein: Cool. I want to make sure we answer evidence expectations. Erin, what do you need as outputs for the review?

[14:53] Erin Caldwell: Three things: 1) written retention policy capability statement, 2) sample audit logs with event types, and 3) a checklist / mapping for SOC 2 style controls. Also, if you have SOC 2 report, we’ll request under NDA.

[15:10] Olga Petrov: We can do that. The baseline pack is meant to cover (1) and (3). For (2) Kevin can provide a sanitized export.

[15:20] Hannah Wu: For the audit export: do you include the actor identity? Like email or ID.

[15:26] Kevin Osei: Yes—actor ID, actor type (user/service), source IP when available, user agent, action, target resource, timestamp, and outcome. If SSO is configured, it maps to the SSO subject.

[15:46] Miguel Alvarez: Does it include request IDs to tie to app logs?

[15:49] Kevin Osei: Some events include correlation IDs. Request logs have request IDs; audit logs have event IDs; there’s a relationship when the action triggers a data plane request (e.g., export generation). We can walk through it.

[16:10] Priyanka Shah: What about key management, KMS? If we use customer-managed keys, does key rotation show up in audit logs?

[16:18] Marcus Lin: Key configuration changes and rotations in our system are audited. For Private, your KMS logs are in your cloud provider and you can merge them into your SIEM.

[16:34] Hannah Wu: Okay. Switching gears: what about the actual content in the compliance pack. Is it “on-demand”? Like we click a button.

[16:42] Markus Klein: The goal is on-demand generation in the console. In the short term, for early customers, we can generate it via internal tooling and deliver it securely. For GA it’ll be self-serve or support-assisted depending on tier.

[17:00] Erin Caldwell: We’re okay with support-assisted as long as it’s timely. What is “timely”? We have procurement timelines.

[17:07] Olga Petrov: For early stage, we’ve been targeting 3-5 business days for a full package including evidence attachments. Once the generator is fully productized, it should be same-day.

[17:21] Tom Becker: Please send that as a commitment you can stand behind. Otherwise we can’t plan.

[17:25] Markus Klein: We’ll send a “current process” timeline and what will be available by the time you’re in contracting.

[17:33] Miguel Alvarez: I want to understand: for Dedicated, are logs stored in your systems or can they be shipped to ours?

[17:39] Markus Klein: Both. There’s default storage in Redwood-managed systems with retention controls, and we can also support forwarding/export to customer-managed SIEM/log bucket depending on integration.

[17:55] Hannah Wu: Do you support “write once read many” style storage?

[17:59] Marcus Lin: For Private, you can implement WORM in your storage layer. For Dedicated, we don’t claim WORM by default, but we can provide integrity controls, access logs, and export. If WORM is required, we’d likely recommend Private with customer-managed storage.

[18:22] Priyanka Shah: That’s helpful; we can route that accordingly.

[18:26] Erin Caldwell: What about deletion exceptions? For example, if there is a billing dispute or operational incident, do you keep logs beyond retention?

[18:34] Marcus Lin: Not by default. The only reasons to extend beyond configured retention would be a documented hold: legal hold or incident hold, both auditable, scoped, and time-bound. Otherwise purge continues.

[18:53] Hannah Wu: And is the hold scoped per data class? Like hold audit logs but not request logs.

[18:58] Marcus Lin: Yes, it can be scoped.

[19:02] Miguel Alvarez: Good.

[19:04] Markus Klein: Let’s talk about your target retention periods. You said 365 for audit. Any specific requirements for request logs or traces?

[19:12] Erin Caldwell: For request logs, we prefer minimal. Ideally metadata only, 30 days. For anything with customer content, we want it off, or at most 7 days for break/fix.

[19:26] Hannah Wu: Traces/metrics can be 30-90 days, but we need to know if they can leak content.

[19:32] Marcus Lin: Our standard posture is no content in traces. Request content logging can be turned off. We can document how we prevent that and where exceptions might exist.

[19:46] Priyanka Shah: For audit, we’ll likely ask 365. If your max is less, that’s a problem.

[19:52] Kevin Osei: For Dedicated/Private, longer audit retention is generally supported. The limit is usually storage sizing and performance; we can set guardrails but 365 is a common ask.

[20:05] Miguel Alvarez: If you’re doing continuous batching or KV cache, does that impact what’s logged? Sorry, I’m mixing performance and logging.

[20:12] Markus Klein: No worries. KV cache is in-memory; it’s not something we persist to logs. Performance optimizations don’t change retention. The logging pipeline is separate.

[20:26] Hannah Wu: Another audit question: do you log failed login attempts and lockouts?

[20:31] Kevin Osei: Yes, authentication events include failures. If you’re using SSO, some of that is in your IdP logs as well.

[20:42] Priyanka Shah: Do you support SCIM provisioning? And does that show up in audit logs?

[20:47] Markus Klein: SCIM is supported for enterprise tiers. Provisioning events are audited.

[20:55] Erin Caldwell: Great.

[20:57] Markus Klein: Any other big gaps we should address?

[21:01] Tom Becker: I’d like clarity on what you can deliver now vs roadmap. If you say “on-demand report pack,” but it’s not ready, we need a plan.

[21:11] Olga Petrov: Totally. For February, we can deliver: retention configuration export, audit log export (time-windowed), and an evidence checklist + narrative. The fully productized “click to generate” pack is in progress; we’ll share expected dates separately.

[21:33] Erin Caldwell: Okay. That might be enough for this cycle.

[21:37] Miguel Alvarez: If you’re Private, can we integrate the purge verification metrics into Prometheus?

[21:43] Kevin Osei: Yes, we emit metrics that can be scraped. We have dashboards for “ttl lag” and “purge errors” and backlog size.

[21:55] Hannah Wu: And alerts? Like if purge fails.

[21:58] Kevin Osei: Yes—alerts for sustained failures and lag above threshold.

[22:06] Marcus Lin: And from a control perspective, those alerts and runbooks are part of “monitoring” evidence.

[22:13] Priyanka Shah: That’s good.

[22:16] Erin Caldwell: I want to go back to “disable logging.” If we disable request/response logging, can your support still troubleshoot?

[22:23] Markus Klein: Good point. We can troubleshoot with metrics and traces that don’t include content. If deeper debugging is needed, we can do a time-bounded “debug mode” with explicit approval, and it’s auditable. But default is minimal.

[22:40] Hannah Wu: And that debug mode is a type of exception/hold?

[22:44] Marcus Lin: It’s an exception workflow, yes. It’s logged and time-bounded. It’s not a “hold,” it’s more like “temporarily increase logging.”

[22:55] Erin Caldwell: That’s acceptable if controlled.

[22:58] Miguel Alvarez: For Dedicated, do you have separate retention by environment? Like prod vs staging.

[23:03] Kevin Osei: Yes, policy can be scoped per environment, and you can set different TTLs.

[23:10] Priyanka Shah: Okay.

[23:12] Markus Klein: Let’s do a quick run through the evidence artifacts we will send.

[23:17] Markus Klein: 1) Retention controls overview: data classes, defaults, configurable range, semantics.
2) Legal hold / incident hold write-up.
3) Audit log event type list + sample export.
4) Compliance reporting pack outline and checklist.

[23:39] Erin Caldwell: Add “data residency summary” please.

[23:41] Markus Klein: Will do.

[23:44] Hannah Wu: For the sample export, please include a retention policy change event, if possible, because that’s a key control.

[23:52] Kevin Osei: Yep, we can include that in the sample.

[23:56] Tom Becker: And what’s the secure channel for sending? Email is sometimes a problem.

[24:01] Olga Petrov: We can use our secure file share link with expiration, or upload to your portal if you have one.

[24:09] Erin Caldwell: We have a portal; I’ll send access.

[24:12] Markus Klein: Perfect.

[24:14] Miguel Alvarez: Any constraints on retention settings that might block us? Like minimum 30 days for audit? we might be okay, but I want to know.

[24:22] Kevin Osei: The main constraints are: audit logs cannot be turned off and have a minimum retention; request content logging can be disabled; and we enforce maximums to prevent unbounded storage in Hosted. For Dedicated/Private, maxima are higher and can be tuned.

[24:44] Priyanka Shah: Okay.

[24:46] Hannah Wu: Are exports immutable? Could an admin edit audit logs?

[24:51] Marcus Lin: Audit logs are append-only in storage; access is controlled. Exported files can be tampered with like any file, but we can provide checksums, and the integrity of underlying logs is protected by permissions and monitoring.

[25:08] Hannah Wu: Checksums would help.

[25:10] Kevin Osei: We can add a checksum file in the package.

[25:14] Markus Klein: Great call.

[25:16] Erin Caldwell: Also, if you do purge, do you purge in backups? This comes up.

[25:22] Marcus Lin: Backups have their own retention. For Hosted/Dedicated, we have backup retention policies and we can document them. In general, backups age out; we don’t do per-record deletion from backups in the short term, but backups expire within a defined window. For Private, backup retention is customer-controlled.

[25:46] Priyanka Shah: That’s important. We’ll need exact backup retention windows.

[25:52] Olga Petrov: We can provide our standard backup retention statement for the relevant tier.

[25:57] Tom Becker: Please do.

[26:00] Miguel Alvarez: For Private, if everything is in our VPC, do you still generate the compliance pack?

[26:06] Markus Klein: We can generate a pack that reflects your config and the product controls, but some evidence (like infrastructure access logs) will be yours. The pack will be a combination: Redwood-provided evidence + customer-provided evidence in the checklist.

[26:23] Erin Caldwell: That’s fine.

[26:25] Hannah Wu: What about redaction? If you give us a sample export, we don’t want real customer names.

[26:30] Kevin Osei: We’ll sanitize. Sample will be from an internal sandbox tenant with fake users.

[26:36] Markus Klein: We’re at about halfway. Any other questions we haven’t hit?

[26:42] Priyanka Shah: Just one: can retention be set by API? We prefer IaC.

[26:47] Kevin Osei: Yes, there are APIs, and for Private we have Terraform modules in progress. If you want day one, API-based config works.

[27:01] Miguel Alvarez: Good.

[27:03] Hannah Wu: RBAC report—what is that?

[27:06] Olga Petrov: It’s basically a snapshot of roles and permissions: who has admin, who can export audit logs, who can change retention, and how those map to least privilege. It’s part of evidence.

[27:20] Erin Caldwell: Nice.

[27:22] Tom Becker: And is SSO required for that? We’ll require it.

[27:26] Markus Klein: For enterprise yes, we support SSO/SAML and we recommend it. We can make it a requirement in your tenant config.

[27:35] Marcus Lin: And audit logs will show SSO configuration changes.

[27:40] Hannah Wu: Perfect.

[27:43] Markus Klein: Let’s do a quick recap then align on next meeting.

[27:48] Markus Klein: Recap: Redwood supports customer-configurable retention by data class with guardrails; request/response content logging can be disabled; audit logs are separate with longer retention. Purge is enforced via jobs with verification metrics and alerts. Legal hold and incident holds exist and are auditable. Audit logs include key admin/security events and can be exported with time windows and filters. We’ll provide a customer-ready evidence package.

[28:18] Erin Caldwell: Sounds right.

[28:20] Markus Klein: Next steps: We’ll send docs tomorrow, and we’ll schedule a Private deployment deep dive. Miguel, do you want to do that next week?

[28:28] Miguel Alvarez: Yes, Tuesday or Wednesday.

[28:31] Markus Klein: Erin, can you send your target retention requirements by data class? You already gave some verbally but we need it written.

[28:39] Erin Caldwell: Yes, I’ll send by end of next week.

[28:43] Tom Becker: And please include timelines for the report pack delivery. That’s important.

[28:49] Olga Petrov: Noted.

[28:52] Hannah Wu: Kevin, please include the event type list; and call out anything that’s “coming soon.”

[28:58] Kevin Osei: Will do.

[29:01] Markus Klein: Cool. We’ve got about 20 minutes left—do you want to go deeper on any specific area? Legal hold, backups, or event coverage?

[29:10] Priyanka Shah: Backups. You said you don’t delete per-record from backups. That’s common but we need to know backup retention is short enough.

[29:19] Marcus Lin: Right. For Hosted/Dedicated, backups have a defined retention window (varies by store). We can provide the standard window and the rationale. The key point is data is not retained indefinitely in backups; it expires, and access is restricted.

[29:37] Erin Caldwell: Okay.

[29:39] Miguel Alvarez: For Private, we can do our own backup policies.

[29:42] Marcus Lin: Exactly.

[29:44] Hannah Wu: Event coverage: do you log “export downloaded” vs “export generated”?

[29:49] Kevin Osei: Both. Generation is one event; download is another. Also failures.

[29:56] Hannah Wu: Nice.

[29:58] Priyanka Shah: Do you log API calls to the retention policy endpoints?

[30:02] Kevin Osei: Yes, changes are logged as audit events, and we can also log read access for sensitive config depending on settings.

[30:12] Markus Klein: Anything else?

[30:15] Erin Caldwell: Maybe just confirm: in Dedicated, is customer data isolated? We’ll handle in a separate call but it’s part of overall risk.

[30:22] Markus Klein: Dedicated is isolated at the compute pool and tenant level; network isolation and storage isolation are part of the offering. We can go deeper in the deployment call.
