[Request: isolate webhook callback traffic from long-poll SSE to prevent 429s during peak backfill]
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports sustained 429s on production for mixed workflows where webhook callbacks (short HTTP POSTs) coincide with a large long-poll SSE workload used for UI presence updates. They believe health-check probes and short callback bursts are being counted against their tenant burst pool and are exhausting tokens during nightly backfills.

Impact: Intermittent 429s for webhook endpoints (callbacks fail, downstream systems see delayed processing) and sporadic client timeouts for SSE consumers. Business impact: delayed webhooks cause missed metering events and degraded UX for customers during the nightly backfill window.

Timeline:
- 2026-03-09 23:00 UTC: ByteFarms begins scheduled backfill (orchestrator spikes SSE connections).
- 2026-03-10 00:05 UTC: First 429s observed for webhook callback endpoint.
- 2026-03-10 00:20 UTC: Customer opens support ticket after retries do not clear 429s.

Environment: prod-us-east on Dedicated pool (tenant_id: BF-10982). Configuration notes provided by customer: single API key used for both SSE and webhook callback requests; ingress via customer-managed proxy -> Redwood edge; Kubernetes readiness/liveness probes to a /health endpoint on the same domain.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1. Start large-scale SSE clients (10k concurrent long-poll connections) that maintain frequent keepalive pings (every 25s).
2. Trigger a batch backfill that emits ~15k webhook callbacks over 10 minutes using the same API key/tenant.
3. Observe HTTP 429 responses from Redwood for webhook POSTs and occasional truncated SSE reconnects.

Observed behaviour: 429s on webhook POSTs with response header X-RateLimit-Reason: tenant_burst_exhausted. Console shows burst credits consumed rapidly; token refill events are visible but not fast enough to prevent rejections. Customer reports health probes and a set of telemetry beacons that run every 30s also correlate with quota depletion spikes.

Expected behaviour: Short webhook callbacks and health probes should be isolated into a separate short-burst pool or exempted from tenant long-tail credits so that long-lived SSE connections don't starve webhooks during scheduled backfills.

Attachments: request logs (sample), edge gateway timestamps, and a short HAR from a failing webhook POST (provided as links in ticket attachments).

comments:
2026-03-10 00:45 - Priya Patel (Support): Thanks for the details — assigning to Infra/SRE to validate burst accounting and route separation. Can you attach a sample failing request ID if available?
2026-03-10 01:10 - Marcus Lee (SRE): Got the sample logs (req id edge: bf-req-20260310-7a2). Initial glance shows correlated token drain during 00:02-00:08 UTC window. Will pull rate-limiter metrics and refill traces from the dedicated pool.
2026-03-10 02:05 - ByteFarms (Customer): Request IDs: bf-req-20260310-7a2, bf-req-20260310-7b9. Also attached kube readiness probe logs. We suspect our readiness probe hits on /health are being counted and would like them excluded if possible.
2026-03-11 09:20 - Marcus Lee (SRE): Reproduced locally using a scaled SSE simulator. Hypothesis: long-lived SSE keepalive pings are being attributed as interactive tokens against the tenant burst bucket because of shared API-key route. Proposing two options: (1) create route-level separation (route tag) for webhook callback path to map it to an isolated burst pool; (2) create a rule to ignore requests from a health-check IP range (requires team approval for exemptions).
2026-03-12 14:12 - Priya Patel (Support): Proposed config change documented below; scheduled a migration window with customer for 2026-03-13 02:00 UTC. Customer approved route-level separation option.

investigation_notes:
Pulled rate-limiter telemetry for tenant BF-10982: saw burst token count drop from 750 -> 0 between 00:02 and 00:07 UTC while refill continued at configured 60 tokens/min.
Metric links: https://metrics.redwood.com/tenants/BF-10982/burst-tokens?from=2026-03-09T23:50Z&to=2026-03-10T00:20Z
Edge logs show 11k concurrent SSEs during the window. Keepalive frequency 25s causes ~440 keepalive requests/sec aggregated (each counted as a request event).
Health checks: kube readiness probes hitting /health every 15s from node IP pool (~50 nodes) generated an extra ~3-4 requests/sec which contributed to token drain under peak.
Verified current tenant configuration: single default route and single burst pool with smoothing enabled. No route-level pool overrides are configured. Config stored in repo: infra/tenants/BF-10982/config.yaml (PR needed to add route mapping).
Risk assessment: Exempting probes at the edge increases risk of accidental abuse by allowing unauthenticated hits to avoid quota; prefer route-level isolation using authenticated webhook callback path.

resolution:
Workaround applied: created a dedicated route tag /webhook/callback mapped to an isolated short-burst pool with higher refill rate and lower per-request weight; updated tenant BF-10982 routing config and rolled out a canary to 5% of edge nodes at 2026-03-12 03:10 UTC. Result: webhook POST success rate increased to 99.8% during a synthetic backfill test. Follow-ups: (1) customer to rotate API keys used by SSE clients and webhook sender so callbacks map to the new route; (2) SRE to prepare a judgement/PR for probe exemption policy if customer requests it in future.

Notes on fix: Changes made in repo (PR 789) and applied to dedicated pool autoscaler to prevent scale-down during scheduled backfills. Monitored for 48h — no repeat 429s for webhooks during scheduled tests. Ticket resolved with recommended permanent configuration steps documented in Confluence.

follow_up_actions:
Customer action: rotate keys for webhook sender and SSE clients as planned (instructions provided).
SRE action: implement a small dashboard to surface route-level burst pool consumption for dedicated tenants (owner: Marcus).
Product action: evaluate a first-class 'health-probe exemption' feature with risk guardrails (owner: Product-Infra).

[Split-DNS views + ECMP path selection causing intermittent service discovery flapping in private deployment]
description:
Customer reports intermittent failures where agent instances in their private deployment fail to resolve control-plane hostnames or resolve to different IPs that intermittently reject TLS handshakes. Symptoms began after a recent network change (added a second transit attachment and enabled ECMP for egress). Failures cause model pulls to fail and gRPC streams to drop for bursts of ~30-90s before recovering.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) From a node in the customer's private subnet run: dig +short control-api.internal.finedge
2) Repeat the dig command several times in quick succession and note alternating A records
3) curl -v --resolve control-api.internal.finedge:443:<ip_from_dig> https://control-api.internal.finedge/health
4) Observe TLS certificate common name and occasional connection resets when dig returns alternate IP
5) Reproduce from multiple AZs/subnets to see AZ-correlated behaviour.

logs:
Customer-provided dig/tcpdump snippets: 
- dig outputs: 10.0.5.21
10.0.8.42
10.0.5.21
- tcpdump on node: DNS requests (udp/53) source=10.0.5.50 -> 172.31.2.10 and -> 172.31.3.11 (alternating)
- openssl s_client -connect 10.0.8.42:443 shows certificate CN=control-api.external.redwood.ai (mismatch)
- kube-agent logs: "x509: certificate is valid for control-api.private.redwood, not control-api.external.redwood.ai"
- Control plane logs show successful connection attempts from IPs in resolver-1 subnet and rejected/handshakes-from resolver-2 subnet

investigation_notes:
Initial hypothesis: split-horizon DNS (resolver sets in two AZs) returns different record sets (one view returns private IPs tied to internal LB with private cert, the other returns an internal CNAME that resolves to an external-facing IP/hostname that presents external TLS cert). Enabling ECMP for egress caused packet flows to be hashed across two NAT paths which send DNS queries to different forwarders / resolvers based on path. Result: same client sometimes gets IP A, sometimes B within TTL window => TLS mismatch when client picks IP with external cert.
What we did: 
- Pulled route tables and observed two active NAT gateway paths with equal-cost routes for 0.0.0.0/0 and DNS traffic to resolver endpoints flowed to different forwarders depending on ECMP hash.
- Captured tcpdump showing DNS queries from same source to two different resolver IPs within 5s.
- Compared resolver responses: resolver-A returns 10.0.5.21 with cert CN control-api.private.redwood; resolver-B returns a CNAME that ultimately resolves to 34.x.y.z (external) with cert CN control-api.external.redwood.ai.
- Reproduced by temporarily forcing egress to a single path: DNS responses stabilized and TLS handshakes succeeded consistently.

comments:
2026-03-12 09:18 - Priya Kapoor (Support): Customer called in after spike of model pull errors. Asked for immediate tcpdump/dig output.
2026-03-12 10:05 - Customer (FinEdge): Provided pcap and dig output, noted network change at 2026-03-11 22:00 (added second transit attachment).
2026-03-12 14:22 - Miguel Santos (SRE): Observed split DNS behavior in provided traces; suspect ECMP+dual-resolver pathing. Requested route table dumps and resolver config from customer.
2026-03-13 08:41 - FinEdge NetOps: Confirmed two NAT gateways + route table entries with equal cost; resolvers are different firewall-forwarders with independent view configs.
2026-03-13 11:30 - Miguel Santos: Suggested temporary mitigation: prefer single egress path for DNS (change route propagation on transit, or add specific /32 route for resolver IP via one NAT), or make both resolvers return the same view (preferred long-term).

resolution:
Mitigation validated: customer changed route preference to pin DNS egress to resolver-A (single path) and restarted agents on nodes. After change, DNS responses stabilized to the private-only view and TLS handshake failures stopped. Root cause: ECMP-induced path selection caused DNS queries to hit two different forwarders with inconsistent split-horizon views.
Permanent fix planned: customer will (a) reconfigure forwarders so both present identical internal views, and (b) update network design to avoid ECMP across resolvers for control-plane traffic. Redwood SRE to add documentation guidance for Private deployments about resolver consistency and ECMP pitfalls.

follow_up_actions:
Create KB entry: private-dns-and-ecmp-runbook (assigned to SRE)
Add validation to onboarding checklist: verify resolvers return identical views from all AZs
Add an outbound-route recommendation to Private deployment docs
Engineering: consider agent-level resolver pinning toggle to prefer a configured resolver IP (feature request filed)

[Happy Eyeballs chooses IPv6 egress through branch proxy that rewrites SNI, causing intermittent artifact TLS certname mismatch in private deploy]
description:
Issue summary: BrightCart is seeing intermittent model artifact fetch failures from serving nodes in their private deployment. Failures manifest as TLS certificate name mismatch (x509: certificate is valid for storage.internal.corp, not artifacts.s3-external.net) when nodes attempt to download shard objects. This happens ~0.3-0.8% of shard fetches, spikes during nightly warmups.

Impact: Inference requests occasionally return 502/5xx or experience longer tail latency while retries happen. Customer reports degraded end-user batch jobs during peak.

Environment: Private deployment (customer-managed VPC peering to our control plane) with egress routed through the customer's branch-office proxy/NGFW. Serving nodes are dual-stack (IPv4+IPv6) and use system default Happy Eyeballs behavior.

Steps to reproduce:
1) Trigger model rollout that causes serving nodes to fetch shard objects concurrently (large model or batch warmup).
2) Observe artifact fetch logs and TLS errors on a subset of nodes.
3) Failures correlate with a resolver returning AAAA records and the kernel selecting IPv6 egress first.

Logs / observations:
- serving-node.log: "GET https://artifacts.s3-external.net/model-12345/shard-0: x509: certificate is valid for storage.internal.corp, not artifacts.s3-external.net"
- tcpdump on node during failure shows TLS ClientHello SNI = "artifacts.s3-external.net" but proxy/NGFW upstream opens TLS to storage.internal.corp endpoint (IPv6 path) and responds with a different certificate.
- DNS responses during failure include AAAA then A; Happy Eyeballs chooses IPv6 path leading to branch proxy path.

Suspected cause: Branch-office egress path for IPv6 is hairpinned through an intermediate corporate proxy that performs SNI rewriting (or routes to an internal storage translator) only for IPv6-preferring flows. IPv4 egress takes a different ISP path that preserves SNI. Happy Eyeballs/dual-stack behavior causes a fraction of connections to use IPv6 and encounter proxy SNI rewrite, producing hostname mismatch.

Temporary workaround: Request customer to either (a) prefer IPv4 on serving nodes (gai.conf / sysctl tweak) or (b) add an exception in the branch proxy to preserve SNI for artifacts.s3-external.net/storage endpoints. We provided exact gai.conf line to prefer IPv4.

Requested next steps:
- Collect pcap and proxy logs from customer for a failing window.
- Confirm proxy rule that rewrites SNI or routes IPv6 traffic differently.
- Consider adding an artifact fetch fallback that retries with IPv4 on TLS hostname mismatch to avoid transient failures.

[Presigned-artifact TLS name mismatch caused by split-horizon DNS rewriting S3 host to internal proxy]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports failing model artifact downloads for large model pulls using presigned S3 URLs from their Private deployment. Errors show TLS certificate name mismatch when the platform attempts to fetch artifacts during model load.

Impact:
- Model pulls fail intermittently, causing pod restart loops and degraded inference capacity for the customer's private deployment in us-east-1.
- Affects production traffic for a single customer (FinSolve Analytics).

Environment:
- Private deployment (customer-managed VPC peering to Redwood control plane).
- prod/us-east-1.
- Model: gptx-13b-v2 (~4.2GB artifact).

Steps to reproduce:
1) Trigger a model rollout that requires a fresh artifact pull (scale up or new node join).
2) Observe model-puller logs in the private deployment agent.
3) Some requests show TLS handshake failures when fetching the presigned URL returned by Redwood Control Plane.

Observed logs (excerpts):
- model-puller: "GET https://finsolve-models.s3.amazonaws.com/artifacts/....?X-Amz-Signature=..."  --> TLS handshake failed: certificate verify failed: hostname '10.10.20.45' does not match 'finsolve-models.s3.amazonaws.com'
- curl --location --verbose against presigned URL from within customer VPC shows: "* Connected to 10.10.20.45 (10.10.20.45) port 443 (#0)" then "* TLS: hostname mismatch (certificate is for internal-cache.company.corp)"

Notes from customer: their on-prem DNS resolver and corporate proxy return an internal IP for the s3 hostname (split-horizon) and forward traffic to an internal HTTPS cache/proxy for inspection and deduplication. The proxy uses an internal cert not matching the S3 hostname.


investigation:
Timeline and diagnostics performed:
- 2026-02-28 09:10 UTC: Support replicated failing model pulls in a staging mirror using customer's forwarded DNS rules.
- Ran dig +short finsolve-models.s3.amazonaws.com against the customer's forwarder -> returned 10.10.20.45 (internal cache IP).
- tcpdump from model-puller container showed SYN->SYN/ACK with 10.10.20.45 then TLS ClientHello; server sent a cert with CN=internal-cache.company.corp and SANs not including the S3 hostname.
- curl -v to presigned URL inside customer VPC reproduced: certificate hostname mismatch and the TLS subject contained internal proxy name.
- Verified presigned URL host was the regional S3 hostname as expected; cert returned by upstream connection did not match.
- Control-plane logs confirm presigned URL generation was correct; Redwood side S3 endpoints unaffected.

Hypothesis:
- Customer split-horizon DNS returns an internal IP for S3 hostnames, routing presigned S3 requests to an internal HTTPS inspection/cache appliance that terminates TLS with its own cert, causing hostname mismatch and client-side verification to fail.

Evidence to support hypothesis:
- Packet captures show internal IP and proxy cert CN.
- Curl and openssl s_client show cert CN mismatch when run from inside customer network; same presigned URL fetched successfully from an external network.
- No signs of S3 or Redwood control plane issuing partial redirects or rewriting hostnames.

2026-02-28 - Support (Nina Patel): Thanks Rajesh — we've captured a pcap and certificate fingerprint. Can you confirm whether your proxy injects a substitute certificate for *.s3.amazonaws.com? Also please share whether you have DNS split-horizon rules for *.s3.amazonaws.com.
2026-02-28 - Customer (Rajesh Kumar): Confirmed: internal resolver returns 10.10.20.45 for bucket hostnames and our proxy performs TLS termination. It's intended for cache/dedupe. We'll escalate to network team to add an exception if recommended.

Short-term workaround: set model-puller no_proxy to include *.s3.amazonaws.com OR add an ACL on proxy to passthrough S3 requests without TLS termination. Permanent: update DNS or use AWS VPC Endpoint (VPCE) for S3 access.
2026-03-01 - Customer (Rajesh Kumar): We added a proxy bypass for S3 hosts and model pulls succeed. We'll coordinate with proxy team to add an explicit passthrough ACL for S3 hosts and update split-horizon rules.
2026-03-01 - Support (Nina Patel): Marking resolved based on customer's confirmation and suggested follow-ups. Created INT-204 to add a runbook note for private deploy customers about split-horizon and presigned URL verification.

resolution:
Workaround applied by customer: added proxy bypass for bucket hostnames and configured model-puller 'no_proxy' to prevent proxy interception of presigned S3 requests. Result: model downloads resumed and nodes stabilized.

Root cause: Customer split-horizon DNS + corporate HTTPS caching appliance was terminating TLS for S3 hostnames, presenting an internal certificate that did not include the S3 hostname. Because presigned URLs are single-use and host-specific, the client's TLS verification failed.

Permanent remediation recommendations provided to customer:
1) Add an explicit passthrough rule on the proxy for S3 regional hostnames used by Redwood (do not terminate TLS for pre-signed artifact fetches).
2) Update split-horizon DNS so S3 hostnames resolve to AWS IPs or configure the model-puller/service to use a VPC Endpoint (VPCE) for S3 to keep traffic inside AWS without proxy interception.
3) Add a startup healthcheck in the agent to validate presigned URL TLS chain and produce actionable error messages (INT-204 created to track runbook change).

[Egress address-mapping appliance rewrites IPv4 dest to IPv6-mapped (::ffff:) causing TLS SNI / certname mismatch on artifact CDN]
description:
Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent failures downloading model/artifact shards from our CDN during Private deployment. Failures started after a third-party egress appliance firmware upgrade.
Impact: Artifact download errors for a subset of hosts in the customer's VPC causing model pull backoffs and degraded inference capacity during nightly batch pulls. Approx 20% of download attempts return TLS/hostname verification errors.
Environment: Private deployment (VPC + VPCE) in us-west-2, traffic egresses through customer-managed transit appliance (vendor: NetPathX, model NX-2100).
Observed behaviour: TLS handshake fails with certificate name mismatch reported by s3 client. Packet captures show destination IP in outbound TCP/TLS frames as IPv6-mapped address (::ffff:10.12.34.56) while SNI contains the original hostname (cdn.redwood-inference.com). The CDN serves a certificate for cdn.redwood-inference.com, but some client libs attempt host validation against the numeric destination IP when the socket peer address is an IPv6-mapped address, causing verification failure.
Expected behaviour: Egress appliance should preserve IPv4 destination addresses (10.12.34.56) in the IP layer when performing NAT/translation or preserve original socket peer for TLS validation, not convert to IPv6-mapped format.
Steps to reproduce: 1) From a serving node in the customer's private deploy, attempt a presigned shard range download via our SDK. 2) Observe intermittent TLS hostname verification failures in the agent logs. 3) Run tcpdump during failing request to inspect IP addressing and TLS ClientHello.
Relevant logs/snippets: see `logs` field for captures and errors.

steps_to_reproduce:
kubectl exec -it serving-node-abc -- curl -v --resolve cdn.redwood-inference.com:443:10.12.34.56 'https://cdn.redwood-inference.com/path/to/shard'
Run tcpdump on node: tcpdump -i eth0 -s 0 -w /tmp/shard-fail.pcap host 10.12.34.56
Re-run download and observe TLS handshake failures in agent logs and PCAP shows ::ffff:10.12.34.56 as destination IP for some flows

OpenSSL s_client output (failing flow): CONNECTED(00000003)
depth=0 C = US, O = Redwood CDN, CN = cdn.redwood-inference.com
verify error:num=62:hostname mismatch
tcpdump excerpt: 14:22:18.123456 IP6 fe80::2 > ::ffff:10.12.34.56: Flags [S], seq 0, win 64240, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 123456 ecr 0,nop,wscale 7], length 0
Agent debug: outbound-dest-address=::ffff:10.12.34.56, SNI=cdn.redwood-inference.com, socket.getpeername() returned ('::ffff:10.12.34.56', 443)

2026-03-13 11:22 - Miguel Ramirez (SRE): Created temp firewall rule recommendation and requested vendor firmware rollback/patch. Linked runbook: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/12845/Egress+Address+Translation+Runbook

investigation_notes:
Confirmed failure class is not SNI stripping or TLS inspection — SNI in ClientHello intact and certificate presented by CDN is correct for hostname.
Socket peer address reported by the agent is ::ffff:10.12.34.56 for failing flows; some languages/libraries (older Go versions, older OpenSSL stacks) validate against numeric peer name if peer is an IP literal rather than hostname, causing mismatch.
PCAP shows appliance rewrote packets on egress: source stays 198.51.100.23, destination was transformed from IPv4 10.12.34.56 to IPv6 ::ffff:10.12.34.56 before sending to upstream transit link.
Scanned customer appliance config; 'enable-ipv4-mapping' flag toggled by default in vendor config template delivered with 3.2.1. Customer confirmed they used default template during upgrade.
No changes required in Redwood runtime — the issue is due to in-path address mangling by customer appliance that triggers host verification edge-cases in client libraries.

hypothesis:
Vendor firmware 3.2.1 introduced an aggressive translation mode that maps IPv4 destinations into IPv6-mapped (::ffff:) addresses for egress to support an ISP IPv6-only peering. The appliance incorrectly applies this mapping to flows that are still IPv4-capable towards the CDN, causing socket peername to appear as an IP literal to the local TLS stack.
Affected client stacks that perform hostname verification against the numeric peer address fail because they do not prefer SNI/hostname when peername is an IP literal. This is intermittent because not all upstream paths trigger the appliance translation (dependent on ISP route selection).

Advise customer to apply vendor hotfix 3.2.2 which disables IPv4->IPv6-mapped rewrite by default (vendor hotfix confirmed 2026-03-13)
Customer to roll hotfix to prod and monitor shard download success rate for 24h

Post-deploy validation: artifact download success rate restored to baseline (99.98%) after full rollout; no further hostname verification TLS errors observed in agent logs.
Workaround used during mitigation: temporarily route a subset of nodes to IGW (bypass appliance) to unblock critical model pulls.
Longer term: added agent-level telemetry to detect IPv6-mapped peer addresses and surface in Console per-route error summaries; documented vendor firmware caveat in runbook.

root_cause:
Third-party egress appliance firmware (NetPathX NX 3.2.1) enabled IPv4->IPv6-mapped address rewrite for certain egress flows, causing socket peer to be an IP literal and triggering hostname verification failures in some TLS client stacks.

[Private deployment: corporate TLS inspection stripping SNI causes certificate mismatch and intermittent model downloads]
description:
Issue summary:
Customer's private deployment (Acme Analytics, private tier) reports intermittent failures when the agent attempts to download model artifacts and make downstream HTTPS calls to model-registry.redwood-internal.net. DNS resolution succeeds for all requests, but TLS handshakes sometimes fail with certificate name mismatch or the client aborts during ServerHello. Small API calls (token checks, pings) usually succeed; large model downloads fail ~30% of the time.

Impact:
- Model pulls for new containers occasionally fail causing model startup retries and longer cold-starts for customers.
- Streaming inference for long responses sometimes resets mid-stream when the model endpoint is reloaded.

Environment:
- Private deployment (on-customer VPC) with VPC endpoint to Redwood's model-registry, routing through corporate perimeter firewall performing TLS inspection.
- Region: us-west-2
- Agent version: 1.12.0
- Serving runtime: rwd-svc-2026-02

Steps to reproduce:
1) Trigger a model pull via the Console or run a job that requires a cold-start for redwood-open-7B-v1.
2) Observe logs in agent (agent.log) and attempt manual curl from a jump host inside the same VPC: curl -v https://model-registry.redwood-internal.net/v1/models
3) Repeatedly issue downloads; intermittent failures observed.

Observed behavior:
- DNS returns correct A records consistently.
- curl -v shows TCP handshake completes, but in failing cases the ClientHello seen by the server lacks an SNI extension (verified via tcpdump on customer network).
- Server returns default certificate (CN does not match expected host) causing client certificate name mismatch error.
- When SNI is present (successful TLS handshakes), connections proceed normally.
- Agent logs: "tls: server certificate does not match expected name" or "handshake aborted by peer" on failing attempts.

Expected behavior:
- TLS ClientHello includes SNI with model-registry.redwood-internal.net and server presents correct certificate for that name, allowing handshake to complete consistently.

Logs / Evidence attached by customer:
- tcpdump (pcap) showing alternating ClientHello packets: some contain SNI extension, some do not.
- curl -v outputs for success and failure cases.
- Agent logs excerpt and model-pull stack traces.

Investigation notes (Support):
- Reproduced handshake mismatch in our lab by removing SNI from ClientHello; server returns default vhost certificate and client fails verification.
- Hypothesis: Corporate TLS inspection appliance (explicit TLS proxy) is either stripping or rewriting the SNI extension when proxying outbound TLS flows, or it is performing a re-encapsulation without preserving the original SNI. This results in the backend load balancer selecting the default certificate.
- Intermittent nature explained by: appliance is stateful and some flows are proxied differently based on session affinity or connection reuse; some agent processes reuse connections that already had SNI preserved.
- Confirmed no rate-limiting or 5xx on Redwood side for these requests during captured windows.

Suggested actions / Workaround:
- Short term: Customer's firewall team to configure TLS inspection to preserve SNI for hosts matching *.redwood-internal.net or create an allowlist so TLS bypass is performed for model-registry endpoints.
- Alternative: Configure the agent to use an internal HTTP proxy that performs TLS passthrough (no MITM) for registry hosts. Agent supports an explicit PROXY env to route only model pulls.
- Customer has provided corporate firewall logs and agreed to test an allowlist.

Next steps / Requested from customer:
1) Firewall/proxy team to confirm whether SNI rewriting/stripping is enabled and test an allowlist bypass for model-registry.redwood-internal.net.
2) Provide an additional pcap after bypass is applied to verify SNI is present in all ClientHello packets.
3) If bypass not possible, confirm whether corporate CA is being injected and whether the agent runtime trusts that CA (note: trusting injected CAs weakens security; preferred solution is bypass for known Redwood endpoints).

Resolution notes:
- Pending customer firewall change. Support has documented exact hostnames and IP ranges to allow. If customer applies the allowlist and problem persists, escalate to Networking Eng (linked INT-1142) and provide fresh pcaps.

References:
- Internal TLS Inspection runbook: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/ENG/pages/9842/TLS+Inspection+Runbook
- Related GH issue updating agent proxy handling: https://github.com/redwood-inference/internal-tools/pull/342

[Operating Lanes Playbook for Cycle Capacity and Staff Rotation]
description:
Summary:
This ticket codifies an operating-lanes playbook for cycle planning: an explicit policy for how we allocate headcount across core lanes (Committed Work, Critical Bugs/Incidents, Platform / Reliability Investment, and Strategic Bets) and a lightweight staff-rotation pattern to spread knowledge and maintain velocity across teams. The playbook aims to give PMs and ENG leads a repeatable method for sizing cycles, provisioning reserves, and making defensible scope cuts tied to OKRs.

Problem statement:
We regularly over-index on optimistic scope, lack consistent surge rules, and struggle to coordinate cross-functional swaps when emergencies or high-priority renewals surface mid-cycle. This results in unplanned context switching, multi-week delays to key initiatives, and uneven risk exposure across teams.

Proposal (operating lanes):
- Define four lanes with clear budgeted % of team capacity per cycle: Committed (55-65%), Reliability & Ops (10-15%), Strategic Bets (10-20%), Tactical Reserve (10%). Exact percentages vary by team maturity and OKR cadence; provide a baseline and per-team tailoring guide.
- Tactical Reserve is budgeted in engineer-days and fractional FTEs, not tasks; it is held as an explicit capacity hedge that PMs can use for escalations, customer escalations, and late-priority bugs.
- Staff Rotation: create a 2-week rotation window for a 10-20% fraction of engineers to be on an "integration" rotation (knowledge transfer + cross-team pairing) enabling faster context switch and reducing single-threaded risks. Rotation assignments are opt-in and compensated in scope credit for the owning team.

Scope-cut rules (decision matrix):
- If an unplanned high-priority request consumes >50% of Tactical Reserve for two consecutive sprints, trigger an intra-cycle scope review: items in Committed lane will be re-prioritized based on customer impact, revenue risk, and OKR delta; PMs must supply a 30/60/90 impact statement.
- Cut order: (1) Unscheduled stretch items in Committed, (2) Strategic Bets lower than OKR impact threshold, (3) Deferrable reliability improvements with documented mitigation, (4) Non-blocking polish / UX nice-to-have.

Operational playbook artifacts (what this ticket produces):
- A one-page "Operating Lanes" template for cycle planning (Google Doc) and editable spreadsheet that computes capacity buckets per team.
- A rotation roster template and onboarding checklist for rotating engineers.
- An intra-cycle scope review checklist and a simple triage rubric for PM/Eng leads.
- A pre-cycle checklist for staffing commitments and a post-cycle retrospective template focusing on capacity variance.

Acceptance criteria:
- Template doc and spreadsheet are published under Confluence and linked in the cycle kickoff playbook.
- At least three pilot teams (infra, console, and embeddings UI) adopt the lanes in Cycle 2025-W12 and provide capacity baselines.
- The rotation roster and checklist are used in pilot teams and a data snapshot (capacity delta, disruptions avoided) is available after run.

Metrics / signals to monitor:
- Planned vs actual capacity by lane (engineering-days) per team.
- Number of intra-cycle scope reviews triggered and time-to-resolution.
- Percentage of incidents that used Tactical Reserve vs required escalation of additional headcount.
- Velocity variance (story points velocity swing) pre/post rotation pilot.

Rollout plan:
- Week 0: Publish playbook + spreadsheet + sample filled templates; align with ML Platform and Infra leads. (Confluence + Drive links in artifacts below).
- Week 1–2: Pilot with three volunteer teams (Infra, Console, Embeddings UI). Running retrospective at end of week 2.
- Week 3–4: Iterate on templates based on pilot feedback; provide recommended % buckets for small vs. large teams.
- Cycle 2025-W12: Optional org-wide adoption guidance; include in cycle kickoff materials and cadence for monthly check-ins.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Teams underutilize Tactical Reserve leading to waste. Mitigation: Require PMs to publish a short justification and planned fallback uses before cycle start; track usage and allow reclaim at mid-cycle checkpoint.
- Risk: Rotation decreases short-term throughput. Mitigation: Limit rotation to 10–20% and only for teams with buffer; award scope credit and treat rotation as planned work in committed lane.
- Risk: Overly prescriptive buckets don’t fit specialty teams. Mitigation: Make buckets configurable and include guidance for one-off exceptions with approvals.

Decision log:
- 2025-02-19: Agreed baseline lanes and target % ranges in cross-functional working group (Isabel, Marco, Naomi, Raj).
- 2025-02-25: Platform requested a larger Reliability & Ops floor for infra-heavy teams; accepted 10–15% per-team configurable floor.
- 2025-03-04: Rotation compensation approved: 0.5 sprint worth of scope credit per rotation cycle for owning team.

Next steps / owners:
- Draft templates: Marco Li (owner) — due 2025-03-06 (done).
- Pilot coordination: Naomi Chen (owner) — pilot runs 2025-03-10 -> 2025-03-24.
- Data capture and dashboard: Eng Analytics (ENG-1842) — dashboard to show capacity by lane.

Notes on trade-offs considered:
- We considered a purely point-based reserve (story points) but selected engineer-days to align with capacity billing and to reduce story point inflation games.
- We debated fixed vs. percentage reserve; a percentage baseline plus small absolute floor worked best across team sizes.


comments:
2025-02-19 - Isabel Moreno: Kicked off cross-functional working group. Documented initial lane percentages; asked infra to validate reliability floor.
2025-03-06 - Marco Li: Templates v1 completed and uploaded to Drive. Linked a sample filled spreadsheet for Console team.
2025-03-10 - Naomi Chen: Pilot kickoff with Infra, Console, Embeddings UI. Rosters created; rotation volunteers submitted.

2025-03-11 - PM Review: Please ensure the intra-cycle review checklist includes required stakeholder SLA (CTO or Head of Product signoff for >75% reserve consumption).

[Cycle Capacity Scenario Matrix and Staff Allocation Simulation]
description:
Problem: Mid-cycle decommits and repeated scope shuffles are costing engineering ~10-15% of delivery velocity and creating churn on cross-team initiatives. We lack a repeatable quantitative runbook that ties staff availability, skill overlap, and contingency buffers to a recommended tranche/trim plan.

Goal: Produce a practical playbook and a lightweight simulation tool (Monte Carlo-backed spreadsheet + quick script) that both PMs and Eng leads can use during planning to: 1) enumerate plausible capacity scenarios, 2) recommend where to place soft-freeze buffers vs. hard commitments, 3) suggest role-level shadowing and surge lanes, and 4) propose scoped cuts that minimize customer-facing risk.

Success metrics: reduce mid-cycle decommit rate from ~18% to <8% across pilot initiatives; increase accuracy of committed scope (features delivered vs committed) from 72% to 85% for participating teams; time-to-decision in planning reduced to under 90 minutes for medium-sized initiatives.

Approach:
- Design a scenario matrix capturing: staffing uncertainty bands, skill pool overlap, dependency criticality, and external risk multipliers (sales commitments, infra incidents).
- Implement a Monte Carlo simulation prototype (Python notebook + Google Sheet wrapper) to produce distributions of completion probability per initiative given different buffer allocations.
- Convert outputs into a decision matrix: for each initiative, recommended commit tier (Guaranteed / Contingent / Deferred), suggested staff shadowing % and minimum surge lanes.
- Author a 1-page playbook summarizing steps, roles, and templates for PM/Eng leads to run during pre-cycle planning.

Deliverables: scenario matrix template (GSheet), simulation notebook (Colab link), playbook PDF in Confluence, trimmed-scope decision checklist, Slackbot workflow to record final tranche choices into the planning board.

Risks: simulation relies on historical velocity distributions which may be sparse for newly-formed teams; cultural resistance to enforced surge lanes; potential misinterpretation of outputs as prescriptive rather than advisory. Mitigations: conservative priors, running two sensitivity passes (optimistic/pessimistic), include human review gate in the process.

acceptance_criteria:
Simulation tool produces probability distributions for initiative delivery under at least 3 buffer configurations.
Playbook and templates published to Confluence with an example run for a cross-team initiative.
Product and Eng leads complete a pilot planning session using the tool and provide structured feedback.

[Cycle orchestration: Scope Fishing Lanes and adaptive capacity allocation]
description:
Purpose:
This playbook defines a structured approach to cycle planning that reserves explicit lightweight 'fishing lanes' — small, time-boxed capacity bands for high-impact emergent work — while preserving committed scope for OKRs and cross-team initiatives. The goal is to reduce mid-cycle chaos, make scope cuts predictable, and improve confidence in hitting OKR commitments.

Background / Problem statement:
- In past cycles we either over-committed and missed OKRs, or we under-allocated and wasted engineering momentum.
- Unplanned customer escalations and legal/regulatory requests frequently arrive mid-cycle and currently disrupt the committed plan.
- Existing tranche and buffer playbooks are broad; teams ask for a lightweight operational protocol that is easy to apply at the team and initiative level.

Proposal (high-level):
1) Define three capacity lanes per cycle at the initiative level: Committed (70%), Flexible (20%), Fishing (10%). Percentages are configurable by project risk profile.
2) Committed lane: items scoped, estimated, and owned by initiative leads. Changes require formal scope-change approval.
3) Flexible lane: planned low-risk stretch items prioritized in backlog; can be promoted into Committed with PM + Eng tech lead signoff.
4) Fishing lane: reserved tickets for high-impact emergent work (customer bugs, legal/security asks, urgent infra fixes). Activation requires on-call PM + Eng approval and a triage ticket with owner and target impact metric.
5) Weekly capacity burn reviews: initiative leads report lane utilization and reallocate within a predefined guardrail matrix.

Scope-cut rules and triggers:
- Soft trigger: when Committed+Flexible burn > 85% of forecast before cycle midpoint -> initiate scope freeze review.
- Hard trigger: when Committed burn > 95% or unexpected Fishing activation > 2x allocated slots -> automatic reprioritization meeting within 48 hours.
- Cut order: non-customer-facing stretch features -> docs/localization -> deferred infra improvements -> last resort: trimmed slices of committed features with rollback plan.

Acceptance criteria:
- Playbook adopted by at least 3 cross-functional initiatives in the next cycle pilot.
- Clear checklist for Fishing lane activation in the console (triage ticket created, owner assigned, impact metric declared).
- Cycle-level dashboard visible to leads showing lane allocations and live utilization.

Rollout plan:
- Week 0: socialize playbook in PM sync and engineering all-hands; update initiative templates.
- Week 1: pilot with two initiatives (one Platform, one Hosting) and provide a short one-pager for squads.
- Mid-cycle: gather feedback and adjust default lane splits.
- Post-cycle: run a blameless retrospective and measure OKR completion delta vs prior cycles.

Notes on sizing and fairness:
- Default 70/20/10 is a starting point — high-risk initiatives (e.g., new infra) may set 60/25/15.
- Leads must document expected candidate items for Fishing lane at beginning of cycle (even if empty) to reduce ad-hoc backlog creation.

Operational integrations:
- Console: add an Initiative view with lane columns and a simple toggle to 'activate fishing slot' that creates a prefilled Linear ticket template.
- Alerts: add a threshold alert to the initiative dashboard for the soft/hard triggers.
- Templates: Confluence PRD template updated with lane allocation fields and decision owner names.

Implementation risks and mitigations:
- Risk: Teams misuse Fishing lane as extra runway for low-priority work -> mitigation: require documented customer/regulatory justification and PM+Eng approval.
- Risk: Overhead of weekly reporting -> mitigation: automate utilization reporting from Linear/Console and provide lightweight default reports.

Ownership and next steps:
- PM owner: Aisha Patel (playbook shepherd).
- Engineering partner: Marcus Nguyen (implementation/console wiring).
- Design: inform UI for 'activate fishing slot' flow (DES-204).
- Next steps: finalize playbook, create console ticket templates, schedule pilot kickoff for 2026-W11.

[Cycle capacity scenarios & rapid-scope-cut playbook]
description:
Playbook and worked examples for allocating product team capacity across cycles, including three capacity scenarios (conservative, baseline, aggressive), a decision tree for mid-cycle scope cuts, and a running checklist for PMs to coordinate with Eng, Design, and Support. The goal is to standardize how we translate OKRs into committed scope, where to cut in-flight work when capacity shortfalls occur, and how to communicate changes to stakeholders and customers.

capacity_model:
Model assumptions: 8 PMs, 30 engineers, 6 designers. Velocity baseline: 30 dev points/cycle per engineering pod. Reserve buffer flavors: none (0%), low (10%), standard (20%). Scenarios: conservative = 20% scope held as staging/backlog; baseline = 10% buffer + 5% contingency; aggressive = 0% buffer, prioritized delivery of OKR path. Includes recommended staffing multipliers for feature work vs. platform/ops work (1.6x engineer headcount for platform projects).

notes:
Guidance summary: 1) Convert OKRs to no more than 3 Tier-1 commitments per product track per cycle. 2) Use the baseline scenario by default; switch to conservative for compliance or hiring churn. 3) For mid-cycle cuts: prefer cutting scope in the 2nd priority set, defer platform refactors that don't block delivery, and never cut security/compliance work. Attach a customer-communication draft when announcing changes. Track net scope moved between cycles in the Cycle Retro doc.

[Cycle workload bucketing and contingent staffing simulator]
description:
Problem statement: during cycle planning we repeatedly under- or over-allocate people across different work rhythms (steady product work, short high-latency spikes like incidents or carrier integrations, and long opaque R&D investigations). That mismatch drives mid-cycle scope churn and emergency reassignments.

Proposal: build a compact 'contingent staffing simulator' + playbook that 1) buckets recurring workload into a small taxonomy (steady throughput, predictable spikes, maintenance ops, exploration), 2) models staffing profiles (core fraction, shadow rotation, reserve pool), and 3) outputs recommended contingent staffing schedules and de-scope triggers for a target cycle. The deliverable is an MVP simulator (not production-grade), a one-page decision canvas for PMs/ENG leads, and a short playbook for after-hours/incident shadow coverage.

Why this helps: gives an evidence-backed, repeatable method for setting soft staffing reserves and defensible scope cuts; reduces mid-cycle firefights; and provides inputs for Dedicated & Private capacity planning analogs (how much safety buffer to reserve for production reliability work).

maria: Heads-up — brainstorming how we should fan out v1 deprecation signals so routing, billing, and the console all behave sensibly. Sketching an approach, want quick feedback before I file the RFC.

aj: SGTM. main goals? minimize alert noise, keep metrics useful, and make rollouts reversible. :+1:

kevin: Current state for context: console shows a static banner when tenant hits a threshold, telemetry emits deprecated=true at the request level, and routing does a hard pin drop when header missing. That causes a lot of noisy samples.

sarah: Proposal: breadcrumbing. Emit a low-cost tag first (deprec_stage=breadcrumb) that flows to metrics and traces but doesn’t change routing/quota. If breadcrumbed usage crosses thresholds, escalate to deprec_stage=notice, and finally deprec_stage=action which unlocks routing/quota changes.

maria: Exactly. I want these pieces: 1) lightweight breadcrumb emit that’s sampled (1% -> 10% -> 100%), 2) metric label enrichment so we can pivot dashboards by stage, 3) console UX with progressive copy (info -> warning -> action), 4) routing/quotas only on stage=action.

kevin: Suggest metric labels: `api_version`, `deprec_stage`, `route_key`. That way we can slice by route and by stage without exploding cardinality. Also keep breadcrumb sample flag `deprec_sample=true` for quick joins.

sarah: Implementation sketch for telemetry (pseudo):
```
// attach to request pipeline
if (request.hasDeprecatedHeader()) {
  if (rand() < sampleRate) {
    telemetry.emit("redwood.deprec_signal", {
      api_version: "v1",
      deprec_stage: "breadcrumb",
      deprec_sample: "true",
      route_key: request.routeHash()
    })
  }
}
```

aj: Nice. A couple notes: 1) don't let breadcrumbing affect billing metering keys (we need canonical token attribution), 2) quota behavior must be explicit: stage=action -> quota enforcement, stage=notice -> console-only.

kevin: For routing: avoid sudden unpin/unroute. When stage=action we should set a soft TTL on pinned routes (e.g., 5m) and a console button to force unpin. That gives customers time to adjust.

maria: UX copy idea for console:
- breadcrumb: "We observed some v1 traffic. No action required — this helps us track the migration."
- notice: "Significant v1 traffic detected. Consider updating clients; click to see impacted endpoints."
- action: "Automatic routing changes pending — update clients or click to opt out."

kevin: One risk: tenants with high route cardinality could blow up label cardinality. Mitigation: only attach `route_key` for routes that exceed a traffic threshold (e.g., >1% of tenant traffic) and otherwise tag `route_key=other`.

aj: Thoughts on rollout plan? My take: feature flag `deprec_fanout_v1` default off. Stage 1 -> emit breadcrumb sampled 1%. Stage 2 -> increase sample to 10% and enable console notice. Stage 3 -> enable action for a small cohort and monitor.

[Catalyst Retail — Multipath reassembly producing duplicate/truncated completions during peak traffic; escalation and post-incident action plan]
description:
Issue summary: During two afternoon traffic peaks on 2026-03-10 Catalyst Retail experienced repeated fragmented and duplicate completions for conversational endpoints. Impact: user-facing duplicates and truncated completions causing business-critical checkout dialogs to fail and a ~30% increase in tokens billed during incident window. Root symptom: multipath reassembly module failed to deduplicate partial fragments when a subset of multiplexed responses were routed across failover paths.

impact:
- Customer-facing duplicate completions and truncated replies for session-based chat flows. - Elevated token consumption leading to billing spike and customer complaint. - Customer reported lost conversions during peak.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Send 4 concurrent streaming chat requests tied to same session affinity token to model rw-instruct-large-8b-quant in us-east during sustained 200 RPS
2) Induce a transient 10-20% packet loss in the router (simulated via iptables) while triggering autoscale events
3) Observe reassembly logic in gateway producing duplicated chunks and out-of-order final completions

logs:
2026-03-10T14:12:03Z router WARN multiplexed-recovery: reassembly timeout for session=cr-session-77
2026-03-10T14:12:04Z serving-runtime ERROR kv-cache: pending-eviction race detected shard=3
2026-03-10T14:12:04Z api-gateway INFO stream: partial-chunk-forwarded path=/v1/chat/stream request_id=req-9f7a

investigation_notes:
Initial triage by SRE (E. Chen): correlation between routing failovers and duplicate fragments; packet loss amplification seen when autoscaler brought up new endpoints.
Observed that reassembly sequence numbers were occasionally replayed when one path responded slower and the other replayed cached prefix.
Hypothesis: concurrent failover + aggressive prefix caching + reassembly logic did not dedupe identical fragment ids across transport paths.
Telemetry: increased retransmit counts (x5) and 429s absent; no CPU/GPU OOM observed.

mitigation:
Applied immediate temporary throttle on concurrent session affinity (config updated in router to cap session fanout to 2)
Disabled cross-path prefix caching for sessions flagged with high fanout
Rolled a hotfix to reassembly module to add fragment-id deduplication and extend reassembly timeout by 250ms (deploy PR #4578) in us-east then eu-west

resolution:
Hotfix merged and rolled to prod (serving-runtime v2026.03.10-hotfix1) across affected regions
Router config change made persistent via runbook and reverted throttle after validation
Billing credit issued to customer for the window (see comments for amount) and formal apology sent
Monitoring alert created to track fragment duplicate rate and token delta

postincident_actions:
1) Schedule deep-dive with reassembly and routing teams on 2026-03-18
2) Add e2e chaos test for cross-path packet loss in CI (ticket INT-91234)
3) Update runbook: on detection of duplicate fragment rate>0.5% auto-apply session fanout cap
4) Audit billing aggregation to detect token deltas and auto-calc credits

customer_communications:
2026-03-10 16:20 UTC: initial acknowledgment to Catalyst Retail support contact (Z. Martinez) confirming we are investigating
2026-03-10 19:05 UTC: detailed incident update explaining failover-induced fragment duplication and next steps
2026-03-11 09:10 UTC: notification of hotfix deployment and planned credit

credit_resolved:
USD 12,500 credited to Catalyst Retail invoice for incident window (approved by Finance on 2026-03-11)

comments:
Z. Martinez (Catalyst Retail): 'This impacted a live promo. Need confirmation that tokens won't be double-counted again.'
E. Chen (SRE): 'Hotfix adds fragment-id dedupe and we observed duplicate rate drop to <0.01% in canary.'
M. Rivera (Support): 'Finance approved a goodwill credit; formal email drafted and queued for 2026-03-11 12:00 UTC.'
K. Olsen (Product): 'Add integration test for session fanout and routing failover to the serving-runtime CI.'

[support]
lina: Hey team, Customer J. Doe reporting streaming chat responses that cut off mid-JSON then client reconnects and sees duplicate billing events. They say it happens behind Cloudflare + ALB. Repro attached.
customer-jdoe: repro: connect to /v1/stream with Authorization header, wait ~30-45s, last chunk silent, client reconnects and receives partial JSON then full new response. Billing shows two charges.
ben: do we have traces/ingress logs? sample request id? :thinking_face:
customer-jdoe: request_id=rr-2026-03-15-81, I attached pcap and nginx access logs. Also seeing 502 from ALB once in tcpdump before reconnect.
srini: quick guess: Cloudflare HTTP/2 connection coalescing + ALB idle probe causing a half-close that our runtime treats as completed chunk. Client sees no final delimiter and reconnects. Could lead to double-count if we record tokens on flush vs final close.
marta: important: is token billing triggered on chunk flush or on connection close in our pipeline? I thought we charge when send_token finishes.
ben: we charge as tokens stream out; but the client reconnecting and resuming a new request causes another set of tokens. The double-charge likely because initial attempt sent tokens but didn't include the final event that marks completion, so the app retried and consumed more tokens.
ops-bot: NOTE: ALB default idle timeout 60s. If Cloudflare holds upstream longer and ALB probes, half-close may happen. Envoy/nginx can also coalesce trailing small writes.
lina: From pcap: after ~37s of silence there is an RST from ALB toward origin, then client reconnect 1s later. Logs show upstream wrote last chunk but it was buffered at the proxy for 18ms then coalesced with a keepalive and dropped when probe hit.
ben: repro steps I can run: curl -i -N -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" https://staging.redwood.ai/v1/stream -d '{"prompt":"..."}'
ben: if I simulate Cloudflare by proxying via h2 and delayed small final chunk, I can reproduce the silent trailing gap.
srini: mitigation options:
- increase ALB idle timeout > 120s for affected services
- disable proxy buffering where possible (nginx: `proxy_buffering off; proxy_http_version 1.1; chunked_transfer_encoding on;`)
- add periodic small heartbeat SSE comment `: hb\n\n` every 15s so proxies don't consider stream idle
- server-side: only mark request complete after final sentinel event, avoid emitting billing/usage until that sentinel is persisted
marta: can we add idempotency marker for streaming so client reconnect can resume without new billing? That's medium effort.
lina: customer asked for temporary workaround. Recommend heartbeat + raising ALB idle timeout + Cloudflare "origin keepalive" config change. Provide exact curl repro and a minimal nginx config change.
ben: nginx snippet we tested:
```
location /v1/stream {
  proxy_pass http://origin;
  proxy_http_version 1.1;
  proxy_set_header Connection "";
  proxy_buffering off;
  proxy_set_header Host $host;
  chunked_transfer_encoding on;
}
```
ben: and client curl command to reproduce:
```
curl -v -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOK" -N https://edge.example.com/v1/stream -d '{"prompt":"x"}'
```
deploy-bot: deploy 2026-03-15T18:42:10 UTC: candidate runtime change to delay billing write until final sentinel persisted -> can be canaried on staging.
srini: action items:
- SRE: try heartbeat and nginx change on staging (ben)
- Product: advise customer on config + request quota refund for duplicated billing (marta)
- Runtime: add guard to not finalize charge until sentinel persisted or 10s idle after last token (queue PR) (deploy-bot assigned)
lina: customer accepted temp workaround, asked for ETA on fix and refund. I'll escalate billing and send follow-up. Thanks all :pray:
marta: I'm on billing, will patch invoice and follow up by EOD.
ben: last note: if you see partial JSON on client side, suggest client side to treat stream as idempotent until final `event: done` or similar marker, and avoid auto-retry within 3s.

Scope:
- New REST endpoints to create/update/delete a staged release manifest (weight schedules, shadow rules, health triggers).
- SDK client helpers (Python/TS) for declarative manifests and transactional apply semantics.
- Idempotency token semantics for CLI/SDK calls to prevent double-apply on retry.
- Fine-grained permission scopes: rollout.create, rollout.modify, rollout.rollback, rollout.shadow.
- Auto-rollback primitives driven by health hooks (latency p95, error-rate, quality regression signals) and pluggable alert sources.
- Audit logging and immutable changelog entries for compliance.
- Backward-compatible behavior for existing rollout routes.

API contract (high level):
- POST /v1/rollouts: create a staged-release resource with optional idempotency_token header. Body includes targets (model:version), schedule (steps with duration + weight), shadow_rules (percentage, routes), health_checks (metrics, threshold, window), and rollback_policy (immediate/cooldown/escalate).
- PATCH /v1/rollouts/:id/apply-step to manually advance/cancel a step (requires rollout.modify).
- POST /v1/rollouts/:id/rollback to trigger manual rollback (requires rollout.rollback).
- GET /v1/rollouts/:id/history returns immutable changelog and audit entries.
- POST /v1/rollouts/simulate for dry-run that returns estimated traffic distribution and expected safety checks.

SDK helpers:
- Context manager style API in Python: with rollouts.staged_release(manifest) as r: r.apply() -> returns operation handle with progress() and wait(timeout).
- Idempotent apply using client-side generated idempotency tokens; SDK reuses token across retries and surface partial-apply state for callers.
- Helper to attach health-hook listeners that can be wired to Redwood Console metrics or external monitoring webhooks.

Idempotency and concurrency model:
- Clients pass Idempotency-Token header on create/modify operations. Server ensures exactly-once semantics for token within 72h window.
- Concurrent patch semantics use optimistic locking with rollout.etag returned in GET; PATCH requires matching etag or explicit force flag (force requires higher permission scope).

Permissions and audit:
- New RBAC scopes defined and added to Console role mappings.
- Audit events emitted for create/modify/step-advance/rollback with actor, token, and diff.
- Sensitive fields (e.g., rollback to model versions with restricted access) require both rollout.modify and model.promote scope.

Safety & auto-rollback behaviour:
- Health checks evaluate metrics over sliding windows and can mark a step as unhealthy when thresholds breach for >2 consecutive windows.
- On unhealthy step, system can either pause rollout and alert, or automatically revert traffic back to previous stable version based on rollout.rollback_policy.
- Auto-rollback can be configured to be 'immediate' (roll back to last stable), 'gradual' (reduce weight back to zero over N minutes), or 'escalate' (pause + page on-call + wait for manual).

Testing and rollout plan:
- Unit tests for idempotency handling and etag concurrency.
- Integration tests against staging Console metrics pipeline to simulate p95 spikes and error rate regressions.
- End-to-end test that creates a rollout, advances steps, injects metric regression, and asserts auto-rollback and audit log entries.
- Feature flag gated behind rollout-api-v2 until we validate across customers.

Artifacts / Specs:
- Design doc: https://docs.redwood.internal/rollouts/staged-release-api (prototype spec and sequence diagrams)
- API proto: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rollouts/blob/main/api/v1/rollouts.proto
- Prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/inference/pull/12345

Acceptance criteria:
- API endpoints implemented and passing unit + integration tests in CI.
- SDK wrappers for Python + TypeScript published to internal package index and sample usage in quickstarts.
- RBAC scopes wired into Console roles and audit logs show a complete changelog for a sample rollout.
- Auto-rollback triggered in staging test harness and logs show correct revert sequence.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- Should idempotency tokens be scoped to org or global? (Current plan: org-scoped to avoid cross-org collisions.)
- How long to retain idempotency token history (72h current default vs 7d for increased safety)?
- Should we support multi-model rollouts (fan-out) in v1 or postpone to v2? (Plan: v1 single model target, v2 multi-target)

Migration notes:
- Existing rollout endpoints remain functional; new staged-release resource will coexist. Migration guide to map existing canary manifests to staged-release manifest will be published in Console docs.

description:
Goal: Ship a repeatable, low-friction controller that runs precision-directed canary and A/B experiments for model versions. The controller should handle experiment setup, traffic fractioning, sequential statistical checks (early-stop / sequential testing), shadow traffic mirroring, and automated rollback triggers. It must be usable from the Console and the API, support both Hosted and Dedicated deployments, and integrate with existing rollout primitives (canary windows, health checks, and model variant routing).

Motivation: Teams keep building ad-hoc scripts to split traffic and evaluate model variants, which results in inconsistent safety gates and long manual rollbacks. A standardized controller reduces incident risk, shortens experiment cycles, and centralizes observability and cost controls.

Scope: MVP covers: experiment definition API, Console experiment builder, traffic fraction scheduler (time-based + event-driven), sequential statistical tests (E-Stop criteria, false discovery control), automated rollback based on configurable metric thresholds, shadow routing for offline comparisons, metrics plumbing to dashboards, and audit logging for compliance.

[session-consistent-lifecycle-gatekeeper-for-experiments-and-canaries]
description:
Context and motivation:
This PR introduces the 'Lifecycle Gatekeeper', a coordinator that unifies canary deploys, A/B experiments, shadow seeding, and automated rollback workflows while preserving session consistency for stateful flows (chat sessions, transactions, etc.). Prod teams requested an out-of-the-box mechanism that: 1) keeps user sessions routed to stable variants during phased rollouts, 2) applies SLO/QA gates driven by telemetry windows, and 3) supports staged shadow traffic with backpressure and replay for testing.

Design summary:
- Lease-based session bonding: the gatekeeper issues short-lived leases tied to session identifiers (cookie/session_id). During ramp phases, existing sessions remain bound to the pre-rollout variant while new sessions may be admitted to target variants per policy. Leases survive process restarts and are persisted in the existing session-store abstraction.
- Telemetry-synced gates: gates evaluate sliding-window metrics (latency, error-rate, hallucination-rate) from the telemetry pipeline. Policies are declarative (promote_if, rollback_if) and accept multiple metric predicates with boolean logic.
- Shadow orchestration with backpressure: we added a staged shadow lane that applies probabilistic sampling, rate-limited replay of shadow responses to a dry-run eval pipeline, and adaptive backpressure if downstream evaluators fall behind. This reduces blast radius when enabling shadow seeding at scale.
- Auto-rollback and recovery: a configurable 'rollback_advisor' synthesizes gate signals and decides whether to auto-backout a roll based on confidence heuristics and trend detection. It supports dry-run recommendations and an automated rollback path if thresholds are exceeded.
- Compatibility & config: new rollout config keys are optional. The default behavior mirrors current rollouts unless 'session_consistency: true' is set. Admins can opt into 'lease_ttl', 'telemetry_window', 'shadow_sampling', and 'auto_rollback_policy'.

Why this is different from existing controllers:
Most previous controllers focused on traffic fractions or cohort anchoring without explicit session affinity or integrated shadow backpressure. This Gatekeeper ties session guarantees and telemetry-driven decisions together so customer-facing stateful features can safely rollout model changes.

Implementation notes (high level):
- services/orchestrator/gatekeeper.go: new coordinator, lease lifecycle, policy evaluator, rollback_advisor hooks.
- pkg/session/lease_store.go: session lease persistence with adapters for redis and the existing postgres-backed session table.
- pkg/telemetry/gates.go: predicate compiler and sliding window aggregator (uses existing meter ingestion topics).
- controllers/rollout/crd.yml: schema updates for the optional lifecycle fields (validated by the CRD conversion webhook).
- e2e tests: integration tests simulate 10k sessions with a staged ramp and assert session stickiness, correct gate behavior, and rollback paths.

Rollout plan:
- Canary in staging using a Director-managed deployment (dry-run mode) for 48h.
- Gradual production ramp: enable session_consistency for a single low-traffic tenant; observe telemetry and smoke tests for 72h.
- If stable, flip default flag for new rollouts. A migration job exists to backfill leases for long-lived sessions if teams choose to opt-in.

Checklist (completed):
- [x] Design doc reviewed by product and SRE (ENG-4210).
- [x] Unit and integration tests added.
- [x] Backwards-compatible config and CRD migration path.
- [x] Basic load-tested shadow backpressure under 2x normal traffic.
- [x] Canary in staging performed.

Open items (follow-ups):
- Add quantile-aware predicates to telemetry gates (follow-up ticket assigned).
- UI for rollout visualization (PM scope).

See the commit list below for granular changes and PR-level squashed commit content.

[Rollout Ethos: traffic steward and policy expression for safe canary strategies]
description:
Implement a new 'traffic steward' component and a lightweight policy expression language to unify canary/A-B/shadow rollout specs across Redwood runtimes. The steward compiles high-level rollout intents (traffic splits, step schedules, cohort classifiers) into enforcement artifacts consumed by the serving control plane and the console. Goals: reduce operator errors in rollout configuration, make guardrails declarative and testable, and enable automatic rollback when composite health predicates fail.

background:
Current canary configuration is scattered across console UI forms, runtime YAMLs, and internal defaults. This leads to divergent interpretations between Hosted and Dedicated runs and frequent human errors (forgotten abort thresholds, inconsistent step durations). We need a canonical, minimal surface for specifying: 1) traffic schedule (percent over time or steps); 2) health signals and predicates (latency p99, error-rate, quality regressions from eval set); 3) cohort scoping (users, routes, regions); 4) rollback/backoff policies. The steward will centralize validation, simulation, and compile targets for runtime executors.

acceptance_criteria:
1) Policy expression language (PEL) v0 implemented with support for: percent schedules (step and linear), time windows, cohort selectors, and basic boolean health predicates
2) Traffic steward service exposes REST endpoints: validatePolicy, simulatePolicy, compilePolicy
3) Controller can consume compiled artifacts and execute staged traffic shifts against a canary variant with automatic pause/rollback when predicates cross thresholds
4) Console shows simulation visualizations and highlights potential guardrail violations before apply
5) Integration tests cover at least: schedule edge cases, simultaneous multiple cohort deployments, and predicate-triggered rollback
6) Documentation and quickstart (examples for A/B, shadow + canary) published in Confluence and linked in PR

tasks:
Draft PEL grammar and examples (Aisha)
Implement validation + simulation API (Marco)
Integrate compile output with runtime admission controller (runtime team)
Console: add policy editor + simulation chart (DX team)
End-to-end test harness that replays synthetic traffic and health metrics (QA)
Security review for policy evaluation sandboxing (Security)
Migration guide for existing canaries to PEL (PM)

technical_notes:
PEL is intentionally small — expressions compile to a JSON artifact containing: ordered steps (percent, duration), cohort selectors (routeRegex, header, region), signals (metric source, aggregation, threshold) and actions (continue, pause, rollback, notify). Use WASM sandbox for evaluation in the console and a trimmed interpreter in the runtime agent to avoid cross-language runtime dependencies. Simulation will run historical telemetry through compiled guardrail predicates to estimate false positive/negative rollback likelihood.

risks:
Overly expressive PEL increases surface area for bugs and security issues when evaluating customer-provided predicates. Runtime evaluation must be deterministic and bounded. Also, migrating existing ad-hoc rollouts to PEL may require one-off migrations for percent calculations historically expressed in console. Need migration tooling and default translation heuristics.

migration_plan:
Phase 1: opt-in PEL editor and simulation in Console; Phase 2: compile-only mode where runtime accepts compiled artifacts but console still permits legacy forms; Phase 3: default creation uses PEL; provide autorewrite tool that converts 80% of existing policies to PEL format and flags complex ones for manual review.

observability:
Add rollout-trace spans and events: policy_id, step_index, applied_percent, signal_values, action_taken. Expose rollout SLO dashboard and per-policy telemetry for cadence analysis. Add an alert when simulated rollback probability exceeds 5% for production traffic.

test_plan:
Unit tests for PEL parser and compiler; fuzzing for predicate expressions; integration smoke that runs a canary in a staging cluster and asserts expected pause/rollback behavior when we inject latency/error signals; load test the steward APIs at 1000 validates/sec to ensure performance.

qa_notes:
QA to create scenarios: 1) health metric flapping (should backoff, not immediate rollback), 2) cohort overlap (ensure crowding doesn't overshoot percent), 3) shadow+canary combo where shadow quality alerts should not trigger rollback but should surface in console.

[Signalboard: per-route rollout dashboard for canary, A/B, shadow and auto-rollback signals]
description:
Problem: Engineering and SRE teams running model rollouts (canaries, A/B tests, shadow traffic) lack a single Console view that correlates per-route traffic splits, signal-level metrics (latency, error rate, token cost, quality metrics), trace drilldowns, and whether an auto-rollback policy would have fired. Current observability is fragmented across per-model dashboards, tracing, and ad-hoc spreadsheets, which slows decisions and increases risk for incorrect rollouts.

Why it matters: Faster, confident rollouts reduce incident surface area and time-to-value for new model versions. Teams need a compact way to compare live cohorts, inspect failing requests, and understand economic impact (tokens/cost) alongside quality regressions so they can decide to promote, pause, or trigger an automatic rollback.

proposal:
Build a Console feature called 'Signalboard' that lives on a per-route rollout page and provides: 
- Unified time-series panel with overlays for traffic splits (canary percentage, A/B buckets, shadow on/off).
- Key metric tiles (p50/p95 latency, error rate, token cost per 1k tokens, model quality score tied to eval prompt sets) for each cohort.
- Cohort comparison strip: percentage delta and statistically-significant flag for each metric.
- Request trace list filtered to cohort with one-click link into full tracing UI and reproduction payload.
- Shadow traffic comparator: show distribution of outputs (token length, top tokens, embedding similarity) between live and shadowed model for sampled requests.
- Auto-rollback simulator & timeline: preview whether current rollback rules would have triggered historically and an ability to run the simulator over a selected time-range.
- Exportable snapshot and annotation capability for post-mortem and approvals.

Implementation notes: UI implemented as a Console route component; backend will aggregate per-route metrics from telemetry pipelines and reuse existing trace links. Add lightweight statistical engine in backend to compute significance and historical rollback simulation. Integrate with rollout control API to surface current policies.

scope:
MVP: Signalboard panel embedded in existing rollout detail page; metric tiles for latency/errors/cost; cohort comparison deltas with significance; trace links; rollback simulator run-on-demand. Exclude full export workflow and rich shadow diff visualizations in MVP.

Out-of-scope for MVP: automated remediation UI to edit rollback rules inline, full export/approval workflow, and long-term retention UI changes.

acceptance_criteria:
Signalboard is accessible from rollout detail page for all rollout types (canary, A/B, shadow)
Time-series panel displays traffic split overlays and selectable cohorts for the chosen time range
Metric tiles surface p50/p95 latency, error rate, and token cost per 1k tokens for each cohort
Cohort comparison shows percent delta and a simple statistical-significance flag (p < 0.05) for each metric
Clicking a cohort item opens a paginated list of sampled requests with a link to the trace view
Rollback simulator can run over a historical window and indicates whether the configured rollback rules would have fired
End-to-end latency for dashboard queries is <3s for 7-day windows at production traffic levels (non-blocking; SLO for iteration 2 if not met in MVP)
