[Safety gates for multi-model orchestration — scratchpad (WIP)]
Purpose:
This is a working scratchpad for defining safety gates, instrumentation, and playbook steps specific to multi-model orchestration rollouts (e.g., routing different model families/variants per traffic slice, ensemble/reranker handoffs, and conditional fallbacks). Focus is operational: how to safely expose new model variants while preserving availability, latency targets, cost envelopes, and quality.

Audience: product owners, rollout stewards, SRE, serving-runtime, applied-ml, solutions engineering.

Scope (what this doc covers):
- Canary and A/B design where the route is model-dependent (not just feature flag).
- Multi-variant experiments (float vs quantized, small vs large model, reranker on/off).
- Observability hooks required to detect model-specific drift or regressions.
- Automated vs manual gates and escalation path.

Non-goals:
- Full statistical primer on A/B math (see stats-team playbook).
- Detailed infra runbook for provisioning GPUs (handled by infra team).

High-level goals for a safe multi-model rollout:
- Catch behavioral regressions early (quality drop, hallucination patterns).
- Preserve latency SLOs and keep cost within budgeted per-request unit economics.
- Provide deterministic, auditable rollback paths per cohort/route.
- Ensure consistent user experience despite model heterogeneity.

Key failure modes we need to guard for (notes):
- Tokenization/normalization mismatch causing truncated outputs or mismatched alt text.
- Reranker/ensemble mismatch: downstream component assumes a distribution that the new model breaks.
- KV-cache incompatibility across model families causing cold-slow latency spikes.
- Undetected semantic regressions that don't show up in simple BLEU-like metrics.
- Cost spikes due to an unintended routing loop or larger model being selected for bulk traffic.

Proposed safety gates (ordered):
1) Preflight (pre-canary)
   - Model card + checklist: known failure modes, dataset provenance, tokenizer, max-seq heuristics.
   - Offline eval against canonical prompt suite (golden prompts): P95 quality metrics, regression delta < X% (TBD).
   - Throughput smoke test on staging with simulated traffic (latency p95, memory, OOM checks).
   - Approval from applied-ml + serving-runtime.

2) Canary activation (micro-slices)
   - Microcohort selection: prefer stable internal traffic or invited testers.
   - Start at 0.5% of the selected slice (or fixed qps floor) for 6–12 hours.
   - Observability checklist running continuously: telemetry below.
   - If any hard-failure (see hard thresholds) -> immediate auto-fallback to baseline.

3) Progressive ramp (guarded)
   - Ramp steps: 0.5% -> 2% -> 10% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% (example; adjust per product).
   - Hold windows at each step (6–24 hours depending on metric sensitivity).
   - At each hold evaluate both safety and business metrics.

4) Post-activation monitoring and bake period
   - Longer term drift checks (7-day rolling) and sampling for human review.

Observability (what we measure) — must be model-aware:
- Latency: P50/P95/P99 for route+model, cold vs warm (cache hit vs miss).
- Error rates: HTTP 5xx, inference failures, timeouts.
- Resource signals: GPU memory pressure, encoder/decoder stall metrics, OOM frequency.
- Quality: evaluation-set score deltas (nlg-metric, preferred-quality-metric), classification/regression accuracy for tasks with ground-truth.
- Behavioral signals: hallucination proxy (contradiction detection), repetition, user fallback rate (users hitting 'regenerate' or undo).
- Cost per request / per token: monitor burn-rate vs expected.
- Downstream impact: reranker score distribution shift, click-through delta, conversion delta (product metric dependent).

Suggested hard thresholds (examples, tune per-product):
- Latency P95 increases > 40% over baseline for the route+model -> rollback.
- Error rate increase (5xx + inference-exception) > 0.5 percentage points absolute -> rollback.
- Quality score regression on golden set > 5% relative -> hold & manual review.
- Cost per active user increases > 25% without measurable quality gain -> pause ramp and cost-investigation.

Composite pass/fail rule: define a weighted score where higher-severity signals (serviceability) are top priority; if any top-tier threshold violated -> auto-fallback. Middle-tier issues trigger human-in-loop review.

A/B testing specifics when routing is model-based:
- Randomization: assign on user-id hash + route salt to ensure stability across repeated sessions.
- Exposure unit: choose user-level exposure (recommended) to avoid contamination when model stateful (chat history).
- Dedupe: ensure experiments respect dedup across devices if user_id is known.
- Sequential testing: apply sequential p-value correction or predefine stopping rules to avoid peeking.
- Bucketing rules must include a model-compatibility layer: if a user has features incompatible with new model variant, exclude or route to baseline.

Multi-model orchestration nuances (important):
- Tokenizer compatibility: enforce canonical token mapping or ensure route translates properly.
- KV cache affinity: if two model variants share cache keyspace, avoid routing split that would thrash cache (prefer sticky routing).
- Fallback mapping: ensure fallback model is compatible with downstream (e.g., if new model produces structured json, fallback must have same shape).
- Ensemble: if scoring model changes distribution, retrain downstream calibrator during canary window.
- Model lineage tagging: every inference must carry model-version, quantization, and kernel metadata for triage.

Instrumentation and sample capture:
- Capture N random examples per minute + all failed traces for first 24h of ramp.
- Flagged-sample queue for human review (ops + applied-ml).
- Golden prompt sweep nightly for first 7 days post full rollout.
- Annotated replay environment for reproducible reruns (include deterministic seeds).

Alerts and Pager integration (ops-friendly):
- Severity-1 alert: service-impacting (mass OOMs, 5xx spike > threshold, auto-fallback triggered) -> oncall page + product-steward notify.
- Severity-2 alert: quality regression on golden set exceeding warning threshold -> slack channel, product review.
- Include runbook links in alert payload and model metadata.

Escalation and rollback playbook (quick steps):
1) Confirm signal: look at model-tagged telemetry & sample captures.
2) If S1 -> trigger immediate routing rule to baseline with canary traffic mapping rollback API (automated).
3) Notify stakeholders (steward + ML owner + SRE).
4) Postmortem: short RCA within 24h, deeper root cause within 5 working days.
5) Remediation options: patch model, adjust tokenization, change routing, or retract feature.

Roles and responsibilities (proposed):
- Rollout steward (owner of activation): coordinates ramp, signs off holds.
- ML owner: accountable for model quality and fixes.
- Serving-runtime / SRE: responsible for latency/availability gates and rollback hooks.
- Product PM: owns downstream business metric evaluation and release decision.
- Observability lead: ensures dashboards and SLOs are configured pre-canary.

Operational checklist (quick):
- [ ] Model card + dataset provenance attached to model artifact.
- [ ] Offline golden-suite regression < threshold.
- [ ] Staging smoke passed (latency + memory).
- [ ] Dashboards: route+model time-series + sample capture visible.
- [ ] Alerts configured with runbook links.
- [ ] Stakeholders notified of ramp schedule and escalation path.
- [ ] Cost guardrail configured for auto-pause.

Example ramp timeline (concrete numbers for a SaaS chat route):
- T0 (00:00): 0.5% invited testers, 12h hold.
- T1 (12:00): 2% internal users, 12h hold.
- T2 (24:00): 10% random U.S. geo, 24h hold + quality sweep.
- T3 (48:00): 25% + run conversion metric test for 72h.
- T4 (120:00): 50% hold 72h.
- T5 (192:00): 100% if all gates green.

Open questions & TODOs (investigate before next iteration):
- What is the canonical golden-suite for reranker-driven flows? (Mateo to draft list)
- How to represent composite score weighting in the console UI so non-stat folks can interpret (Anika + Observability)
- Define cost-pause vs cost-rollback boundaries (need input from finance).
- Decide default microcohort size for models with stateful session histories.
- Integration test for tokenizer mismatch detection (can we detect automatically?).

Notes to self / friction points we've seen in past rolls:
- When we split routing by model_id only, downstream DB joins that expect certain text shape blow up. Need schema compatibility validation.
- Small traffic (0.5%) sometimes lacks statistical power to detect subtle quality regressions; supplement with targeted golden prompts.
- Auto-fallbacks must not cascade: ensure single-rollout flip doesn't trigger unrelated rollouts.

Reference quick links (local):
- Confluence: Model-Orchestration-Playbook
- Stats primer: "Sequential testing for product experiments"
- Infra PR: github.com/redwood/infra/pull/212

If you are reading this and want to help: add concrete metric thresholds for your product route — put numbers under the "hard thresholds" section and tag me.

[Tool-call diff + schema-drift detector for safe model rollouts]
description:
Background: As we increase use of structured outputs and function/tool-calling across customer workloads, even small changes in model behavior can break downstream tooling. Existing rollout controls focus on latency/error rates and token-level diffs; we need an automated detector that verifies compatibility of structured outputs and function calls during canary/A-B/shadow rollouts and triggers safe fallback/auto-rollback when regressions are detected.

Goal: Implement a runtime-compatible tooling layer that: 1) validates model responses against a supplied JSON schema and function-call contract, 2) computes lightweight function-call diffs and a schema-drift score, 3) surfaces per-route compatibility metrics in the Console, and 4) plugs into existing rollout policies (canary/A-B/shadow) to pause or rollback when thresholds are exceeded.

Scope (this ticket):
- Design and implement an in-path "compatibility detector" that can run in parallel with normal inference (shadow mode) and as a gating check in canaries.
- Provide a compact, time-bounded schema validator optimized for common patterns (nullable fields, unions, typed arrays) with performance budgets to avoid SLO impact.
- Implement a function-call diff estimator: compares callee name, argument keys, basic argument types, and presence/absence of optional arguments; computes a numeric compatibility score.
- Expose metrics and alerts to Console rollouts: compatibility_score, schema_errors_pct, function_diff_rate, and per-field error examples.
- Hook detector outputs into rollout policies: configurable thresholds for pause/rollback, and an automatic rollback runbook.

Out of scope for this ticket: full semantic equivalence checks, heavy-weight AST diffs of nested arguments, and UI polish beyond basic Console widgets.


acceptance_criteria:
Detector runs in shadow mode during a rollout and produces compatibility metrics for every request without increasing p99 latency by >10% on the canary path
Schema validator flags structural violations and returns machine-readable error types (missing_field, type_mismatch, extra_field)
Function-call diff calculates a normalized score in [0,100] and flags dropped/renamed function calls and redacted argument changes
Console shows per-route compatibility_score and an anomaly timeline; alerts are triggered when schema_errors_pct > 2% or function_diff_rate > 5% over a 5-minute window
Automated rollback is triggered when configured thresholds hit for two consecutive evaluation windows and the rollback action is recorded in rollout audit logs
Unit and integration tests cover the validator and diff logic; a canary runbook doc is added and linked

steps:
Design schema validator API and lightweight error taxonomy (Sofia, 2025-02-13)
Prototype function-call diff algorithm and benchmark using historic function-call logs (Alejandro, 2025-02-14)
Add detector hook into runtime request path in shadow mode; ensure non-blocking execution and bounded CPU usage (ENG runtime team)
Instrument metrics (promcounter/gauge) for compatibility_score, schema_errors_pct, function_diff_rate
Integrate metrics into Console rollouts: widget + alerting config (Console team)
Add rollout policy configuration options (pause_thresholds and auto_rollback) and implement state machine transition
Run staged canary against internal staging models and record false positive rate; tune thresholds
Documentation: runbook, examples for customers to attach schemas and function contracts

rollout_policy_proposal:
Default: run detector in shadow for initial 10% traffic for 24h; if schema_errors_pct < 0.5% and function_diff_rate < 1% promote to 50% traffic. Auto-rollback: pause + evaluate if schema_errors_pct > 2% or function_diff_rate > 5% for 5m window twice. Allow per-customer overrides and a 'lenient' mode that only alerts.

[HTTP/3 (QUIC) artifact downloads stall due to MSS clamping by customer WAN optimizer on private deployment]
description:
Issue summary: Customers report large model artifact downloads (several MBs) initiated from private deployment nodes frequently hang during the HTTP/3 (QUIC) handshake or immediately after transfer start. Smaller artifacts succeed; downloads over ~1200-1400 bytes commonly stall and eventually time out.

Impact: Model pulls for new serving nodes and periodic artifact refreshes fail, causing increased cold-start times and degraded scaling for NimbleAnalytics' private deployment. Customer reports multiple failed rollouts and a production impact on inference availability.

Environment: Private deployment connected to Redwood via VPCE and a customer-managed WAN optimizer appliance for egress. Client: node-exporter on private serving nodes using our artifact fetcher (default HTTP/3 where available). Region: us-west-2 (customer-controlled egress).

Steps to reproduce:
1) Trigger model rollout on private serving pool (pull model artifact ~10MB).
2) Observe artifact fetch attempt in agent logs; client negotiates HTTP/3 with Redwood S3-presigned endpoint.
3) Transfer stalls shortly after start; repeated retries eventually fall back to HTTP/1.1 or time out depending on retry window.

Observed logs/traces:
- Agent logs: "download: http3_stream stalled after 0x1a0 bytes, retrying"
- h3 / quicserver logs: repeated PTOs (probe timeouts) and early connection closure with ERROR_TRANSPORT(0x1)
- tcpdump from customer edge (captured): multiple UDP Initial packets with QUIC token, followed by ICMP "Fragmentation needed" not seen in path; customer-managed WAN optimizer shows MSS rewrite to 1200 bytes and strips ICMP type 3 messages.
- VPC Flow Logs: no obvious packet loss on underlying ENIs; retransmits seen at optimizer interface.

Initial hypothesis: Customer WAN optimizer or edge middlebox is clamping MSS / rewriting TCP/UDP segmentation parameters and also suppressing ICMP PMTU messages. QUIC relies on PMTU discovery and large initial UDP frames — when PMTU discovery is blocked and MSS/MSS-clamping reduces allowable payloads but the optimizer does not properly re-segment or generate CLAMP-correct behavior for UDP/QUIC, QUIC initial packets are dropped or cause PTOs leading to stalls. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 (TCP) fallback works more often because TCP path can negotiate smaller MSS or be retransmitted in a way the appliance handles.

Requested from customer: packet capture (pcap) at WAN optimizer ingress/egress with timestamps, configuration snippet showing MSS/MTU rewrite rules, and confirmation on whether ICMP Type 3 (Fragmentation Needed) is blocked or dropped.

2026-03-09 15:30 - SRE (Miguel Ramirez): Reviewing pcap: QUIC Initial packets sent with ~1350-1400B UDP payloads; appliance rewrites/forwards UDP but drops/doesn't forward subsequent large packets. No ICMP Type 3 seen leaving optimizer toward Redwood. Hypothesis: MSS/MTU clamp + ICMP suppression causing PMTU blackhole for QUIC.
2026-03-09 17:04 - Support (Aisha): As a near-term workaround, we can force artifact fetches to use HTTP/1.1 for your private pool (will increase latency). Would you like us to enable HTTP/1.1 fallback on your deployment while you work with the optimizer vendor?
2026-03-09 18:20 - Customer: Please enable HTTP/1.1 fallback for the rollout window. We'll engage our network team and vendor to test disabling MSS clamping / allowing ICMP.

investigation:
- Packet-level findings: Initial QUIC Initial packets from our edge to client show client sends ACKs for small amounts then stalls. The optimizer rewrites MSS to 1200 and appears to fragment or drop large UDP datagrams. No ICMP Fragmentation Needed messages are forwarded from inside customer network to Redwood; vendor config shows 'suppress-pmtu-icmp true'.
- Reproduction on support side: In a lab with a simulated optimizer set to clamp MTU to 1200 and suppress ICMP, HTTP/3 downloads fail to complete for large payloads while HTTP/1.1 completes after retransmit.
- Instrumentation: Added additional retry telemetry in artifact fetcher to record protocol used and time to fallback; early telemetry shows fallback occurs after multiple PTOs (~6s).
- Short-term mitigation validated: Forcing HTTP/1.1 path for artifact fetch increases success rate to ~99% in customer topology.

resolution:
- Workaround applied: Support enabled HTTP/1.1-first artifact fetch policy for NimbleAnalytics' private serving pool to avoid QUIC path; this reduces stalls during rollouts (applied 2026-03-09 20:15).
- Permanent fix recommended for customer: disable MSS clamping for traffic toward Redwood endpoints and allow ICMP Type 3 (Fragmentation Needed) to pass, or configure optimizer to properly re-segment UDP/QUIC flows.
- Product follow-up actions: 1) Add a config knob to force artifact fetcher to use TCP-only for private deployments as an operator-level toggle (tracked in GH PR referenced). 2) Add detection telemetry that flags likely PMTU/ICMP suppression when QUIC PTOs spike during artifact downloads.
- Customer validation: NimbleAnalytics network team scheduled vendor change for 2026-03-11 to allow ICMP and disable MSS clamp; tentative follow-up planned after vendor test.
- Status: Workaround in place; awaiting customer network changes to restore HTTP/3 native path.

[Regional tapered launch and A/B sentinel notes (WIP)]
Purpose:
This doc captures a lightweight operational pattern we want to experiment with for region-first launches and A/B experiments where capacity and user signal lag differ across geographies. The idea: a tapered regional activation combined with a small set of instrumented "sentinel" cohorts that reveal early quality/cost regressions before broad exposure.

High-level concept (one-liner):
- Tapered launch: gradually increase exposure per-region on a half-life schedule (traffic doubles every N hours until target).
- Sentinels: small, persistent cohorts (1–3% of region traffic) routed to an instrumented fork of the model+routing stack containing extra telemetry and tighter fallbacks. Sentinels act as the early-warning system for each deployment wave.

Why this (why different):
- Regional heterogeneity: latency, user intent, and content distribution vary by region; a global canary can miss region-specific failure modes.
- Cost-aware cadence: avoid heavy early exposure in expensive regions while still surfacing quality drift.
- Faster rollback decisions: sentinel metrics are tuned for sensitivity (high recall) so we catch regressions with minimal user impact.

Scope / when to use:
- New model variants, quantized builds, or routing changes with potential regional performance regressions.
- Multi-model experiments (A/B of model families) where traffic shaping needs to respect cost and capacity quotas per region.
- Not recommended for purely UI experiments or business-metric-only A/Bs.

Principles:
- Minimal blast radius: start small, maintain an escape hatch per-region.
- Observability-first: sentinels must expose granular prompt-level and token-level signals (latency hist, token-cost, model-confidence proxies).
- Simplicity of automation: automation should be able to pause/scale back based on a single aggregated stability score.
- Human-in-the-loop for ambiguous alerts: automatic halt for clear breaches, manual review for borderline cases.

Cohort definitions:
- Sentinel cohort (S): 0.5%–3% of region traffic. Instrumented with additional logging, golden prompt probes, and strict timeout policies.
- Pilot cohort (P): next 5% of region traffic after sentinels. Production routing but with daily manual check-ins.
- Warm cohort (W): intermediate ramp group (10%–25%) to validate scale.
- Open cohort (O): remaining traffic.

Taper schedule (example):
- Day 0: S at 0.5%
- +6 hours: evaluate signals; if green, S -> 2% and open P at 3%
- Every 12 hours: double exposure for P/W until reach target or hit a guardrail
- Full open only after 72 hours of green signals across sentinels and pilot cohort

Telemetry & sentinel signals (stability score inputs):
- Latency p95 and 99 (region-specific baselines)
- Token-cost per request (avg/95th)
- Regression probes: a small set (50–200) of golden prompts with expected ranges (tokens, quality rubric)
- Safety flags: content-moderation hit rate, hallucination proxy (e.g., contradiction detector)
- Business signals: conversion delta (if available quickly), feature-specific error rates
- User experience signals: retry rate, abandonment (client-side)

Scoring model (sketch):
- Each signal normalized to region baseline; weighted sum -> StabilityScore in [0..100].
- Example weights: latency_p99 25, token_cost95 15, probe_quality 30, safety 20, retry_rate 10.
- Thresholds: <60 -> immediate rollback; 60–75 -> pause ramp + human review; >75 -> continue ramp

Automated actions mapped to score ranges:
- Score < 60: automatic traffic reweight to fallback model by region + page the rollout-steward and oncall
- Score 60–75: pause further ramp, start 2-hour observation window, trigger async quality audits
- Score > 75: continue as scheduled, post an automated progress note in #rollout-ops

Fallback ladder (per-region):
1) Soft fallback: swap to cheaper/older variant for non-critical routes (automatic)
2) Hard fallback: route sentinel + pilot cohorts to stable model globally (manual if ambiguous)
3) Quarantine: shrink to sentinels-only while creating hotfix patch

Capacity & quota guardrails:
- Reserve 10% warm capacity for rapid rollbacks in each region to avoid cascading throttles.
- Cost cap per-region per-day that, when breached, triggers a throttle on non-sentinel traffic.

Pre-launch checklist (operational):
- Confirm sentinel instrumentation shows raw prompt/response payloads and golden-probe results (Samir)
- Create rolling chartboards for each region with StabilityScore and raw signals (Riley)
- Coordinate time windows with infra (warm-up periods for GPUs)
- Post-runbook and oncall rota for rollout-steward & SRE
- Add experiment to experiment ledger (OPT-4821) and tag related PRs

Simulation plan (small lab before real user exposure):
- Use rollout-sim repo to replay a 24h snippet of region traffic (synthetic distributions) -> run hack: PR 46 combines noise injections and latency spikes.
- Inject a 5% hallucination pattern and ensure sentinel probe precision catches it within 6 hours
- Validate automatic reweight logic in sandbox with fake PagerDuty endpoint

Measurement windows & cadence:
- Real-time: 1m fresh metrics for latency, token-cost, safety flags
- Short-term: 6h evaluation window (post-change) for initial decision
- Medium-term: 72h stabilization window before full open
- Postmortem: 7-day retrospective with regression corpora attached

Human roles & responsibilities:
- Rollout steward (product): owns hypothesis, communication, and final go/no-go
- Observability lead (SRE/observability): ensures dashboards, alerts, and probes are green
- Experiment owner (ML/product): triage quality heuristics and golden-probe failures
- Oncall (SRE): executes automated rollback or manual fallback if escalation occurs

Comms templates (quick):
- Automated progress note: "[REGION] +4h: StabilityScore 82; ramp to next stage scheduled at T+8h unless breached."
- Incident: "[REGION] ABORT: StabilityScore 52; swapped to fallback variant; paging @oncall; retrospective scheduled."

Open questions / unknowns:
- Golden probe design: how to craft probes that are representative across languages and locales without biasing model tuning?
- How to tune weights of the StabilityScore for different product surfaces (conversation vs. completion vs. rerank)?
- What is the minimal sentinel size in low-traffic regions to maintain statistical power?

Next steps / action items:
- (Samir) Draft golden-probe list for APAC and LATAM by 2024-11-12
- (Riley) Wire up a per-region StabilityScore chartboard prototype in Grafana sandbox by 2024-11-18
- (Elena) Open experiment ledger entry and tag rollout-sim PRs (OPT-4821) by 2024-11-10
- (Priya) Coordinate infra warm capacity reservation with platform-engineering (internal ticket: INF-2072)

Notes to self / operational reminders (informal):
- Lean towards higher sentinel sensitivity (more false positives) early in adoption; we can tune down noise after a few runs.
- Watch for cohort starvation: if sentinels get insufficient traffic, create synthetic probe cadence to preserve signal.
- Document any bespoke regional configs (timeouts, quantization profiles) in the experiment ledger.

Appendix (short templates):
- Experiment ledger fields we use: hypothesis, region list, sentinel_size, ramp_schedule, fallback_ladder, StabilityScore_weights, golden_probes, linked_PRs, owners
- Quick rollback command (internal): curl -X POST https://internal-api/rollouts/{region}/reweight -d '{"target":"fallback","pct":100,"reason":"stability_score<60"}'

If this looks reasonable we'll try a single-region taper in EU-west first (low cost, high traffic) and iterate based on simulation outcomes.

References / links:
- OPT-4821 (experiment ledger stub)
- Confluence: REGIONAL-TAPERED-LAUNCH-1298 (design notes)
- rollout-sim PR: github.com/redwood-inference/rollout-sim/pull/46

[Homepage hero: technical assurances and fallback experiments]
OVERVIEW:\nThis is a compact messaging brief + experiment plan for adding technical reassurance and graceful-degradation/fallback language to the homepage hero and product blurbs. Goal is to test whether explicit operational assurances (latency SLOs, fallback model paths, private deployment options) improve trial conversion for engineering buyers without alienating product/PM audiences who prioritize simplicity.\n\nGOALS (primary):\n- Increase API trial activation rate for teams evaluating production inference (measured as signups that test inference within 7 days).\n- Reduce mid-funnel bounce on product pages (time on page and click-to-try).\n- Collect qualitative feedback from pilot accounts on whether fallback assurances are decision-relevant.\n\nTARGET AUDIENCES (primary to secondary):\n- Platform/ML engineers evaluating inference runtime (care about latency, determinism, model controls).\n- Backend engineers / infra leads (care about SLA, isolation, VPC).\n- Product engineers / PMs (care about time-to-value and cost predictability).\n- CTO/VP Eng (enterprise purchase triggers: compliance, auditability).\n\nPRINCIPAL MESSAGE PILLARS (to weave into hero and supporting copy):\n1) Predictable performance: \"Engineered for production latency and throughput — configurable SLOs and dedicated capacity.\"\n2) Cost control: \"Options to optimize per-token unit economics with batching, quantization, and routing policies.\"\n3) Reliability & graceful degradation: \"Automated fallbacks and model routing keep apps online under load.\"\n4) Deployment flexibility: \"Hosted, reserved dedicated pools, or private VPC/on-prem with customer key control.\"\n5) Observability: \"Token-level breakdowns, per-route tracing, and regression alerts.\"\n\nWHY THIS IS DIFFERENT:\n- Existing homepage variants focus heavily on speed/cost/value hooks. We hypothesize a sizable segment of engineering evaluators drop out because they don't see operational guarantees up front. Adding compact, explicit assurances (one-liners + micro bullets) may bridge that gap without adding complexity.\n\nHERO COPY VARIANTS (3 short experiments)\nVariant A — \"Production-first inference. Ship faster, keep costs down.\"\n- Subhead: \"Predictable latency and cost controls for teams running LLMs in production. Hosted, dedicated, or private.\"\n- Micro-CTA: \"Start a free inference test\"\n- Technical micro-strip under CTA (smaller font, one line): \"SLOs, model fallbacks, and per-token tracing out of the box.\"\n\nVariant B — \"Keep your app online when traffic spikes.\"\n- Subhead: \"Automatic model routing + dedicated pools ensure low latency and smooth degradation.\"\n- Micro-CTA: \"Run a synthetic load\"\n- Technical micro-strip: \"Fallbacks to compatible variants, region-aware routing, and burst capacity.\"\n\nVariant C — \"Control cost, control quality, control deployment.\"\n- Subhead: \"Transparent unit economics + model governance for production teams.\"\n- Micro-CTA: \"See a cost demo\"\n- Technical micro-strip: \"Batching, KV caching, quantization suggestions, and private deployment options.\"\n\nSUPPORTING HERO ELEMENT (design notes):\n- Include a compact badge row under the hero with 3 short chips (Latency SLOs • Dedicated GPU pools • Private VPC). Each chip opens a micro-modal with 1–2 sentences and a link to a product page.\n- Keep hero visual minimal — use a small sequence diagram that shows request routing -> runtime -> fallback. Avoid heavy product screenshots in test.\n\nPRODUCT PAGE SNIPPETS (short blocks for landing page sections)\nRedwood Hosted (one-liner + 3 bullets):\n- One-liner: \"Get started in minutes with curated models and transparent performance profiles.\"\n- Bullets: \"Streaming + function calling, built-in rate limiting, usage analytics.\"\n\nRedwood Dedicated (one-liner + 3 bullets):\n- One-liner: \"Reserved GPU pools for predictable throughput and isolation.\"\n- Bullets: \"SLA-backed latency targets, configurable autoscaling, burst capacity.\"\n\nRedwood Private (one-liner + 3 bullets):\n- One-liner: \"Bring inference into your VPC or on-prem with audit logs and KMS/HSM integrations.\"\n- Bullets: \"Customer-managed keys, private control plane, air-gapped packaging available.\"\n\nTECHNICAL REASSURANCE BLOCK (short, scannable)\n- Latency SLOs: \"Pick a 99th percentile latency SLO per-route; we surface violations to tracing and alerting.\"\n- Graceful degradation: \"Automatic fallback to verified compatible model variants when capacity or latency constraints occur.\"\n- Responsible default policies: \"Rate limits, adaptive batching, and token-level cost visibility enabled by default for new accounts.\"\n- Security & governance: \"Encryption at rest/in transit, KMS/HSM support, audit logs, and SOC-ready controls for Private deployments.\"\n- Model provenance: \"Model catalog entries include tokenizer, quantization profile, and performance trace for common request shapes.\"\n\nCOMPETITIVE NOTES (quick mental model for copy and objection handling)\n- Generic cloud vendors (managed endpoints): often simple to start but lack production tooling for cost/latency controls. This document is a compact, sales-facing playbook for engaging risk-sensitive prospects (finance, healthcare, regulated SaaS) who require an evidence-led pilot and clear pricing guardrails. - Objective: Convert a 4–8 week pilot into a committed deployment (Dedicated or Private) by demonstrating safety, latency, cost predictability, and compliance controls.
- Key buyer personas: Platform/infra engineers, Head of ML, Security/Privacy Officer, Health IT/Integrations, Procurement.

-----------------------

Pilot scope: recommended configuration

  - Latency: P95 < 200ms, P99 < 350ms for typical 512-token requests.

[Healthcare Messaging Framework (v1) — PHI-adjacent & regulated workloads]
## Purpose
This messaging framework is the approved, compliance-reviewed source of truth for positioning Redwood Inference to healthcare prospects with PHI-adjacent or regulated workloads. It is designed for the Vertical ABM pilot and for sales-led discovery, security reviews, and pilot/POC scoping.

**What this is:** persona pains, positioning pillars, approved claims, objection handling, and use-case talk tracks specific to healthcare.

**What this is not:** legal advice or a promise of compliance certification. Use the security FAQ and evidence pack for substantiation.

---

## Definitions (use consistently)
**PHI-adjacent workload:** A workload that *touches* clinical workflows, patient/member communications, or billing/coding context, but may or may not require direct PHI processing (e.g., patient support content with de-identified inputs).

**PHI workload:** A workload where protected health information may be processed, stored, or logged.

**Regulated healthcare buyer:** Typically includes HIPAA-covered entities and business associates in the US; additional privacy/security regimes may apply (state privacy laws, contractual security addenda, internal risk controls).

---

## Audience / ICP hypotheses (ABM pilot)
Primary targets:
- Health systems and IDNs (security + app platform teams)
- Payers (member support, claims operations)
- Revenue cycle / medical billing organizations (coding, documentation workflows)
- Digital health / telehealth (patient communication, clinical summarization)

Common triggers:
- Moving from experimentation to production with security review requirements
- Need for private networking, auditability, and predictable performance for patient/member experiences
- Consolidating scattered “model endpoints” into a standard inference platform

---

## Core positioning (healthcare-specific)
### One-sentence positioning
**Redwood Inference provides production-grade LLM inference with deployment flexibility (hosted, dedicated, private) and operational controls (auditability, access controls, retention/residency levers) that healthcare teams need to ship regulated workloads with predictable latency and cost.**

### Pillars (prioritize by persona)
1) **Control for regulated environments**
- Private deployment options (VPC / on-prem patterns)
- Encryption and key management integration options (KMS/HSM patterns)
- Audit logging and access control capabilities to support internal security requirements

2) **Production reliability + predictable performance**
- Latency/throughput predictability for patient/member-facing experiences
- Capacity isolation (Dedicated / Private) to avoid noisy neighbor risk
- Operational tooling: rollouts, fallback, and observability

3) **Economics without sacrificing quality**
- Batching/caching and cost controls with visibility
- Model/version pinning and rollout controls to prevent regressions

---

## Deployment guidance (what to recommend when)
Use this section to align the “right” Redwood deployment mode with PHI risk and procurement constraints.

### Recommended mapping (high-level)
**Hosted API**
- Best for: non-PHI or de-identified workloads; prototyping; low friction evaluation
- Typical buyers: innovation teams, product teams that need speed
- Key message: fastest path to benchmarks and value; strong performance + developer experience

**Dedicated (reserved capacity)**
- Best for: regulated workloads needing **capacity isolation** and predictable SLOs; some customers’ security requirements without full private control plane
- Typical buyers: platform teams scaling to production; teams with strict latency/throughput requirements
- Key message: predictable throughput and isolation + Redwood operational tooling

**Private (VPC / on-prem)**
- Best for: PHI workloads or strict network/data boundary requirements; customers requiring private connectivity, customer-managed networking controls, or on-prem constraints
- Typical buyers: health systems, payers, and billing orgs with high security review bar
- Key message: deploy Redwood’s inference platform within your security perimeter; maintain consistent runtime + operations

### Guidance for PHI conversations (do this every time)
- Ask early: **“Will PHI be included in prompts, outputs, logs, or stored datasets?”**
- If *yes or uncertain*, default positioning toward **Private** (VPC / on-prem) until Security confirms requirements.
- If *no (de-identified)*, you can lead with **Hosted** or **Dedicated** depending on SLO and isolation needs.

---

## Compliance + security requirements (translate into Redwood-friendly language)
Use these as “requirements we commonly see” and map to Redwood capabilities + evidence artifacts.

Common healthcare requirements:
- **Access control:** RBAC; SSO/SAML; user provisioning/deprovisioning expectations (e.g., SCIM)
- **Auditability:** immutable audit trails for admin actions and data access patterns; export for SIEM
- **Encryption:** encryption in transit; encryption at rest; customer key control requirements (KMS/HSM patterns)
- **Retention controls:** ability to define retention windows for logs and stored artifacts; deletion workflows
- **Residency:** constraints around region/VPC boundaries and where data transits
- **Vendor risk:** SOC 2/ISO posture, incident response practices, subprocessors transparency

Approved phrasing (use verbatim where possible):
- “Redwood supports the security controls commonly required for regulated workloads, including encryption, role-based access controls, audit logging, and private deployment options.”
- “We can share our security FAQ and an evidence pack index under NDA to support your security review.”
- “We’ll align deployment mode (Hosted, Dedicated, or Private) to your data classification and network boundary requirements.”

**Do not over-claim:**
- Avoid implying a certification or guarantee of compliance (see ‘Do not say’ list).

---

## Retention & residency considerations (healthcare-specific talk track)
Healthcare prospects often conflate “data retention” across multiple layers. Use this structure:

1) **Request/response content**
- Clarify whether content is stored, cached, or logged and under what controls.
- Emphasize data minimization: “We encourage sending only what’s required; de-identify when possible.”

2) **Operational logs / audit logs**
- Explain the purpose: accountability and security monitoring.
- Confirm export patterns: “Audit logs can be exported to your logging platform/SIEM depending on deployment.”

3) **Regional / network boundaries**
- Ask: “Do you require data to stay within a specific cloud region or within your VPC/on-prem environment?”
- Position Private for strict boundaries.

Suggested discovery questions:
- “What retention window do you require for application logs vs security audit logs?”
- “Do you require customer-managed keys or HSM-backed key custody?”
- “Do you have a policy restricting PHI from leaving your environment?”

---

## Personas and what they care about
### 1) CISO / Security & Privacy
Primary concerns:
- PHI exposure risk (including logs)
- Auditability (who did what, when)
- Identity and access controls
- Incident response posture; vendor risk management

Value props:
- Private deployment option for strict data boundaries
- Audit logging + export patterns
- Enterprise security review readiness (FAQ + evidence pack index)

Proof points (safe):
- “We support security reviews with a standardized FAQ and evidence pack workflow to reduce turnaround time.”

CTA:
- “30-minute security architecture review”

### 2) Platform Engineering / ML Engineering
Primary concerns:
- Latency and throughput predictability
- Operational visibility and rollout safety
- Integration complexity (networking, auth, logging)

Value props:
- Dedicated/Private for consistent performance
- Console visibility into cost and latency
- Rollouts and fallbacks to reduce downtime risk

CTA:
- “Benchmark + reference architecture session”

### 3) Clinical Ops / Informatics / Product Owners
Primary concerns:
- Clinical safety and quality drift
- Workflow fit (summarization, coding assistance)
- Governance and review steps

Value props:
- Version pinning and controlled rollouts
- Structured outputs and guardrails (pattern-based)
- Operational monitoring to detect regressions

CTA:
- “Use-case scoping + quality plan (prompt set + eval outline)”

### 4) Procurement / Vendor Management
Primary concerns:
- Contract terms, security addenda, SLAs
- Evidence availability; timeline predictability

Value props:
- Clear deployment options and support tiers
- Standardized evidence pack request process

CTA:
- “Security review checklist + timeline alignment”

---

## Example use cases (healthcare) + guardrails
Use these examples to anchor the conversation; always pair with guardrails to demonstrate responsible posture.

### Use case A: Member/patient support assistant (chat + routing)
Examples:
- Benefits questions, appointment FAQs, coverage explanations
- Escalation to human agent with summarized context

Where Redwood fits:
- Low-latency chat inference with routing/fallback
- Cost controls for high-volume traffic

Guardrails to state:
- Start with **de-identified** inputs where possible.
- Avoid generating medical advice; include policy-based disclaimers and escalation paths.
- Define a “no-PII/PHI” boundary for Hosted; use Private if PHI is in scope.

Suggested success metrics:
- P95 latency target for first token + steady-state streaming
- Deflection rate with human escalation safety checks

### Use case B: Clinical note / chart summarization (clinician productivity)
Examples:
- Summarize longitudinal notes for review
- Highlight medications/problems with structured output

Where Redwood fits:
- Private deployment patterns for strict data boundaries
- Version pinning and controlled rollouts to prevent quality regressions

Guardrails to state:
- Human-in-the-loop review for any clinical-facing output.
- Use structured outputs to reduce hallucinated formatting.
- Maintain a prompt/eval set and monitor regressions during rollouts.

Suggested discovery questions:
- “What’s the source system and what PHI fields are included?”
- “Do you require on-prem or VPC-only processing?”

### Use case C: Coding assistance / revenue cycle (ICD/CPT suggestions)
Examples:
- Draft coding suggestions from documentation
- Summarize claim context for back-office workflows

Where Redwood fits:
- Batch throughput optimization for back-office processing
- Observability for unit economics (cost per document)

Guardrails to state:
- Treat outputs as suggestions; final coding approval remains with staff.
- Ensure traceability: store prompts/outputs per policy; audit access.
- Clarify retention: what must be logged vs what must not be stored.

Suggested success metrics:
- Throughput (docs/hour) and cost per document
- Accuracy proxy metrics defined by customer (e.g., agreement with human coder)

---

## Claims and language guidance (approved vs. do not say)
### Approved claims (safe)
- “Private deployment options (VPC/on-prem patterns) support strict network boundary requirements.”
- “Audit logging and access controls support regulated operational requirements.”
- “Dedicated capacity provides predictable throughput and isolation for production workloads.”
- “We support security reviews with an FAQ and evidence pack workflow.”

### Use with qualification (ask Security/Legal; do not improvise)
- Any mention of **HIPAA**, **BAA**, “HIPAA-ready,” “HIPAA-compliant,” or “certified.”
- Any claim about **data retention defaults** or specific residency guarantees unless confirmed for the prospect’s deployment mode.
- Any claim implying “we never store anything” or “no logs.”

### Do not say (verbatim)
- “Redwood is HIPAA compliant.”
- “We can sign a BAA for any deployment.”
- “We don’t log anything.”
- “Your data never leaves your environment” (unless Private deployment is confirmed and Security has validated the exact architecture).

---

## Objection handling
### Objection: “We can’t send PHI to an external API.”
Response:
- “Understood. For strict data boundary requirements, we typically recommend Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem patterns). We can walk through a reference architecture and the controls your security team will expect, including identity, audit logging, encryption, and retention options.”

Next step:
- Schedule security architecture review + confirm network topology requirements.

### Objection: “We need full audit trails and SIEM integration.”
Response:
- “That’s common in regulated environments. We can review our audit logging approach and how customers export logs into their SIEM. We’ll also provide the evidence pack index under NDA so your team can see exactly what artifacts are available.”

### Objection: “We’re worried about model drift and clinical safety.”
Response:
- “We design for controlled rollouts and operational visibility. We’ll align on a prompt/eval set, pin model versions, and use staged rollouts so you can validate quality before expanding.”

### Objection: “We need predictable latency for patient-facing experiences.”
Response:
- “That’s a key reason customers choose Dedicated or Private: predictable throughput and isolation. We can define P95/P99 targets and validate with a short benchmark pilot using your traffic shape.”

---

## Discovery checklist (healthcare-specific)
Use in first call to qualify for Private/Dedicated and avoid rework.

1) Data classification
- Will PHI be present in prompts/outputs? In logs? In stored datasets?

2) Deployment constraints
- Must run inside customer VPC? On-prem requirements? Private connectivity?

3) Identity and access
- SSO/SAML requirements? SCIM provisioning expectations? Admin separation?

4) Audit + monitoring
- Required audit log fields? SIEM destination? Retention windows?

5) Performance and workload shape
- Interactive vs batch? Peak QPS? Token lengths? Concurrency?

6) Procurement timeline
- Security questionnaire timeline; NDA requirements; contracting sequence

---

## Suggested talk tracks (by stage)
### Initial outbound (security-forward)
- “Teams building healthcare assistants and summarization workflows often hit a wall at production: security review, auditability, and predictable performance. Redwood supports regulated deployments with Dedicated and Private options plus operational tooling (audit logs, access controls, rollouts). Are you open to a 20-minute architecture + security fit check?”

### First meeting (problem framing)
- “Before we talk models, we align on (1) whether PHI is in scope, (2) the required data boundary, and (3) the audit/identity controls your security team will require. Then we map you to Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private and validate latency/cost with a short benchmark.”

### Security review (set expectations)
- “We’ll share a security FAQ and evidence pack index under NDA and walk through what is available. Where requirements are deployment-specific, we’ll confirm the exact architecture before we commit to language.”

---

## Asset mapping (what to send when)
- Security FAQ (regulated): use for security teams; link to evidence pack index.
- Evidence pack index: use under NDA; clarify restricted sharing.
- Regulated workloads deck: use for exec + platform alignment.
- One-pager (healthcare): use after first call to summarize architecture + pilot plan.

---

## Internal escalation rules (do not skip)
Escalate to Security (Naomi Feldman / Olga Petrov) when:
- Prospect asks for HIPAA/BAA language, subprocessor lists, incident history, pen test results, or any “certification” claim.
- Prospect requests specific retention/residency commitments or “no logging” commitments.

Escalate to Legal (Michael Grant / Sofia Mendes) when:
- DPA/security addendum requires changes or custom language.
- Prospect requests liability terms or bespoke SLA beyond standard tiers.

Escalate to Product/SE (Vivek Kulkarni / Markus Klein) when:
- Prospect needs a confirmed Private deployment topology, on-prem constraints, or audit log export details beyond the FAQ.

---

## Version notes
**v1 (2025-05-16):** Initial ABM pilot release. Includes PHI-adjacent definitions, healthcare use cases, and approved language aligned with regulated workloads security FAQ. Updates should route through PMM + Security review before publishing.

[Proxy-branch rate-limited shadow mirroring with tenant chargeback]
description:
Problem: We need a safe shadow-mirroring pipeline that lets teams run canary and A/B experiments with realistic production traffic while guaranteeing cost isolation and preventing noisy tenants from exhausting mirror budgets. Current ad-hoc mirroring approaches either (a) duplicate all traffic which blows budget, (b) lack per-tenant throttles leading to noisy neighbor effects, or (c) reuse production caches and contaminate observability.

Proposal: Implement a proxy-branch component in the edge router that performs sampled request duplication into a dedicated mirror plane. The proxy-branch will enforce per-tenant budget tokens (chargeback-aware), support adaptive sampling (priority based on recent drop in model quality or rollout phase), and attach metadata that keeps mirrored requests logically and cache-isolated from primary runtime. The mirror plane will be backed by separate compute pools and billing meters so mirrored compute is chargeable to tenant cost centers. Include automatic quarantine and rollback triggers when mirrored traffic cost or error rates cross thresholds.

acceptance_criteria:
Proxy-branch duplicates a sampled subset of live requests to a dedicated mirror endpoint without adding >1ms median latency to happy path
Per-tenant mirror budgets are enforced: tenants can set monthly mirrored-token budgets and mirror requests are denied/logged once exhausted
Adaptive sampler supports three modes: fixed-rate, priority-based (error/quality-driven), and exploratory (uniform for early canaries)
Mirror plane uses separate KV prefix namespaces and does not share production KV caches (no cache pollution)
Billing records for mirrored compute appear in tenant chargeback reports and are available in Console cost breakdown within 24 hours
Auto-quarantine policy triggers when mirrored compute for a tenant exceeds configured rate-of-spend or when mirrored model regression >= configured threshold; quarantine must prevent further mirroring and notify SRE and customer owner

tasks:
Design proxy-branch API and open RFC (include sampling knobs and token-bucket semantics)
Implement proxy-branch middleware in edge-router (duplicate path, async fanout, minimal headers)
Add mirror-budget store: per-tenant token bucket with replenishment window and admin APIs
Create mirror plane runtime configs: isolated KV namespaces, separate model pools, and separate metrics tags
Instrument billing pipeline to include mirror compute and store chargeback dimensions
Implement adaptive sampler service to adjust sampling weights from Console/experiment config
Add quarantine controller that listens to cost/quality signals and flips tenant mirror allow=false
E2E tests: latency impact, quota exhaustion, cache isolation, correct billing labeling
Create runbook and Console UI surface for tenants to manage mirror budgets and view mirror spend

rollout_plan:
Phased rollout: 1) dev-only testing against synthetic traffic (2 weeks), 2) internal dogfood with platform team (2 weeks) using fixed-rate sampling at 0.5% and strict budgets, 3) limited external beta for trusted customers with explicit chargeback and opt-in, 4) GA when billing, monitoring, quarantine and docs are complete. Each phase will publish a short checklist; gate to next phase requires no critical regressions and stable mirror billing for 48h.

monitoring:
Latency-Delta: distribution of proxy latency before/after branch to ensure <1ms median overhead
Mirror-Cost-Per-Tenant: daily spend and token consumption metrics
Mirror-Error-Rate: per-model/per-tenant divergence in error/latency
Cache-Pollution-Check: KV hit-rate on prod namespace compared to baseline
Quarantine-Events: counts and reasons; alert on repeated quarantines

[Blackout rehearsal: tiered load-shedding, circuit-breaker validation, and atomic restore certification]
description:
Objective: Validate end-to-end behavior of an active-passive evacuation where the primary region experiences a sudden blackout. Exercise tiered load-shedding, per-route circuit-breakers, and an atomic restore from KV snapshots while preserving SLOs for high-priority customers. This drill focuses on: 1) exercising automated circuit breakers and policy escalations, 2) proving KV snapshot restore produces consistent model-serving state, 3) exercising rollback and progressive traffic ramp-down/up, and 4) collecting signals to update runbooks and tuning guidance.

success_criteria:
1) High-priority routes remain within SLOs (p95 latency < 200ms for host-tier-1) during and after failover. 2) KV and tokenstore consistency checks report zero divergence for pinned model versions and session state within 5 minutes of completion. 3) Circuit-breaker thresholds trip at expected loads and recover according to policy. 4) Restore validation harness verifies data integrity and checksums. 5) Post-drill action items created and owners assigned.

preconditions:
- Backup snapshots for tokenstore/KV taken within last 15 minutes before rehearsal window.
- DR ops team on-call assigned and paged.
- Canary traffic generator configured to simulate tiered customer mixes.
- Monitoring dashboards and SLO alerts are enabled and annotated.
- A non-production but production-like cluster and a dedicated test customer org are reserved for the exercise.

runbook_steps:
Phase 0 - Preparation:
1) Confirm snapshots exist and are uploaded to s3://redwood-dr-snapshots/2026-03-13/ENG-59713.
2) Notify observability and support teams; set experiment tags in datadog:drill=ENG-59713.
3) Start canary traffic generator with baseline profile and capture baseline metrics for 10m.

Phase 1 - Simulated Blackout:
4) Trigger failover: use orchestration playbook 'failover/trigger_active_passive.sh --target passive-region=eu-west-1 --reason=simulated-blackout --tag=ENG-59713'.
5) Immediately raise global circuit-breakers to tiered thresholds: invoke admin API /admin/v1/circuit-breakers with payload to set p95-latency cutoff and request-per-second caps.
6) Monitor for automatic routing: ensure smart-routing redirects eligible requests to eu-west-1 and that fallback model variants are used for low-tier plans.

Phase 2 - Load-shedding and CB Verification:
7) Ramp canary traffic by +3x in 2 minutes and observe which routes get shed. Verify that shed order follows priority map (free -> standard -> enterprise).
8) Validate circuit-breaker trip metrics and log events in /metrics/cb-trips. Expected: 5-10 trips among low-tier routes, zero for enterprise.

Phase 3 - Atomic Restore and KV Validation:
9) After failover stabilizes, perform atomic restore from snapshot: 'restore/atomic_restore --snapshot s3://redwood-dr-snapshots/... --target eu-west-1 --dry-run=false'.
10) Run data-integrity check: 'validation/kv_consistency_check --left active-kv --right restored-kv --allowed-drift=0'.
11) Run session replay tests for long-lived sessions and streaming reconnect tests.

Phase 4 - Rollback and Cleanup:
12) If restore fails checks, initiate rollback to snapshot pre-state and re-run restore with alternate snapshot.
13) Gradually lower circuit-breaker thresholds and ramp traffic back to normal patterns in 30m windows.
14) Terminate canary traffic and mark experiment complete.


validation_checks:
- SLO dashboard: runtime/slo/host-tier-1 shows p95 < 200ms.
- KV checksums match: sha256(restored) == sha256(snapshot)
- Tokenstore session replay success rate >= 99%
- No unhandled 5xx spikes > 2% sustained for > 5m
- Audit logs contain explicit restore command and actor IDs


rollback_plan:
If critical validation fails (data mismatch, >5% 5xxs, or enterprise SLO breach):
1) Pause traffic routing to passive region.
2) Revert to last-known-good snapshot using restore/atomic_restore --snapshot s3://redwood-dr-snapshots/last-known-good.
3) Use emergency routing policy to send traffic to warm standby in us-east-1.
4) Open a Sev with postmortem owner and start forensic capture for at least 24h.

Dashboards: https://dashboards.redwood.ai/runtime/slo/ENG-59713, https://dashboards.redwood.ai/kv/consistency/ENG-59713.

notes:
Design decision: prefer atomic snapshot restore to avoid partial state that confuses model-serving runtime. Trade-off: atomic restores can take longer and increase initial latency during reintegration; mitigations include progressive traffic ramping and serving degraded model variants.
We will use a reserved non-prod account that mirrors customer auth to avoid exposing production customer data. KMS keys for snapshots are accessible to DR engineers via temporary role for the exercise.

[GPU availability surface — weekly snapshot (2026-05-21)]
content:
Purpose: weekly export of the ‘availability surface’ view used by infra and SRE to track true usable GPU capacity across clusters and pools (sample window: 2026-05-14 to 2026-05-20). This is an intermediate sheet-format export (derived from Grafana timeseries + pool scheduler logs).

Definitions / methodology:
- time window: 7-day rolling (Mon 2026-05-14 00:00 UTC to Sun 2026-05-20 23:59 UTC)
- avg_util: average active vcore-equivalent GPU utilization per pool (weighted by instance-hours)
- p95_util: 95th percentile instantaneous utilization across the window
- headroom_pct: fraction of pool capacity that was idle and immediately schedulable (accounting for fragmentation)
- wasted_slots: estimated percentage of slots that could not be used due to instance size mismatch or partial fragmentation
- data sources: grafana panel id: gpu-availability-surface, scheduler logs (slot-alloc events), capacity catalog

High level findings:
1) Fleet-level avg_util: 71% (weighted by GPU-seconds) with p95 at 91% during the 2026-05-18 afternoon surge. This is marginally up (+4ppt) vs the previous week.
2) Region breakouts: us-west1 remains the tightest (avg_util 82%, p95 96%), eu-west1 sits at 68% avg, apac-southeast1 at 62% avg but with highest fragmentation/wasted_slots.
3) Fragmentation spike: apac pools with mixed T4/RTX-share instances show ~16–20% wasted_slots during nights (local business hours for APAC customers cause fragmentation with long-running training jobs).
4) Emergent risk: cluster-alpha (us-west1) had two 30–45m windows where the scheduler reported <5% instantaneous idle but autoscaler failed to spin additional burst nodes due to quota throttling (see linked Linear ticket).
5) Reserve policy suggestion: add a 6% soft headroom target to us-west1 pools for next 2 weeks to reduce request latency for high-priority routes; implement gradual bump rather than instant commit.

Per-cluster quick snapshot (short bullets):

[Reserved capacity GPU exhaustion causes batched request failures and latency spikes]
description:
Issue summary: BrightCart observed a sharp increase in 5xx errors and token latency for requests routed to their reserved pool between 2026-03-12T09:40 and 2026-03-12T11:05 UTC. Impact: ~22% of batched requests returned 500/502 within the window, median token latency increased from ~45ms to ~420ms, and several long-running streams were terminated by the serving runtime. Environment: Dedicated capacity (reserved pool id rp-44), prod us-east-1, cluster sku: 8xA100, autoscale policy: conservative-burst-v2. Steps: See steps_to_reproduce. Logs and telemetry attached below. Initial hypothesis: sudden saturation of GPU memory/KV cache by a single noisy tenant causing eviction storms and scheduler thrashing, which cascaded to failed batch allocations and queue timeouts. Resolution summary: applied temporary isolation by moving the noisy tenant to a different pool, increased pool GPU headroom and lowered max_batch_size for affected routes, and deployed an autoscaler fix to back-pressure noisy-tenant allocation. Follow-ups: post-incident audit of tenant scheduling and new quota-based scheduling enforcement.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Send 100 concurrent batched requests (batch size 16) to /v1/generate on BrightCart's reserved pool rp-44 using open-7b-q4 model.
2) Observe request queue growth beyond configured max_queue_ms and increased token generation latency after ~15 minutes.
3) Repeat with a single high-memory streaming workload (long context, prefix cache hits) to replicate KV cache eviction pattern.
4) Monitor metrics: gpu_utilization, gpu_memory_used, serving_batch_alloc_errors, scheduler_queue_length.
5) Confirm 5xx error spike aligns with GPU memory OOM and batch allocation failures in logs.

logs:
2026-03-12T09:43:12Z rp-44-node-7 serving-runtime: BatchAllocError: allocation timeout after 12000ms (requested 4g, available 0g)
2026-03-12T09:43:12Z rp-44-node-7 gpu-manager: GPU memory pressure: 98% (A100-40GB), KV-cache entries evicted=3124
2026-03-12T09:44:01Z autoscaler: scale_event: prevented_scale_up pool=rp-44 reason=insufficient_gpu_headroom
2026-03-12T09:45:05Z scheduler: queue_delay_ms route=/v1/generate median=375 max=1234
2026-03-12T10:02:33Z proxy: downstream 502 from serving-runtime on rp-44-node-3 during streaming connection

investigation_notes:
Metric analysis: serving_batch_alloc_errors correlated with gpu_memory_used > 92% and KV eviction spikes. Three nodes (rp-44-node-3/5/7) showed repeated allocation timeouts.
Heap: The noisy tenant's streaming workload retained large KV caches (~8GB per worker) due to long-context inference pattern and lacked prefix caching TTL in user config.
Scheduler behavior: When allocation timeouts occurred, scheduler attempted to rebalance batches which increased queue delay and caused downstream 502s from timeouts.
Autoscaler observation: conservative-burst-v2 policy prevented immediate scale-up because it evaluates aggregated queue signal and saw transient oscillation; this created a feedback loop where allocation failures blocked scale triggers.
Customer config: BrightCart had max_batch_size=64 and aggressive prefetch settings; lowering batch size reduced per-batch memory and improved headroom.
Related incidents: SUP-51777 documented intermittent GPU availability that had similar symptoms but different root cause (eviction due to kernel memory leak). Linked for historical context.

resolution:
Applied temporary tenant isolation by moving the noisy evaluation job to a separate reserved pool, increased pool headroom by adding one GPU to rp-44 for 1 hour, lowered max_batch_size for the affected routes to 16, and deployed an autoscaler patch to break the prevention loop. Customer confirmed error rate returned to baseline and median token latency dropped back under 70ms. Incident marked resolved after 30m of stable metrics.

1) Enforce per-tenant KV-cache memory quotas in the serving-runtime (Owner: Diego) - target ETA 2026-03-26
2) Add quota-based scheduling to autoscaler to avoid allocation/prevention loops (Owner: Priya) - target ETA 2026-03-19
3) Update dedicated capacity onboarding checklist to include recommended max_batch_size and prefix TTL settings for streaming workloads (Owner: Maya) - target ETA 2026-03-18

[Erratic 5xx pulses during slow-client keepalive bursts causing API gateway accept-queue collapse]
description:
Issue summary: Multiple customers (largest: StreamlineAI) reported short-lived waves of 5xx responses on streaming and embedding endpoints. Impact: customer requests during bursts receive 502/503/504 with high variance in first-byte times; some long-lived streaming sessions drop mid-stream. Environment: prod us-east serving dedicated fleet for StreamlineAI (reserved capacity). Observed pattern: errors occur in short pulses lasting ~30-120s, often in evenings, correlated with a small subset of upstream runtimes cycling and API gateway accept-queue growth.

steps_to_reproduce:
1) Run sustained mixed traffic: many long-lived streaming connections (keepalive HTTP/2) interspersed with embedding upload batches from a small client pool.
2) Introduce a client behavior that sends delayed window updates and occasional tiny payload bursts (simulates slow consumer with sporadic writes).
3) Observe apigw accept-queue length and backend handshake times; monitor for 5xx pulses on edge and runtime restarts.

logs:
Mar 10 18:21:12 apigw-44ab accept_queue=193 peer=svc-ephemeral-12 result=queued
Mar 10 18:21:35 runtime-ephemeral-12: SIGTERM triggered due to watchdog timeout during prefetched-model lock (nvml reset)
Mar 10 18:22:01 apigw-44ab proxy: upstream 10.0.12.8 reset while reading response header (502)
Mar 10 18:22:15 apigw-44ab accept_queue=28 drain=fail reason=connect_timeout
Mar 10 18:22:32 srx-scheduler: backpressure=on prefetch_thrash=high

investigation_notes:
Initial triage: Pattern suggests accept-queue growth at apigw followed by short upstream restarts (watchdog timeouts) rather than a single sustained overload.
SRE observation: CPU on apigw hosts spikes concurrently with keepalive churn; fd usage climbs but not full exhaustion. Accept queue length correlates with 5xx pulse start times.
Runtime logs: One runtime process hit a GPU driver reset and triggered a local restart; subsequent reshuffling of ephemeral workers increased connection handoffs.
Hypothesis 1: Slow-client windowing causes partial reads at the proxy, leaving sockets tied up and causing accept-queue pressure; when accept queue backpressure increases, the apigw amplifies retries to upstreams causing transient overload and runtime watchdog timeouts.
Hypothesis 2: Small number of long-lived streaming sessions from StreamlineAI are unevenly distributed across apigw nodes; when a node experiences runtime restart, the rebalancing amplifies ephemeral load onto neighbors, creating a short 5xx pulse.
Observed mitigations tried: temporarily shifting customer route weight off the hot apigw hosts decreased pulse frequency; adding a short client-side keepalive threshold on StreamlineAI reduced connection churn in testing.

comments:
Support (Aisha): Customer reports 5xx pulses ~18:20-18:25 local time yesterday. They provided a sample timeseries and a pcap of a single streaming session (attached to ticket). Asked SRE for initial log sweep.
SRE (Diego): Pulled apigw host metrics and runtime logs. Found accept_queue spikes and a runtime GPU reset on runtime-12. Suspect prefetched model lock contention contributed to watchdog timeouts. Investigating fd leak hypothesis.
Eng (Marta Novak): Noted a recent ingress-proxy tweak (PR #7891) changed the read timeout semantics for half-closed streams. Will review if this increased partial-read retention. Linking PR: github.com/redwood/pr/7891
Support (Aisha): Customer confirmed they perform periodic tiny writes from an SDK under poor network conditions (mobile). They can try increasing their client-side keepalive frequency for a test window.
SRE (Diego): Scoped mitigation: increased apigw accept-queue cap on the affected AZ and temporarily diverted 30% of StreamlineAI traffic to a healthy pod group (route weight change). Monitoring for recurrence.
Eng (Ethan Shaw): Adding a short-term circuit in the ingress to penalize connections that emit long tail windowing behavior. Drafting patch (WIP) and load test plan.

resolution_notes:
Workaround: shifted StreamlineAI route weights away from three saturated apigw nodes and applied a temporary ingress policy to drop half-closed idle streams after 45s. Customer applied a conservative SDK keepalive fix during the window. Result: 5xx pulses frequency dropped to zero during the monitoring window. Next steps: eng to land ingress PR to tighten partial-read retention and backpressure handling; SRE to add alerting threshold for accept-queue growth and autopurge policy. Postmortem scheduled.

[Inflight request preemption by priority rebalancer causing elevated 5xx rate]
description:
Issue summary:
We observed a sustained increase in 5xx responses for customer Vernon Analytics (dedicated tenant) originating from api-gateway and upstream serving-runtime restarts. Error rate spike started 2026-03-13 14:12 UTC and correlated with an automated priority rebalancing job executing across the ingress-prioritizer fleet.

Impact:
- ~12% of requests for the tenant returned 5xx over a 22-minute window; clients reported failing streaming sessions and aborted generation jobs.
- Customer reported production degradation for a data-processing pipeline (affects business analytics dashboards).

Environment:
- Dedicated pool: prod us-east-1 (tenant pinned to a subset of GPU nodes).
- Components involved: api-gateway -> ingress-prioritizer -> serving-runtime pool (cuda nodes).

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Priority rebalancer runs and recalculates per-tenant priority buckets based on recent QPS and SLA weights.
2) In-flight lower-priority requests are preemptively evicted to rebalance capacity.
3) Evicted clients retry immediately (no jitter) causing a rapid burst against api-gateway.
4) Api-gateway queues spike, backpressure increases, and several serving runtime workers exceed allowed KV cache thrash limits leading to watchdog restarts and OOM-like termination (SIGABRT).
5) Subsequent requests receive 502/503/504 depending on proxy path and timing.

Observed behavior & logs (selected):
- apigw logs (us-east-1, 2026-03-13 14:12:30 - 14:34:00): repeated upstream 502s; connection resets followed by 429s at the gateway when token buckets hit zero. Link: https://dash.redwood.com/apigw/errors?svc=us-east-1&window=2026-03-13T14:10:00Z_2026-03-13T14:40:00Z
- ingress-prioritizer: job "rebalance-cycle-2026-03-13-14:11" completed in 18s. Logs show mass eviction events for tenant id t-vernon-11 with reason PREEMPTIVE_REBALANCE.
- serving-runtime: repeated worker watchdog restarts with stack traces indicating rapid KV cache invalidation and repeated memory pressure before abort: "runtime: aborting worker due to kv-evict-loop". Kernel-level OOMs were not recorded, but process exit codes were non-zero.

Investigation notes:
- Hypothesis A: Preemptive eviction without backoff caused retry amplification; retries hit the gateway burst limit and queue saturation triggered upstream timeouts.
- Hypothesis B: The rebalancer's immediate eviction approach did not signal the runtime to gracefully finish in-flight streams, causing partial state corruption of runtime's KV caches and subsequent instability when those requests retried.
- Correlated metrics: request retry rate increased 6x immediately after rebalance completion; average per-request queue time at apigw jumped from 12ms to 420ms.
- Cross-checks: No infra-level node interruptions recorded in cloud provider metrics; node CPU/GPU utilization increased but did not show sustained saturation prior to restarts.

Temporary mitigation performed (timeline):
- 14:25 UTC: Support escalated to SRE and Engineering.
- 14:32 UTC: Rolled back automated priority rebalancer for the us-east-1 ingress-prioritizer cluster to stop further evictions (hotfix toggle).
- 14:40 UTC: Applied short-term gateway rate-smoothing for tenant t-vernon-11 via dynamic token-bucket increase to allow graceful retries with jitter.
- 14:55 UTC: Performed rolling restart of 6 serving-runtime workers handling the tenant to clear the kv-cache thrash cycles; error rate began to fall.
- 15:10 UTC: Error rate returned to baseline for the tenant; monitoring shows stabilized queue times and reduced restart frequency.

Customer communication:
- CS notified customer at 14:36 UTC; provided update at 15:20 UTC confirming mitigation and next steps. Customer accepted working-with-engineering for root cause follow-up.

Next steps / recommended permanent fixes:
1) Add a grace-window in the priority rebalancer that avoids preemptive eviction of actively streaming sessions for X seconds and instead marks for low-priority tail-preemption.
2) Implement client-visible retry-jitter guidance and server-side retry token smoothing when eviction events are emitted.
3) Add a safety-check in ingress-prioritizer to not evict more than N% of in-flight requests within a single cycle.
4) Enhance runtime KV cache eviction metrics and add an automated alert when eviction storms correlate to worker restarts.
5) Postmortem & runbook update: record exact mitigation toggles and make hotfix toggle accessible to on-call without engineer approval.

Work items created:
- github.com/redwood/ingress-prioritizer/pull/129 (smoothing + grace window)
- ENG-TASK-1122: telemetry for kv eviction spikes and runtime restarts
- DOCS: update runbook confluence.redwood.com/KB/priority-rebalancer-runbook with emergency toggle steps

Resolution notes (so far):
- Root cause appears tied to the rebalancer eviction policy interacting poorly with streaming workloads and runtime cache behavior. Hotfix rollback and smoothing mitigations reduced customer impact; engineering will deploy a targeted code change to ingress-prioritizer to enforce eviction rate limits and grace periods.

Assumptions:
- Models are pre-warmed in snapshot images and can be instantiated on compatible instance types within 90–120s per worker for cold starts; continuous-batching and KV cache optimizations reduce steady-state spin-up time for many workloads.
- Customer data flows (logs, request metadata) replicate asynchronously to an immutable ledger in a separate region; log replication lag target <60s under normal load.

Failover sequencing (simplified):
1) Detection: regional health probes + control-plane anomaly detection raise an incident. Automated routing policy evaluates latency & capacity and triggers policy execution.
2) Automated fallback: requests for compatible model variants are routed to next-best region/tier (platform-level routing switch within 60s). For dedicated customers with cross-zone replication configured, routing pins to warm-standby pool.
3) Capacity ramp: orchestration boots reserved or burst-capable GPUs in target region; model containers restore KV cache from persisted snapshots where available. Recommended warm-standby config keeps minimal pre-warmed workers to meet baseline throughput.
4) Traffic reflow: once backpressure is acceptable, traffic is progressively returned to normal regions; we prefer incremental reweighting to avoid cascading cold-starts.
5) Failback: after root cause remediation, we execute an orderly failback with state reconciliation windows and can coordinate a maintenance window with the customer.

Target RTO / RPO by product mode (typical):
- Hosted API (standard): RTO (automated routing + degraded capacity) = 60s for control-plane switch; full throughput recovery (steady state) 5–10 minutes; RPO for control-plane metadata & logs <60s.
- Dedicated (reserved): RTO (warm-standby enabled) = 2–5 minutes to restore throughput to committed levels; if warm-standby not enabled, boot times dominate (5–12 minutes). RPO for committed tenant metadata <60s.
- Private (on-prem / VPC): RTO depends on customer infra; our orchestrator supports scripted failover sequences and we provide runbook templates. Typical guidance: aim for <15 minutes if pre-provisioned.

Data consistency notes:
- Model KV caches are treated as ephemeral caches; we persist model state snapshots periodically but not every in-flight token. Session reconstruction requires application-level sticky sessions or short-lived session replay tooling.
