[Budgeting & Contract Milestones: Forecast-to-Revenue Playbook]
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines the end-to-end process for aligning budgeting and forecasts with customer contract milestone billing and revenue recognition rules. It is intended for Finance (Revenue Accounting, FP&A), Sales Ops, Legal, and Procurement partners who manage contracts that include milestone-based billing, partial deliveries, or multi-period performance obligations.

Scope: Applies to all customer contracts where billing or revenue recognition is driven by discrete milestones, acceptance events, or usage thresholds. Excludes standard monthly subscription-only contracts covered by the Subscription Billing policy.

Key principles

- Single source of truth: Contract milestone definitions in Contract Repository (CR-ID) are authoritative for billing triggers and recognition schedules.
- Forecast fidelity: FP&A forecasts must reflect the expected timing and recognition method for each milestone (deferred, over time, or at point-in-time).
- Change discipline: Any change to milestone timing, acceptance criteria, or billing triggers must follow the change-management steps below and be reflected in both the FP&A forecast and RevRec schedules within 48 business hours.

Definitions

- Milestone: A contract-defined deliverable or event that triggers billing or a portion of revenue recognition (e.g., delivery, acceptance, onboarding completion).
- Billing trigger: The event that authorizes invoicing (often tied to milestone completion or customer acceptance).
- Performance obligation (POB): The promised good/service to be delivered; revenue recognition method is determined per POB.

Who owns what (responsibilities)

- Sales / Account Executive: Ensure contract milestone definitions and acceptance criteria are clearly captured at signing. Provide amendments via Sales Ops.
- Legal: Review milestone language for enforceability and clarity; advise on acceptance language.
- Sales Ops: Record contract metadata into Contract Repository and flag non-standard billing or recognition clauses.
- RevRec / Revenue Accounting (Finance): Maintain journal schedules, deferred revenue buckets, and recognition rules. Final sign-off on recognition treatment.
- FP&A: Incorporate milestone timing and recognition method into revenue forecast and monthly re-forecast.
- Procurement (if vendor-managed deliverables): Coordinate acceptance confirmation and provide evidence for recognition.

Process: From contract to forecast (high level)

1) Contract intake and tagging (Sales Ops)
   - At contract signature, Sales Ops creates/updates the CR-ID record and tags each milestone with: milestone_id, acceptance_criteria, billing_trigger, billable_amount, recognition_rule (e.g., immediate, ratable over N months), and expected_date.
   - Non-standard clauses (e.g., contingent billing, customer escrow, delivery-dependent refunds) must include Legal sign-off.

2) Initial FP&A mapping (FP&A)
   - FP&A maps milestones to forecast lines: recognized revenue (by period), deferred revenue schedule, and cash collection forecast.
   - Add notes: probability adjustments (if milestone is contingent) with rationale and link to contract clause.

3) Invoice & recognition execution (RevRec)
   - When billing trigger occurs, Sales Ops or Billing team issues invoice using billing system and tags invoice with milestone_id and CR-ID.
   - RevRec posts invoice to AR and creates/adjusts deferred revenue schedule if recognition is over time.

4) Monthly alignment cadence
   - FP&A and RevRec run a joint monthly reconciliation: compare milestone expectations vs. activity, adjust forecasts, and publish delta analysis to Leadership.

Detailed procedures

A) Contract tagging checklist (Sales Ops)
   - Confirm presence of: milestone acceptance definition, billing trigger, net amount or price schedule, remedies/credits for failure to accept, and termination/force majeure clauses affecting timing.
   - Enter fields to Contract Repository: contract_id, customer_id, milestone_id, expected_date, bill_amount, recognition_method, supporting_doc_link.

B) Billing trigger execution (Billing team)
   1. Verify milestone completion evidence (QA report, customer acceptance email, deployment logs).
   2. Log acceptance evidence to CR-ID and attach to invoice.
   3. Create invoice using billing CLI or UI and include metadata flags: --contract CR-1234 --milestone M-2 --billing-trigger "acceptance" --amount 50000 --invoice-date 2026-03-01.

   Example CLI (billing):
   redwood-billing create-invoice --contract CR-1234 --milestone M-2 --amount 50000 --date 2026-03-01 --evidence-url https://cr.company/contrib/CR-1234/evidence.pdf

C) RevRec posting rules (Revenue Accounting)
   - Point-in-time recognition: Record revenue on invoice date when POB satisfied on that date.
   - Over-time (ratable) recognition: Create deferred revenue schedule and amortize monthly (or as specified).
   - Contingent milestones: Do not recognize until contingency resolved; reflect in FP&A as probability-weighted pipeline.

   Standard journal entries (examples):
   1) Invoice with ratable recognition (on invoice date):
      Dr Accounts Receivable 50,000
      Cr Deferred Revenue (liability) 50,000

   2) Monthly recognition (first of month):
      Dr Deferred Revenue 16,667
      Cr Revenue 16,667
      (Assumes 3-month ratable schedule)

D) Forecast update and re-forecast rules (FP&A)
   - Weekly rolling forecast updates for the next 90 days; monthly comprehensive re-forecast for quarters.
   - Trigger an immediate forecast update if any of the following occur: milestone slips > 14 calendar days, customer rejects acceptance, scope change > 10% of milestone value.
   - When a milestone is delayed, FP&A applies an adjustment entry in the forecast with one-line narrative: "CR-1234 M-2 delayed due to acceptance testing — impact: -$50k recognized revenue, move -$50k from Q2 to Q3 forecast."

E) Contingency handling and credits
   - If contract includes customer credits or rollback clauses tied to failed acceptance, Sales Ops must: 1) record the credit template in CR-ID, 2) notify Billing and RevRec, 3) create a credit memo referencing the original invoice.
   - Accounting treatment: book credit memo to reduce AR and adjust deferred revenue if previously recognized. Work with RevRec for retrospective adjustments if recognition timing spans prior periods.

Tables & quick reference

Milestone to Forecast mapping (example):
| Milestone ID | Billing Trigger | Bill Amount | Recognition Method | Forecast treatment |
|--------------|-----------------|-------------|--------------------|-------------------|
| M-1          | Delivery        | $75,000     | Ratable over 3 mo  | Move $25k to recognized rev/mo for contracted months |
| M-2          | Acceptance      | $50,000     | Point-in-time       | Recognize in month of acceptance; include in cash forecast same month |
| M-3          | Usage threshold | $10,000     | Contingent          | Probability-weighted in forecast until threshold met |

Escalation & exception workflows

- Minor timing variance (<= 14 days): FP&A notes in rolling forecast; no formal escalation.
- Material slip (> 14 days or > $100k impact): Sales Ops files JIRA ticket to "REV-FORECAST" board and notifies RevRec and Sales leadership within 48 hours.
- Disputed acceptance: Escalate to Legal within 24 hours; place invoice on hold if dispute > 7 days and potential credit > 20% of invoice amount.

Communication and reporting

- Monthly Revenue Alignment Pack (owner: RevRec): Includes: planned vs actual milestone completions, deferred revenue roll-forward, forecast delta table, and open disputed invoices. Delivery: 3rd business day of month.
- Quarterly Executive Forecast Review (owner: FP&A): Narrative on material changes in milestone timing, probability assumptions, and any accounting policy judgment calls.

Controls and audit evidence

- Required evidence for recognition: signed acceptance, deployment logs, support ticket closure, or customer confirmation email. Upload evidence to CR-ID within 72 hours of the billing trigger.
- Segregation of duties: Billing cannot modify recognition method; RevRec approves recognition posting.
- Audit trail: All invoice and recognition metadata must be retained in the Contract Repository and GL for at least 7 years.

Operational examples (short)

1) Use case: Beta delivery billed $60k, ratable over 4 months
   - Invoice: create-invoice CR-345 --milestone M-BETA --amount 60000 --date 2026-05-05
   - Journal: Dr AR 60,000 / Cr Deferred Revenue 60,000
   - Monthly recognition: 15,000 per month for 4 months (Dr Deferred Revenue / Cr Revenue)

2) Use case: Acceptance contingent on third-party cert. Cert delayed 6 weeks
   - FP&A: move $40k expected recognition out 6 weeks, notify Sales Ops and Legal
   - Sales Ops: log contingency status and attach vendor cert correspondence
   - RevRec: hold recognition until acceptance evidence posted

Implementation notes and tooling

- Contract Repository (CR) fields required: contract_id, customer_id, milestone_id, expected_date, signed_date, bill_amount, recognition_method, evidence_link, legal_signoff.
- Billing CLI/UI must support metadata flags for contract and milestone IDs; invoices without metadata will be rejected at AR staging.
- FP&A forecasting model templates (spreadsheet and BI layer) will include flag columns for "probability" and "deferred_bucket_id" to allow roll-ups by recognition timing.

Appendix: common recognition scenarios and sample journal codes

- Code table: REV: 4000, DEFERRED_REV_LIAB: 2100, AR: 1100, CREDIT_MEMO: 1200

- Sample retrospective adjustment (when recognition criteria found to be unmet after posting):
   1) Reverse previously recognized revenue: Dr Revenue 20,000 / Cr Deferred Revenue 20,000 (if within same fiscal period) or post adjustment with commentary and CFO approval if cross-period.

- Evidence naming convention: CR-<contract_id>_M-<milestone_id>_<yyyy-mm-dd>_<type>.pdf

Questions & next steps

- Action item: Sales Ops to validate that all active milestone contracts have CR-ID and required fields populated by 2026-04-20.
- Action item: RevRec and FP&A to publish the first "Revenue Alignment Pack" for March activity by 2026-04-05.

Contact owners for clarifications: Marcus Lee (Revenue Accounting), Aisha Patel (FP&A), Liam Chen (Sales Ops).

- 2026-04-05: Revised after initial cross-functional review; added CLI examples and escalation thresholds


[Operational Controls and Request Templates: Access, Changes, Data, Procurement, Vendors, Travel]
Summary
--------
This playbook collects company-wide operational controls and standardized request templates for common cross-functional processes: access & permissions, change management, data management, procurement & expenses, vendor onboarding/management, and travel reimbursements. The goal is to provide a single, actionable reference for requesters, approvers, and operational owners to reduce friction, accelerate approvals, and ensure compliance with security and finance controls.

Audience and scope
------------------
- Audience: all Redwood employees, managers, approvers, IT, security, finance, and procurement partners.
- Scope: applies to host-based and cloud access, configuration changes to production and infra, data classification and retention decisions, purchase orders and expense flows, third-party vendor relationships, and business travel booked on company funds. Exclusions: specialized customer contracts (see finance-legal).

High-level principles
---------------------
1. Least privilege by default. Grant the minimum access required and set expirations.
2. Segregation of duties. Requester, approver, and implementer should be different where practical for privileged actions.
3. Evidence-first approvals. Approvals should include justification and relevant risk mitigations.
4. Standardized templates and SLAs. Use the templates below to ensure consistent triage and predictable processing times.
5. Risk-based exceptions. Temporary exceptions require documented compensating controls and explicit approval by Security or Finance depending on domain.

Section A — Access & Permissions
--------------------------------
Purpose: Define how employees request, approve, and audit access to systems, data stores, and vendor consoles.

Access types and owners
- Identity (Corp Google/SSO): People Ops (onboarding/offboarding lifecycle).
- Cloud console & infra (AWS/GCP/Azure): Cloud Platform team (eng-infra) + Security for privileged roles.
- Production service access (SSH, SRE Consoles): Eng SRE (eng-sre) and service owners.
- Data access (analytics warehouse, S3 buckets): Data Platform + Data Security.
- Third-party vendor consoles: Procurement + Security.

Request process (standard flow)
1. Requester fills the Access Request template (see template A).
2. Request routes to the manager and the resource owner for approval.
3. Security reviews high-privilege requests (see privilege thresholds).
4. Provisioning is executed by Cloud Platform or delegated delegation owners.
5. Access records automatically expire as requested; tickets are created for renewals.

Privilege thresholds requiring Security review
- Any role granting admin/root in production services.
- Access to data classified as Confidential or Restricted (see data classification).
- Permanent cross-org role grants (e.g., org-wide billing).

Access audit cadence and responsibilities
- Quarterly automated access review for all privileged roles (Owner: Security).
- Managers must attest to team access lists on employee promotions and role changes (Owner: People Ops).

Template A: Access Request (copy into ticket system)
```
Title: [Short] Access Request: <Resource> for <User>
Requester: <Name / Email>
Manager: <Name / Email>
Resource owner: <Service / Team>
Purpose: <Business reason and duration>
Role requested: <role name / scope>
Expiration: <date or 90 days default>
Compensating controls (if any): <MFA, jump box, audit hooks>
Security review required: yes/no
```

Section B — Change Management
-----------------------------
Purpose: Ensure controlled, auditable, and low-risk changes to production systems, infra, and tenant-facing routing.

Change categories
- Routine (non-impacting config that can be automated): fast-track via CI/CD with tests and monitoring.
- Standard (pre-approved, repeatable ops tasks): documented runbook and approved cadence.
- Major (config, schema, or infra changes with potential service impact): requires Change Advisory Board (CAB) review.
- Emergency (outage mitigation): post-hoc documentation required within 24 hours.

Approval matrix (summary)
1. Routine: implementer + automated gates. SLA: immediate.
2. Standard: team manager + service owner. SLA: 2 business days.
3. Major: service owner + infra lead + CAB (Security, SRE, Product). SLA: 5 business days for scheduled window.
4. Emergency: engineer + oncall lead; CAB post-facto review.

Change request template
```
Title: Change Request: <Service> - <Short desc>
Requested by: <Name>
Impact: <low/medium/high>
Rollout plan: <steps, smoke tests>
Rollback plan: <steps>
Monitoring and success criteria: <metrics to watch>
Change window: <date/time>
Approvers: <list>
Risks & mitigations: <list>
```

Pre-deployment checklist (required for Major)
- Run unit/integration tests in staging.
- Load test if change affects performance-critical paths.
- Notify downstream teams and schedule oncall coverage.
- Create automated alerts and dashboards (SLO error budget guardrails).

Section C — Data Management and Classification
---------------------------------------------
Purpose: Provide a simple taxonomy for data handling, retention, and approved storage locations.

Data classification table
| Classification | Examples | Storage requirements | Access rule |
|----------------|----------|----------------------|-------------|
| Public | Marketing pages, public docs | Any public cloud bucket with public-read | No restrictions |
| Internal | Internal docs, Slack history | Encrypted corp storage | Manager-approved, least privilege |
| Confidential | Customer PII, contractual docs | Encrypted at-rest and transit; limited to vault-backed stores | Requires Data Owner + Security approval |
| Restricted | Health data, regulated datasets | Air-gapped or VPC-only, HSM/KMS-backed keys | Requires Data Owner + Legal + Security approval |

Retention and deletion
- Default retention: 3 years for Internal, 7 years for Confidential unless otherwise specified by Legal.
- Data deletion requests must include dataset path, owner, justification, and cross-checks to backups. Data Platform executes deletion and logs actions.

Data access approval process
1. Determine classification.
2. Use Access Request template and mark as Confidential/Restricted when required.
3. Data Owner and Security approve; Data Platform provisions view- or copy-only access where feasible.

Section D — Procurement & Expenses
----------------------------------
Purpose: Standardize approvals, thresholds, and required documentation for purchases and reimbursements.

Spend thresholds and approvers
- < $1,000: Requester + Manager.
- $1,000 - $10,000: Requester + Manager + Budget owner (Product/Finance).
- > $10,000: Requester + Manager + Finance Director approval + Procurement review.
- Annual contracts > $100,000: Procurement + Legal + VP signoff.

Required documentation for purchases
- Business justification and expected ROI or use-case.
- Vendor quote and SOW (if applicable).
- Cost center and GL code.
- Security assessment checklist for SaaS vendors (if the product processes company or customer data).

Template B: Purchase Request (PO initiation)
```
Title: Purchase Request: <Vendor> - <Product>
Requester: <Name>
Cost center: <code>
Amount: <$X>
Business justification: <short>
Vendor contact & SOW: <link>
Security assessment: <completed/skip>
Billing cadence: <monthly/annual>
Desired vendor start date: <date>
Approvals required: <list>
```

Expense reimbursement rules
- Use corporate card where possible. If personal card used, submit expense within 30 days with receipts.
- Per diem caps: domestic $75/day, international $125/day (exceptions require manager approval).
- Hotel: book standard room; upgrades allowed with manager pre-approval.

Section E — Vendor Onboarding & Management
-----------------------------------------
Purpose: Ensure consistent risk assessment, contract terms, and operational controls for third-party providers.

Vendor onboarding checklist (minimum)
1. Business owner identifies need and budget.
2. Procurement collects vendor profile and references.
3. Security completes initial security questionnaire (applicable for SaaS/files/data access).
4. Legal reviews contract terms and data processing addenda (DPA) if PII is involved.
5. Finance establishes payment terms and GL codes.
6. Vendor access: provisioned as least-privilege and time-limited.

Ongoing vendor controls
- Quarterly vendor risk review for high-impact vendors (Owner: Procurement + Security).
- Contract renewals flagged 90 days before expiry.
- Incident playbook and notification timelines must be in contract for data-impacting vendors.

Template C: Vendor Intake Summary
```
Vendor name: <vendor>
Business owner: <team>
Service provided: <description>
Data scope: <none/customer/employee>
Security tier: <low/medium/high>
Contract term: <months>
Primary contact: <name/email>
Key SLAs: <availability, RTO>
```

Section F — Travel Policy (business travel)
------------------------------------------
Booking and approval
- All business travel requires a Travel Request (Template D) and manager approval before booking.
- Use corporate travel vendor or approved booking tool to capture company rates.

Per diems and allowable expenses
- Domestic meals: up to $75/day (receipts optional under per diem).
- International: up to $125/day.
- Ground transportation: economy rideshare or taxi; car rental: compact only unless pre-approved.

Safety and duty of care
- Employees must share itinerary and emergency contact with People Ops when traveling internationally.
- Company-provided travel insurance covers medical evacuation for approved trips; People Ops must be notified for high-risk regions.

Template D: Travel Request
```
Traveler: <Name>
Purpose: <meeting/conference>
Dates: <start - end>
Destination: <city/country>
Estimated cost: <USD>
Manager approval: <Name>
Health & safety notes: <any restrictions>
```

Section G — Internal Templates and Automation Tips
--------------------------------------------------
- All templates above should be copied into the ticketing system (Jira/ServiceNow integration) and configured with appropriate routing and SLAs.
- Where possible, use ephemeral credentialing (e.g., AWS STS, short-lived tokens) and automation for provisioning to reduce manual work and expiration drift.
- Integrate access and change requests with audit logs and email/SMS alerts for high-severity events.

Exception and waiver process
---------------------------
1. Submit an Exception Request (same format as corresponding template plus \"Compensating Controls\").
2. Exceptions are limited to 30 days by default. Longer exceptions require escalation to Security or Finance and documented compensating controls.

Operational SLAs and metrics to track
- Access requests: 90% handled within 2 business days.
- Change requests (Major): 95% scheduled within 7 business days.
- Procurement PO creation: 95% within 3 business days for approved requests.
- Vendor review cycle completion: 100% for high-impact vendors within 30 days of intake.

Roles and ownership table
- People Ops: onboarding/offboarding, travel approvals, per diem policy owner.
- Security: privileged access review, data classification owner for Confidential/Restricted, security questionnaire.
- Procurement: vendor onboarding, contract lifecycle, high-value negotiations.
- Finance: spend approvals, PO issuance, GL coding and expense policy.
- Cloud Platform / Eng-SRE: provisioning, change implementation, runbook maintenance.

FAQ (short)
Q: Who can approve a tool purchase for developer productivity at $2,500?
A: Requester + Manager + Budget owner. If the vendor stores customer data, add Security review.

Q: How to request access to a customer dataset labeled Restricted?
A: File an Access Request and select "Restricted" classification; obtain Data Owner + Legal + Security approvals.

Appendix: Useful links and references
- Ticketing templates: /confluence/policies-and-process/internal-ticket-templates (see templates for Jira).
- Security RBAC guidelines: /confluence/security-and-compliance/rbac-and-auth.
- Legal contracting checklist: /confluence/finance-and-legal/contracts-and-legal-process.

Change history
- 2024-11-18: Initial draft published.
- 2025-02-03: Added Procurement thresholds and Travel per diem updates.

Contact and escalation
- For questions about this playbook, contact People Ops (people-ops@redwood.com).
- For urgent security or vendor incidents, follow the Incident Response playbook in /confluence/security-and-compliance/incident-response-security.

[Forecast Sensitivity & Contract Alignment Playbook — Finance Controls]
Summary:

This playbook defines the standardized approach Redwood Inference uses to: (1) perform forecast sensitivity analysis for revenue and expense line items, (2) align contract milestones and procurement events to forecast and revrec treatment, and (3) operationalize controls and escalation points for deviations that impact recognized revenue or cash timing. This document is intended for Finance, Legal, Sales Ops, Revenue Ops, and Procurement partners.

Purpose & Scope:

- Purpose: Reduce month-to-month volatility, ensure contract terms are reflected accurately in both forecasts and revenue recognition, and provide deterministic triggers for reforecasting and control escalation.
- Scope: Applies to all customer and vendor contracts, multi-period SaaS arrangements, reserved capacity / Dedicated contracts, Private deployment licensing, professional services statements of work (SOWs), and procurement commitments above the approval threshold. Excludes one-off immaterial purchases (below $5k).

Primary owners and stakeholders:

- Finance (Forecast owner): Maya Patel (Finance Controller) — overall playbook owner and reforecast coordinator.
- Revenue Ops: Liaison for contract schedules and bill-run configuration.
- Legal: Contract intake, clause interpretation, and amendment approval.
- Procurement: Purchase order timing, vendor payment terms.
- Sales/Account Exec: Contract milestone confirmation.

Guiding Principles:

1. Single Source of Truth: Contract schedules (ARR, one-time fees, credits) must be captured in the contract repository and referenced by the forecast model.
2. Materiality Thresholds: Use quantitative thresholds to avoid churn — reforecasting required only if impact on quarterly revenue > 1.5% or absolute delta > $200k.
3. Timely Alignment: Contract amendments or PO commitments that change cash collection timing must be reflected in the next weekly forecast update.
4. Segregation of duties: Contract negotiation owned by Sales/Legal, forecast adjustments owned by Finance, procurement approvals owned by Procurement and delegated approvers.

Forecast Sensitivity Framework:

- Cadence:
  1) Weekly topline checkpoint (Finance + Revenue Ops): quick checks for bookings, major amendment notices, and procurement events.
  2) Monthly reforecast (detailed): replaces prior month’s micro-forecasts with refreshed numbers.
  3) Quarterly planning: scenario refresh and board/planning slides.

- Scenario definitions (minimum):
  - Base: Management best estimate using signed contracts + pipeline conversion assumptions.
  - Conservative (-10%): Contracts with pending signatures and renewals at risk; adjust churn + price pressure.
  - Upside (+10%): Accelerated renewals / increased upsells.

- Key levers for sensitivity analysis (examples):
  - Sales conversion lag (days) — default 30; sensitivity at +/- 15 days.
  - On-prem / Private deployment start delay — default 45 days; sensitivity +/-30 days.
  - Reserved Dedicated capacity ramp — step function: 0/25/50/100% capacity on fixed dates.
  - FX movement: apply 3% and 6% shocks for non-USD revenue.

Triggers that require an immediate reforecast (examples):

- Contract amendment or cancellation with revenue impact > $250k or change to billing timing > 60 days.
- Procurement commitments (CAPEX/contracted infra) that increase monthly costs > $150k.
- Pipeline conversion slippage causing expected ARR recognition to move across quarters.
- Collections deterioration: DSO increases by > 10 days quarter-over-quarter.

Contract Alignment and Mapping to Forecast / RevRec:

1. Contract intake checklist (required fields captured in contract repository):
   - Effective date, billing cadence, payment terms, renewal terms, termination rights, data residency/KMS clauses, SOW milestones, deliverable acceptance criteria, and liability/escrow clauses.

2. Mapping rules (standardized):
   - Recurring subscription (hosted API) = recognized ratably over service period, subject to ASC 606 performance obligations.
   - Dedicated reserved capacity = allocation between hardware/service (if separately priced) and subscription; split per negotiated percentages or estimated fair value.
   - Professional services (enablement, onboarding) = allocate where distinct; if not distinct, bundle with subscription and recognize over contract period.
   - One-time implementation fees with acceptance criteria = defer until acceptance or when services are distinct.

3. Contract amendment workflow (3-step):
   - Step 1: Sales logs amendment in CRP (Contract Request Portal) and flags change type: timing vs. quantum.
   - Step 2: Legal reviews clause implications and tags revenue treatment.
   - Step 3: Finance updates the forecast schedule and notifies Revenue Ops to update billing runs.

Approval thresholds and escalation:

- Standard approval matrix:
  - <$250k: Sales Director + Procurement (if PO needed).
  - $250k–$1M: Sales VP + Legal + Finance.
  - >$1M or changes to data-residency/escrow/KMS clauses: CRO + CFO + Legal Partner.

- Escalation path if thresholds breached at signing: Notify CFO within 24 hours, freeze recognition until sign-off.

Procurement timing & CAPEX vs OPEX considerations:

- Procurement obligations that obligate future payments (multi-year support contracts, hardware for Dedicated pools) must be recorded in the procurement register and reflected in cash-flow forecasts.
- Capitalization policy summary: Hardware purchases > $50k with >12 month useful life => CAPEX (amortize over 36 months); other purchases are OPEX.
- Vendor payment terms: Standard net-45 unless negotiated otherwise. Extended payment terms (>net-90) require Finance + Procurement sign-off and must be modeled in working capital.

Revenue Recognition & Billing Policy Exceptions:

- Standard revrec treatment is governed by ASC 606 principles: identify performance obligations, determine transaction price, allocate, and recognize when satisfied.
- Common exceptions:
  - Free trials and credits: model as contra-revenue and adjust recognized ARR when trial converts.
  - Variable consideration (usage billing): apply expected value approach and update each month with actual usage; cap estimates if significant reversal risk.
  - Customer acceptance clauses: defer until acceptance or expiry of acceptance window.

- Material judgment checklist (required for monthly close when non-standard items exist):
  1) Evidence of transfer of control (logs, access metrics).
  2) Acceptance sign-off or test results from customer.
  3) Clear pricing terms for performance obligations.

Monthly Close & Reconciliation Procedures (high level):

1. Pre-close (day -5 to 0): Finalize contract change log, capture new POs, validate billing runs.
2. Close day 1–3: Post invoice batches, reconcile AR subledger to GL, run deferred revenue roll-forward.
3. Day 4–7: Review churn and credit memos, update forecast with realized deltas, prepare commentary for CFO.

Sample deferred revenue roll-forward (text table):

Columns: Period | Opening Deferred | Cash Invoiced | Revenue Recognized | Adjustments | Closing Deferred
Example row: Q1 | $1,200,000 | $500,000 | ($450,000) | ($25,000) credit | $1,225,000

Controls and Audit Evidence:

- All contract approvals must have an auditable trail in the contract repository including sign-off stamps from Legal and Revenue Ops.
- Random monthly sample (10 contracts) for internal audit: validate mapping from contract pricing to forecast line items; target exceptions <3%.
- Journal entry approvals: All non-standard revrec JEs must be reviewed by Finance Manager and CFO.

Reporting templates and signal dashboards (owner: Finance Reporting):

- Weekly topline checkpoint dashboard: Signed ARR, Pending signatures > 30 days, Net New ARR, Bookings by sales rep.
- Forecast variance dashboard: Actual vs Forecast by product line and region; alert if variance > 5% for two consecutive weeks.
- Procurement cash runway: Rolling 12-week commitments vs available cash.

Decision Log and Escalation Examples:

- Example: Customer A requests a 180-day delayed start for a Private deployment (impact $800k ARR). Because the delay changes billable start date across quarters and exceeds $250k, Sales logs the amendment, Legal tags the clause, Finance recalculates quarter recognition and executes an immediate reforecast. CFO signs off on recognition treatment.

Appendix — Quick reference artifacts:

1) Sample journal entries (text):
   - Invoice for subscription: Dr. Accounts Receivable $100,000 / Cr. Revenue (deferred portion) $100,000 (then monthly recognitions).
   - Defer implementation fee until acceptance: Dr. Cash $50,000 / Cr. Deferred Revenue $50,000; upon acceptance: Dr. Deferred Revenue $50,000 / Cr. Revenue $50,000.

2) Example sensitivity calculation (simple):
   - Base ARR for quarter = $4,500,000.
   - Trigger: 5% conversion lag results in $225,000 shift out of the quarter -> reforecast required if > $200k threshold.

3) Useful templates and reference links:

   - RevRec policy: /finance-and-legal/revrec-and-billing/revrec-policy-2024

[Pallisade Industrial AI]
Summary: Pallisade is evaluating Redwood Dedicated + Private for a factory-floor assistant and telemetry summarization pipeline. Primary ask: predictable throughput guarantees and strict latency SLOs for operator chat and alerting. They want dedicated GPU capacity (reserved) with fallbacks to hosted during maintenance windows.

Workload profile: mostly short interactive chat (operator queries, status checks) and periodic batch summarization of telemetry windows. Peak concurrency expected 350-500 concurrent operator sessions during daytime shift; baseline 60-100 overnight. Avg response length 40-120 tokens; some long summaries up to 4k tokens.

SLO & throughput targets (asked on call):
- P95 latency <= 200ms for short chat responses (<= 128 tokens).
- P99 tail latency target <= 350-400ms; they want wording in SLA about p99 and sustained load handling.
- Sustained throughput goal: 400 reqs/s steady-state with 1.2k reqs/s burst for 30s windows.

Reserved GPU planning notes:
- Initial estimate: 4-6 H100-class slots for baseline; plan for 8 slots for burst headroom. They asked for modeling of token/sec economics across 4/8/16 GPU commitments.
- Want explicit guidance on autoscaling/burst capacity policies and transparent preemption behavior when committed capacity is exhausted.

Model-specific tuning requirements discussed:
- Context length: 32k for telemetry summarization POC; need guidance on memory vs throughput tradeoffs and recommended kernel profiles.
- Quantization profiles: Will try 4-bit quant for large model variants; ask for Redwood's recommended quant profiles and fallback variants (int8 / fp16) for latency-sensitive routes.
- Batching & KV cache: Close coordination with their inference engineers. They prefer small, latency-minded batching (batch size 8-16 for interactive) and aggressive KV caching for long-context sessions to avoid re-encoding prefixes. Need POC configs to test cache hit rates and how cache invalidation ties into their session model.

Security / compliance: Must run in customer VPC for PII telemetry. Require KMS-integrated keys in Private deployment and audit logs forwarded to their SIEM. Data residency restriction: US only.

Commercial / SLA negotiation points:
- They want explicit credits if p99 latency exceeds agreed threshold across monthly rolling windows.
- Request a 12-month committed tier with breakpoints at 6/12 months for additional GPU add-ons.
- Need a clear escalation path and runbook for failover to Redwood hosted catalog models in case of private capacity outage.

Recent timeline / activity (high level):
- 2026-01-12: Intro + requirements call (Fireflies ff_call_2026_01_12_873).
- 2026-02-05: Architecture deep-dive with infra and security teams; provided preliminary network diagrams.
- 2026-02-21: Perf targets call; agreed to run baseline perf bench with 30k context and 4-bit quant profile. (Fireflies ff_call_2026_02_21_214)
- 2026-03-01: Shared POC pricing v2 (Drive link).
- 2026-03-09: Internal Redwood prep: generate GPU commitment cost model and draft SLA language for CX review.

POC milestones for evaluation:
- Perf bench (week 1): validate p95/p99 under synthetic traces matching operator load.
- Model tuning (week 2-3): test 32k context, verify KV cache hit improvement, iterate quant profiles.
- Live pilot (week 4-6): run on two factory sites in PRD-like network; measure SLOs and operational playbooks.

Customer quotes / call snippets: "If we can't get consistent p99 under 400ms our operators won't adopt it."; "Need a clear cost model that shows us break-even vs. self-hosting at 12 months."

Next steps (short): finalize dedicated sizing recommendation, deliver SLA draft, schedule POC kickoff for 2026-04-15, confirm billing/account team for committed contract.

[POC: SLO definition, workload profiling & evaluation tactics]
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-04-03
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Rodriguez (Redwood SE), Evan Brooks (Orchid Labs VP Eng), Priya Nair (Orchid Labs ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (Orchid Labs SRE)

Summary (auto):
Quick kickoff to agree POC success criteria for latency/throughput SLOs. Focus on traffic categorization, sampling plan, TTFT vs TPOT tradeoffs, p95/p99 targets, and measurement harness. Agreed next steps and owners.

Topics: 1) Success criteria & acceptance gates 2) Workload profiling and traffic buckets 3) Measurement approach (TTFT vs TPOT) 4) Benchmarks, runbook and timeline 5) Security/operational constraints

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining — uh — let's do quick intros, then we'll jump into what success looks like for the POC. Maya and I are from Redwood.
[00:10] Evan: Evan here, VP engineering at Orchid. Great to meet you. We're trying to validate that downstream chat features meet strict latency targets before we scale.
[00:18] Priya: Priya, ML engineering. I'll be owning the sample sets and baseline prompts.
[00:22] Liam: Liam, SRE. I'll own the infra constraints and be the bridge to our network/security team.
[00:28] Maya: awesome. Quick agenda: alignment on SLOs and acceptance criteria, what traffic looks like, proposed sampling and benchmarks, and decide measurement tooling and schedule.
[00:36] Samir: first question — what's your top-level success criteria? Is it user-facing latency, throughput cost per 1k tokens, or both?
[00:44] Evan: user-facing. p95 under 350ms for short chat messages is the main ask. If we can keep p99 under 700ms that's ideal. But we also need a predictable cost per 1k tokens for budgeting.
[00:56] Priya: just to add, we have a mix of short prompts (single question) and multi-turn contexts — about 70% short, 25% medium, 5% long. The long ones push token counts and KV cache behaviour.
[01:08] Maya: good, and do you have an existing metric for first-token latency? Or are you measuring total response time?
[01:15] Priya: we collect end-to-end response time now; we haven't separated TTFT. We could instrument for TTFT but need guidance on where to sample.
[01:23] Samir: that's core to this scoping. For POC we recommend measuring both TTFT (time-to-first-token) and TPOT (total-per-token) because they capture different user experiences and resource econs.
[01:34] Evan: can you explain the user impact differences quickly? I heard TTFT favors faster perceived responsiveness, TPOT affects throughput/cost.
[01:40] Maya: exactly. TTFT captures how fast the first token shows up — perceived latency. TPOT measures aggregate per-token generation time, which affects cost and throughput when you have many concurrent sessions. In a chat app, TTFT matters for perceived snappiness, TPOT matters when you need to sustain bursts.
[01:58] Samir: so for acceptance we'll propose a hybrid SLO: p95 TTFT <= 250-350ms for short prompts, and p99 TPOT per-1000-tokens budget target that maps to expected concurrency. But we need Orchid's traffic profile to pick enforcement buckets.
[02:15] Liam: our concurrency profile is spiky. Peak concurrency is roughly 420 concurrent sessions in Eastern region during our morning. Average is closer to 60. We also have backend batching that aggregates user messages occasionally.
[02:28] Priya: also note user payload variance — about 8% of requests are embeddings/analysis that are larger. We'll tag those out of the baseline sampling.
[02:36] Samir: perfect. For traffic categorization we usually split into: short (<= 32 tokens), medium (33-256 tokens), long (>256 tokens), and heavy analytics. That seems to align?
[02:46] Priya: yes that matches our histogram. Short is the bulk.
[02:50] Maya: okay so SLO draft: for "short" prompts TTFT p95 <= 300ms, TTFT p99 <= 650ms; for "medium" TTFT p95 <= 600ms; for TPOT, we propose p95 per-token ms under a threshold that keeps your cost per 1k tokens within target.
[03:06] Evan: do we have example numbers for TPOT that you can map to cost? We're sensitive to doubling costs at peak if quantization is not used.
[03:14] Samir: example: on an 8k context LLM variant, TPOT average per token might be 12-18 ms on our hosted runs; with int8 quantization it can drop 20-30% depending on kernels. We'll produce a model-comparison matrix in the PoC.
[03:28] Liam: will the PoC run against your hosted infra or our private deployment? Network egress and VPC peering will affect TTFT.
[03:36] Maya: good point. For this PoC we recommend Redwood Dedicated in-region to mimic production network hops, but there's also an option for a Private VPC peering test. Which do you prefer?
[03:46] Evan: we'd prefer Dedicated in our cloud region to avoid dealing with peering for the initial run. If results look good we'll evaluate Private deployment later.
[03:54] Priya: what about caching? We use prefix caching heavily for multi-turn; can you measure with cache warm and cold?
[04:01] Samir: yes, benchmark runbook will include cold-start, warm-cache, and steady-state phases. We'll also toggle KV cache and measure impact on TTFT and TPOT.
[04:10] Maya: measurement windows: we recommend micro-benchmarks (isolated synthetic runs) for kernel-level comparison, and end-to-end emulated traffic runs that replay sampled production traffic for acceptance. Both are needed.
[04:22] Priya: about sampling — we can export 14 days of anonymized request logs, but we need a script/template from you for stratified sampling.
[04:30] Samir: we'll share a sampling script that buckets by token length, user action type, and time-of-day. The goal is 10k representative requests for the end-to-end replay with a heavier tail sampling to capture rare long requests.
[04:42] Evan: how long does a standard benchmark sweep take? We have limited maintenance windows.
[04:46] Maya: depends on concurrency matrix. A baseline sweep (three phases: cold, warm, steady) at target concurrency for short prompts typically runs ~2 hours. If we do multiple model variants and quant configs, plan for a 6-8 hour run, ideally off-peak.
[05:00] Liam: can we run in smaller batches overnight? Our egress caps reset at 02:00 UTC.
[05:04] Samir: yes we'll collaborate with you to schedule. We'll provide a runbook and a preflight checklist so nothing surprises SRE.
[05:10] Priya: metrics — besides TTFT and TPOT, can we capture token counts, CPU/GPU utilisation, memory, kernel stalls, and tail queuing?
[05:18] Maya: absolutely. Redwood Console exposes per-route token breakdowns, GPU load, batching depth, and per-request traces. For the PoC we'll give you an evaluation dashboard and raw CSVs.
[05:28] Evan: SLA-like acceptance — do we need p95/p99 to hold across a 30-minute window or over the whole run?
[05:34] Samir: recommended acceptance gate: metric thresholds must hold for at least 90% of 15-minute windows across a 2-hour steady-state run. For p99 we usually use larger sample windows because p99 is noisy — we'll specify sampling confidence intervals in the runbook.
[05:49] Priya: what's the proposed p95/p99 numeric defaults again for our short prompts?
[05:52] Maya: p95 TTFT <= 300ms, p99 TTFT <= 650ms; p95 TPOT per 1k tokens keep within X ms — but we'll translate that to a cost per 1k token not to exceed your budget target. Samir will include the cost mapping in a spreadsheet.
[06:06] Liam: how do you handle burstiness? Our traffic has 30s bursts of high concurrency every 10 minutes because of a batch job.
[06:13] Samir: we'll simulate bursty patterns in the traffic replay and also test graceful degradation policies — e.g., fallback models, queueing with prioritized short prompts, or prefetched responses for certain flows. We'll show routing policies in the demo.
[06:27] Evan: security question — if we send sample traffic to Redwood Dedicated, how is data protected? We need SOC2+ and encryption at rest + KMS integration.
[06:36] Maya: Redwood Dedicated supports customer-managed KMS for key rotation and audit logs. We'll attach the SOC2 and ISO docs to the security packet. Samir will send the security link.
[06:45] Priya: instrumentation detail — for TTFT we need server-side timestamps: request-received, model-first-token, model-last-token, response-sent. We'll add those headers to the replay harness.
[06:55] Samir: yes, include those. We'll also capture at least two clock sync methods (NTP vs monotonic) to avoid skew.
[07:02] Liam: about p99 instability, if sample size is small, p99 can be dominated by outliers. Are you doing bootstrapped CIs?
[07:09] Maya: yes, the runbook proposes bootstrapped confidence intervals for p99 and median-absolute-deviation based outlier treatment — we'll surface raw traces for investigation.

[POC Kickoff - Data Handling & Benchmarks]
summary:
Kickoff for a 6-week POC to validate Redwood inference for PineBridge's customer-facing insight pipeline. Main priorities: PII handling, redaction in telemetry, retention windows for prompt storage, workload sizing for peak batch vs low-latency queries, and benchmark plan for latency/cost. Agreed next steps: security pack + architecture doc, sample dataset for sanboxing, 2-week benchmark run, and pricing outline for reserved capacity if needed.

topics:
PII detection & redaction
Prompt storage and retention settings
Telemetry/logging: what we keep vs scrub
Workload sizing and throughput targets
Benchmark plan and success criteria
Timeline and pilot acceptance criteria

transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-12-09
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam (Redwood Perf Eng), Aisha (PineBridge - Data Privacy), Marco (Platform), Ravi (ML), Sofie (Procurement)

Auto-summary (auto gen): POC kickoff focusing on privacy and bench architecture, with emphasis on redaction rules and retention durations.

[00:00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick check — can you hear us ok?
[00:00:05] Aisha: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks Jordan.
[00:00:08] Jordan: Sweet. I'm Jordan, AE on the account. With me are Priya, our solutions engineer, and Liam who runs the benchmarking work. We're here to scope the POC — specifically around data handling, retention, and benchmark targets. Can each of you do a 30-second intro?
[00:00:22] Marco: Marco, platform engineering. We're responsible for the infra side — VPCs, networking, and deployment ops.
[00:00:26] Ravi: Ravi, ML lead. I'll own the model selection and evaluation criteria.
[00:00:30] Aisha: Hi, Aisha — data privacy. I'll be defining what's considered PII and what must be redacted before logs leave our environment.
[00:00:36] Sofie: Sofie from procurement, here mostly to track timelines and contracts.
[00:00:00] Jordan: Great, thanks. Priya, do you want to kick with the proposed POC scope?
[00:00:42] Priya: Sure. High level: six-week pilot. Week 0-1: environment setup and security review (SSO, KMS, network). Week 2-3: benchmark run with our synthetic workload and your sample traces, focusing on latency p95 and cost per 1k tokens. Week 4: redaction/telemetry verification. Week 5-6: final pass and success criteria verification for acceptance. Benchmarks include both bursty low-latency queries and steady-state batch throughput.
[00:01:10] Ravi: Quick clarification: by "batch" do you mean async bulk scoring? Or chunked streaming inference?
[00:01:16] Liam: Good question. For us batch is async scoring — high throughput with throughput targets around X tokens per second. We'll also run streaming latency tests that emulate chat-style calls.
[00:01:28] Marco: On the security side I wanted to call out that we likely need a VPC deployment or Private control plane because of our data residency rules. Is that supported for a short pilot?
[00:01:36] Priya: We can do a Private deployment into a customer-managed VPC for the pilot. Usually for a short POC we spin up a temporary private control plane with strict networking rules — customers can bring their own KMS or use Redwood's managed keys if allowed. Aisha, which KMS mode would you prefer?
[00:01:50] Aisha: We need to review KMS integration. Ideally customer-managed keys — we don't want any plaintext storing on Redwood side.
[00:01:57] Priya: Totally understood. We support external KMS/HSM integrations. We'll include a KMS design in the security pack.
[00:02:05] Jordan: Let's talk data flow. Ravi, can you describe what PII typically looks like in your prompts and telemetry?
[00:02:12] Ravi: Most of our prompts are customer-support transcripts that include names, account numbers, last4s, occasional addresses. We strip obvious tokens client-side but we're looking to quantify residual sensitive tokens that slip through and test our redaction rules. Also want to see how Redwood logs inputs — e.g., do you persist full prompts in telemetry by default?
[00:02:32] Priya: By default our hosted logs keep a trace id and model metadata. For Private deployments we can configure prompt retention to zero or to an encrypted store with the retention window you set. We also have an optional prompt-scrubbing pipeline that runs regex and NER-based redaction before logs hit disk.
[00:02:50] Aisha: Can you be more specific about what "optional" means? We need guarantee we won't have free-text prompts logged in plaintext anywhere.
[00:02:58] Priya: Understood. For the POC we can enable the scrubbing pipeline and set telemetry retention to 0 days for raw prompts. We will still retain minimal telemetry such as request ids, model version, token counts, latency metrics. Anything that could identify a user we can either hash or redact. We'll document where keys and hashes are stored.
[00:03:18] Marco: And what about KV cache? Our use case involves retrieval augmented generation with session state. Is the KV cache persisted to disk? That's a sensitive surface.
[00:03:26] Liam: KV cache in our runtime is in-memory by default for performance. We do have optional checkpointing for longer sessions — but for the POC we recommend in-memory only to avoid persisting session tokens. That will also give you the best latency numbers.
[00:03:40] Aisha: Ok, in-memory only is preferable. However we need to test a failure scenario where a node is restarted — does the system repopulate without writing prompts to persistent logs?
[00:03:49] Priya: Good test. We can simulate node restart during the benchmark and confirm the behavior; we'll capture only aggregate metrics, not raw prompts.
[00:03:58] Ravi: On retention windows: we'll need a configuration where prompt retention is 0, but we want to keep derivation metadata for 90 days for debugging. Is that workable?
[00:04:07] Priya: Yes. We separate "prompt_payload" retention from "telemetry meta" retention. Prompt_payload can be set to never persist. Telemetry meta can be retained up to 90 days — and can be encrypted and access-controlled.
[00:04:20] Aisha: Who has access to that telemetry meta? Is there audit logging for readers?
[00:04:24] Priya: Yes, RBAC integrates with your SSO; we can configure roles so only your security and RM teams have read access. All reads are auditable and we can ship audit logs to your SIEM.
[00:04:35] Marco: Good. On workload sizing, we gave you the QPS distribution in the pre-call doc but to summarize: peak concurrent requests of ~800 qps during batch windows, avg 120 qps, median latencies target p95 < 250ms for streaming small prompts — can you size GPU/eval for that?
[00:04:51] Liam: We'll take that offline for precise sizing but initial thought is a mix of T4-equivalent nodes for batch and A100-class for latency-sensitive lanes. For Private we can provision mixed pools and route by policy (cost vs latency). We'll detail a recommended cluster topology in the Perf plan.
[00:05:09] Jordan: Success criteria — what would make this POC a success from your perspective, Ravi?
[00:05:13] Ravi: Three things: (1) p95 latency on chat flow under 300ms for our 90th percentile prompt size, (2) redaction catches > 99% of defined PII tokens in test corpus, (3) cost per 10k tokens under our target threshold — we have internal number but we can share after call.
[00:05:29] Aisha: Add (4) zero retention of raw prompts and provable access logs for telemetry reads.
[00:05:35] Jordan: Perfect. We'll capture those as acceptance criteria.
[00:05:38] Sofie: From procurement — how long will the trial resources be billed and what's the estimate if we need reserved capacity?
[00:05:45] Jordan: For a pilot we typically offer a timeboxed usage agreement — you pay for the infra you provision. If you decide to move to reserved capacity we can provide a committed quote for monthly usage; Liam can follow up with ballpark numbers.
[00:05:58] Liam: I'll prepare a cost sensitivity matrix: reserved commit vs on-demand vs mixed.
[00:06:03] Marco: On encryption at rest — will Redwood hold any plaintext on your side?
[00:06:07] Priya: No, if you choose customer-managed KMS, we never have the plaintext keys. Anything at rest will be encrypted with your key. We'll include a diagram showing key flow in the security pack.
[00:06:20] Aisha: What about redaction accuracy — you said NER-based scrubbing. Do you have a way to fold our custom regex and a blocklist?
[00:06:28] Priya: Yes, the scrubbing pipeline supports pluggable rulesets: built-in NER models + customer regex/blacklist. For the POC we can ingest your blocklist and run an evaluation over your sample traces and report false positive/negative rates.
[00:06:44] Ravi: We'll provide a sanitized sample of 20k prompts and a second set of 5k with known PII tokens to test recall.
[00:06:51] Jordan: Great. Timeline confirm — six weeks total, with benchmarks in weeks 2-3. Any blockers to that schedule?
[00:06:58] Marco: We need internal approvals to open the VPC peering and to allocate a service account for KMS access — that could take 5-7 business days.
[00:07:06] Priya: We can front-load the security review so networking approvals can happen in parallel with the baseline infra.
[00:07:12] Aisha: Also need legal review for data processing addendum — we have a template. Sofie will coordinate.
[00:07:18] Sofie: Yes, I'll send the DPA template after this call.
[00:07:22] Jordan: Perfect. Bench specifics — Liam, what's the benchmark plan shape?
[00:07:25] Liam: We'll run two suites: a latency suite (chat-style, many short prompts, measure p50/p90/p95) and a throughput suite (bulk scoring with synthetic tokens to stress throughput). For latency we recommend a replicated client across 10 ephemeral clients to emulate concurrent users. For throughput we'll run sustained 1-hour and 4-hour runs. We'll also run a failure/chaos test to simulate node restarts and confirm no prompt persistence.
[00:07:50] Ravi: Will you run the benchmark against our model or your curated open models? We plan to test a fine-tuned model — can that be loaded?
[00:07:58] Priya: We support customer model artifacts in Private deployments; you'll provide the container or model weights and we can stage it in the private environment. For hosted we have restrictions. For the POC if you want private loader, we'll coordinate artifact transfer via a secure bucket.
[00:08:12] Marco: Artifact transfer will need the signed S3 policy.
[00:08:15] Priya: We'll send an artifact transfer guide.
[00:08:19] Aisha: A couple of edge questions — do you tokenize differently in different quantization profiles? Could that affect PII detection?
[00:08:27] Liam: Tokenization doesn't change by quantization. However, certain quantized kernels might alter output fidelity in edge cases; for PII detection we run scrubbing pre-tokenize so it's not impacted. We'll outline the pipeline order: pre-scrub -> tokenize -> inference -> post-filter.
[00:08:44] Jordan: Any competitors or alternatives you're evaluating that we should be aware of?
[00:08:47] Marco: We're also looking at a few others — Anthropic's infra offering and an internal infra team doing on-prem hosting.
[00:08:52] Aisha: Also smaller managed vendors for redaction-centric products.
[00:08:55] Jordan: Good to know. We'll highlight where Redwood differentiates — unified runtime, configurable retention, and inlined scrubbing.
[00:09:03] Sofie: For contract stuff — if we go into reserved capacity what's the minimum term?
[00:09:07] Jordan: Standard reserved terms are 3 or 12 months; we can do a 3-month bridge pilot if you'd like.
[00:09:12] Sofie: Noted.
[00:09:14] Priya: On observability: we'll provide trace-level dashboards showing token counts, per-request latency, per-model cost, and a telemetry feed where we can redacted-sample the prompts if you opt in. This feed can be routed to your SIEM.
[00:09:28] Marco: Can we get sample dashboards ahead of time?
[00:09:30] Priya: Yes — I'll drop a dashboard link and the sample JSON.
[00:09:34] Jordan: Ok wrapping — let's restate concrete next steps and owners.
[00:09:40] Priya: Action items I'll record: 1) Security pack including KMS diagram and audit flow (Priya). 2) Perf plan and cost matrix (Liam). 3) Artifact transfer guide and S3 policy (Jordan). 4) PineBridge to share sanitized sample prompts and PII blocklist (Ravi/Aisha). 5) Procurement/Legal to share DPA template (Sofie).
[00:09:58] Aisha: We'll aim to deliver samples within 3 business days.
[00:10:01] Sofie: Legal will try to turn around the DPA in a week.
[00:10:04] Marco: I'll start the VPC approval request today — expect 5-7 business days.
[00:10:09] Jordan: Great. Anything else?
[00:10:12] Ravi: One last ask — can you run a small test to show redaction false positives? We want to see cases where names get redacted incorrectly.
[00:10:19] Priya: Yes, we'll include a quick false-positive report during the scrubbing eval.
[00:10:24] Jordan: Alright, thanks everyone. We'll send a recap and the security pack by EOD tomorrow.

[Permission shadowing, canary rollback signals, and customer opt-in migration plan for RBAC v2]
description:
Goal: introduce a lightweight 'permission shadowing' mode that writes RBAC v2 state in parallel but does not change enforcement for a customer cohort, instrument fine-grained observability probes for divergence and regression detection, and define canary rollback signals and a customer opt-in/off window for safe cutover. This ticket coordinates engineering work (dual-write, backfill throttling, reconciliation sampler), observability (telemetry, dashboards, alert thresholds), and customer-facing opt-in UX and comms.

acceptance_criteria:
Dual-write enabled for 5% canary cohort with shadow enforcement only
Divergence sampler deployed that flags >0.1% permission mismatches per 24h for canary
End-to-end test harness that replays 50 representative API flows against v1 and v2 and asserts functional parity
Rollback automation that disables v2 enforcement and re-routes reads to v1 within 3 minutes and verifies successful state re-sync
Customer opt-in toggle in Console with audit trail and email template for comms

tasks:
Implement permission-shadow flag and dual-write plumbing (auth-service & role-store)
Add per-request tagging (rbac-v2-shadow=true) for sampling and metrics
Build reconciliation sampler job and dashboard (grafana panel + alert)
Create canary cohort selector and rollout controller (region, org size filters)
Integrate audit-log hooks to capture v1 vs v2 decision context in S3/Pulsar
Implement rollback playbook and CLI automation (ops-runbook)
Prepare customer opt-in Console flow and consent logging
Coordinate security review and threat model updates

technical_notes:
Shadowing approach: write canonical grant/deny records to v2 store and annotate requests; enforcement remains on v1 unless opt-in flag present
Backfill throttling: use token-bucket per-org with adaptive slow-start to avoid cache stampedes; default 50 orgs/minute configurable per release wave
Reconciliation: deterministic diff algorithm based on (principal, resource, action, grant_id); tolerates eventual order differences by using tombstones for deletes
SSO mapping: user/group IDs must be normalized via canonical SAML NameID mapping layer to avoid mismatches; mapping verification job included
Audit logs: each decision must include trace_id, policy_version, principal_hash (pseudonymized), and decision_source (v1|v2|shadow)

risks:
Permission divergence causing accidental escalation if shadowing accidentally flips to enforcement
Backfill-induced DB throttling on peak churn orgs
SAML name-mismatch leading to false-positive divergence alerts
Customer confusion if opt-in UX not clear about enforcement semantics

rollback_plan:
Primary rollback: flip canary cluster flag to disable v2 enforcement and stop writes to v2 enforcement index; trigger reconciliation job with high priority to merge fixes back to v1 if any. Ops-runbook has scripted steps: 1) disable enforcement flag, 2) switch routing for read evaluation to v1 (3min target), 3) run divergence sampler and publish report. Secondary rollback: global feature-flag kill-switch and DB-level write-block if automated rollback fails.

monitoring_and_alerting:
Metric: rbac.v2.shadow.divergence_rate (count per 24h)
Alert: divergence_rate > 0.1% sustained for 6 hours => P1 oncall
Alert: backfill_write_errors > 0.5% per minute => auto-throttle backfill and page ops
Dashboard: canary/org-level heatmap with per-org divergence, top failing principals, recent SAML mapping errors

communications:
Customer-facing: 2-week opt-in window email + Console banner explaining shadow vs enforcement
Internal: Slack #rbac-migrations daily updates during canary weeks, weekly engineering sync with PM and Security
Support runbook: FAQ for customers about access regressions and how to opt-out quickly

[Streaming responses freeze mid-generation for Arcadia Health (SSE stalls, request never completes)]
description:
Issue summary:
- Customer reports streaming chat responses intermittently stop mid-generation. Client keeps the HTTP connection open; server stops emitting SSE tokens and never sends [DONE].

Impact:
- Production incident for Arcadia Health’s support-agent. End users see partial completions and stuck spinners.

Environment:
- Dedicated pool in us-east.
- Client uses OpenAI-compatible streaming endpoint.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Start streaming completion with max_tokens ~800.
2) After ~10–40 seconds, stream stalls mid-sentence.
3) No further bytes, no close, no error.

Investigation notes:
- Correlates with longer generations + high concurrent streams.
- Gateway shows upstream still open; runtime logs show request context cancelled late or not at all.
- Suspected backpressure interaction between token streamer + gzip + chunked transfer.

Workaround:
- Customer can set client-side read timeout and retry with idempotency key.

Resolution:
- Rolled out gateway change: disable gzip for SSE responses and flush after each token chunk.
- Added runtime guard: heartbeat/flush every 2s while streaming.

References:
- Slack: #support thread_ts 1769084201
- Customer emails in Ava Chen mailbox (thread_id gth_9a3f1b0a)

comments:
Ava Chen: Customer escalation via email + screenshot of stalled curl. They see it ~1 in 20 requests; worse at peak.
Alex Martinez: Seeing similar symptoms in perf-canary when gzip enabled. I can reproduce in staging with 200 concurrent streams.
Dylan Brooks: Gateway fix in progress; will ship a config toggle for SSE gzip off by default.
Ava Chen: Confirmed with customer: after change, no stalls observed over 2 hours of load test. Closing with workaround note still recommended on client side.

[Streaming chat sessions go silent mid-generation when prefetch throttle and corporate SSL proxy coincide]
description:
Issue summary: Several customers using Dedicated capacity reported streaming chat responses (SSE) that silently stall mid-generation. Impact: end-users see chats freeze with no final token and client-side eventually shows timeout/reconnect. Environment: Dedicated pool in us-east, traffic routed through customer corporate SSL proxy; client uses SSE over HTTPS. Steps to reproduce: 1) Start a long chat generation (>800 tokens) to redwood/gpt-medium-qa-v1 pinned on dedicated pool. 2) Repeat under corporate network that performs TLS interception and connection reuse. 3) Trigger high prefetch and KV-cache warmup by sending concurrent warmup requests (~20 concurrent). Observations/Logs: - Server shows continuous generation in runtime traces but no bytes reach client after ~40-120s. - Proxy logs show intermittent TLS session renegotiation and connection splice events. - Serving runtime reports prefetch-throttle events and worker backpressure in same timeframe. - Client SSE shows no close event; connection remains open but silent until client-side timeout. - No 5xx from edge; connections show long idle periods.

investigation_notes:
Timeline: 2026-03-09 first customer reports; 03-10 reproduce attempt in house. Metrics: surge of prefetch_throttle.count and serving_runtime.write_retries correlate with streaming silence windows. Hypotheses: 1) Corporate SSL proxy performs mid-stream TLS re-negotiation or connection splice that leaves long-lived HTTP/1.1 SSE connections in a half-open state leading to kernel-level write stalls. 2) Prefetch throttling causes the runtime to batch tokens longer, so there are fewer writes; combined with proxy coalescing this increases chance of proxy-triggered connection state change during quiet periods. Evidence: packet captures show server-side FIN+ACK after proxy splice while runtime still had queued bytes. Reproducible in staging with simulated TLS-interceptor that triggers renegotiation after idle intervals. Affected subset: Dedicated pools with aggressive KV-prefetch enabled and customers behind TLS inspection proxies. Observed that websocket clients show similar but less frequent symptoms due to different keepalive patterns. Logs and dashboards: link: https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/streams/streaming-silence?var=pool=dedicated-us-east

resolution:
Workaround: 1) Advise customers to allow passthrough of long-lived SSE/WebSocket streams at proxy level or configure proxy to avoid mid-stream renegotiation. 2) Temporary server-side mitigation deployed: enable frequent SSE heartbeat (every 8s) and force token-chunk flush on emission for the affected dedicated pool to reduce quiet windows. Fix: Implemented more robust socket-handling in serving-runtime to detect silent write backpressure and proactively close and retry stream with a short reconnect advisory (launch PR linked below). Rollout notes: mitigation rolled to 2 dedicated nodes in us-east on 2026-03-14 09:15 UTC, monitoring for 48h. Follow-ups: - Create advisory for customers behind TLS interceptors describing recommended proxy config. - Add a runtime metric to track proxy-splice events and increase test coverage by simulating TLS-intercept in CI.

description:

2) Simulate burst of concurrent requests (50-100) to the same model variant within a 30s window.
3) Observe SSE stream: after initial tokens, stream becomes silent for 5-30s.
4) Either stream resumes with a block of tokens or connection resets.

Selected log excerpts (sanitized):
- request_id=rid-7f3b, trace=tr-11a: chunk_emit at t=0.12s, last_chunk at t=0.84s, then no chunks until t=24.3s.
- worker=pool-3/worker-21: 'batch-resync initiated' at 2026-03-12T23:41:02Z; 'kv-cache-evict start' at 23:41:02.223; 'inflight-split lock' acquired.
- scheduler: 'adaptive_batch_respin: triggered for model gpt-4o-mini-v2, reason=latency_skew'
- tcp: FIN from client at 2026-03-12T23:41:27Z; upstream reset from worker at 23:41:27.310

Attached metrics: SSE_chunk_interval_p50/p95 spiked from 40ms/120ms to 1.2s/18.4s during windows correlated with autoscaler events and worker respins.

investigation_notes:
Chronology: Customer reported 2026-03-12 23:50 UTC. Support triaged and escalated to SRE and Serving team. We reproduced in staging by replaying burst traffic and toggling adaptive_batch_window.

Hypotheses considered:
- 1) Network intermediary (corporate proxy) buffering: unlikely — multiple customers and internal smoke tests show same pattern.
- 2) Application-level keepalive missing: keepalives present but behavior persists.
- 3) Adaptive batching/resynchronization (batch-respin) causes worker to serialise inflight batches, evict KV cache, and block chunk emission until kernel warm-up completes — this matches timing and 'kv-cache-evict' logs seen.
- 4) Preemption/noisy neighbor: some worker eviction noted but not enough to explain ~3% frequency.

Key evidence: 'batch-resync initiated' log aligns with silence start; p95 token emit gap ~18s matches worker re-init path (quantized kernel load + KV refill). Reproduced by forcing a batch-resync during inflight generation in staging.

Edge/proxy configuration on streaming routes can prematurely close connections under certain backpressure/idle patterns, especially during/after edge rollouts. Model layer errors are typically not present.

[Runbook (2026): Streaming timeouts caused by large request headers + proxy buffering (ALB/API Gateway)]
## Purpose
This runbook covers diagnosing and mitigating intermittent streaming inference failures (typically 502/504) that occur during long-lived streaming completions (40–180s), most commonly when request headers are large and/or change frequently (e.g., rotating Cookie headers) and the edge tier buffers streaming responses.

This pattern was confirmed in customer production (Lexicraft AI, dedicated, us-east-1) under SUP-90147 and has recurred historically under similar conditions.

## Symptoms (what you will see)
- Client reports: streaming stalls mid-response; connection closes with 504 (ALB) or 502 (API Gateway).
- ALB access logs: entries with HTTPCode_ELB=504 and/or error_reason like "Target timed out".
- API Gateway logs: intermittent 502 with messages consistent with upstream connection close / timeout.
- Serving runtime logs: typically clean (no worker crash/OOM). Token generation may still be happening server-side, but the client does not receive chunks.
- Failure rate: often low single digits (e.g., 1–10%), increases during bursts or when customers rotate auth/session cookies frequently.

## Primary causes (current understanding as of 2026-03-20)
1) Large request headers (most often Cookie + tracing headers) increase edge/proxy processing and can trigger buffering/translation behaviors.
2) Proxy buffering on streaming routes (API Gateway or intermediate proxies) can prevent timely flush of chunks, creating apparent “idle” periods at the ALB connection.
3) ALB idle timeout too low for long streams when downstream buffering delays chunk delivery, leading to ALB-initiated connection resets and 504s.

Notes:
- Header size alone is not always sufficient; the problematic cases frequently involve a combination of (a) large headers and (b) long-lived connections with intermittent chunk delivery.
- In SUP-90147, correlation was strongest when total request header size exceeded ~8–12 KB and the Cookie header changed during sessions (auth refresh / rotation).

## Scope / where this applies
- Environments: most commonly production dedicated clusters behind ALB -> API Gateway -> mesh -> serving runtime.
- Protocols: observed with HTTP/1.1 chunked streaming; translation from HTTP/2 at the edge can exacerbate buffering behavior depending on gateway config.

## Decision tree (fast triage)
1) Are failures 502/504 and clustered on long streaming requests (>60s)?
   - If yes: continue.
2) Do failing requests have large headers (Cookie, x-client-trace, x-trace-cookie, large Authorization/JWT)?
   - If yes: continue.
3) Is proxy buffering enabled on the streaming route/stage?
   - If yes: disable buffering (see Mitigation A).
4) Is ALB idle timeout < expected worst-case stream duration + buffering jitter?
   - If yes: increase idle timeout for the streaming target group (see Mitigation B).

## Data to collect (before changes)
Collect these artifacts for the incident/ticket:
- 5–10 failing request IDs with timestamps and target group name.
- ALB access log lines for failing requests (include request_processing_time, target_processing_time, response_processing_time, target_status_code, elb_status_code).
- API Gateway request/response logs for the same request IDs.
- Approximate header sizes from gateway logs (or request samples) with focus on:
  - Cookie
  - Authorization
  - x-client-trace / x-trace-cookie / baggage / traceparent
- Serving runtime metrics: token throughput, worker restarts (confirm “no” for crash loops).

## How to confirm header-size correlation
Indicators:
- Failures disproportionately occur on requests with large Cookie/tracing headers.
- Replaying the same prompt with reduced headers reduces or eliminates failures.

Practical methods:
- Ask customer to temporarily disable cookie rotation (or reduce cookie payload) for a controlled window.
- Replay a failing request in staging with:
  - Original headers
  - Minimized headers
  Compare stream stability and TTFB.

## How to confirm proxy buffering
Indicators:
- Upstream (runtime) is emitting chunks, but the client sees delayed/accumulated output (large TTFB, then burst output, or no output until timeout).
- Gateway configuration shows buffering enabled for the streaming route.

## Mitigations
### Mitigation A (preferred): Disable proxy buffering for streaming endpoints
Goal: ensure chunks are flushed as they are generated.

Actions (implementation depends on gateway/proxy stack):
- API Gateway stage/route config: ensure streaming mode is enabled and response buffering is disabled for the streaming completion routes.
- Confirm any intermediate proxy does not buffer (e.g., equivalent of "proxy_buffering off" / "X-Accel-Buffering: no" behavior where applicable).

Validation:
- After change, confirm client receives tokens continuously (no long silent gaps) on a test stream lasting >120s.
- ALB target_response_time should no longer cluster near idle timeout.

Rollback:
- Revert stage/route config to previous version.

### Mitigation B: Increase ALB idle timeout for streaming target groups
Goal: avoid ALB closing long streams during occasional delivery pauses.

Recommended settings (current):
- Streaming target groups: 180s idle timeout (minimum), with consideration for 300s on high-latency workloads.
- Non-streaming target groups: keep defaults unless otherwise required.

Notes:
- Increasing idle timeout treats symptoms if buffering still exists; it should be paired with Mitigation A when possible.

Validation:
- Confirm 504s drop immediately on streams that previously timed out around 60–120s.

### Mitigation C (customer-side): Reduce header size and header churn
When our edge changes cannot be applied immediately or customer headers exceed safe limits.

Recommended guidance to customers:
- Keep total request headers under 8 KB (soft limit); investigate aggressively above 12 KB.
- Avoid rotating large Cookie values during a single long-lived streaming request.
- Prefer compact auth tokens; avoid embedding large JSON blobs in cookies.
- Keep tracing baggage minimal; avoid duplicative trace headers.

## Permanent remediation (platform defaults)
As of 2026-03-20, the platform remediation direction is:
- Default: streaming routes MUST have buffering disabled.
- Add header-size telemetry at the gateway and emit per-request metrics (p50/p95/p99 header bytes).
- Add guardrails:
  - Warnings at >8 KB header bytes.
  - Investigation threshold at >12 KB.
  - Optional enforcement policy (by org/cluster) if chronic.
- Update docs and support playbooks to include “header size + buffering” as first-line checks for streaming 502/504.

## Operational checks (after mitigation)
Monitor for at least 24–72 hours:
- ALB 5xx rate on the affected target group.
- API Gateway 5xx rate on streaming routes.
- P95/P99 stream duration and disconnect rate.
- Customer-reported completion success rate.

Success criteria:
- 504s attributable to idle timeouts drop to near zero on the affected workload.
- Streaming output shows steady chunk delivery (reduced long silent intervals).

## Communication template (support-facing)
We believe your intermittent streaming timeouts are correlated with large and frequently changing request headers (notably Cookie/tracing) interacting with edge buffering/timeouts. We can mitigate on our side by disabling proxy buffering for streaming routes and increasing the load balancer idle timeout for long-lived streams. In parallel, we recommend keeping total request headers below ~8 KB and avoiding rotating large cookies during long streaming requests.

## Appendix: What to look for in logs
ALB access logs (common patterns):
- elb_status_code=504 with error_reason containing "Target timed out"
