[Economics and SLOs Optimization Roadmap — Q2 2027]
Summary
-------
This document describes the Q2 2027 roadmap for the Economics & SLOs Optimization initiative: a coordinated product and engineering program to reduce per-token inference cost, make SLOs more transparent and actionable for customers, and provide bundled pricing changes that align economic controls with reliability guarantees. It combines a short PRD, high-level design notes, pricing and packaging considerations, release plan, and an operational rollout playbook.

Background and motivation
-------------------------
- Customers have asked for clearer cost controls that do not force sacrificing latency SLOs.
- Internal telemetry shows 14% of hosted requests experience tail latency > target for routes with high token churn, leading to missed SLOs and increased incident work.
- Current pricing is per-token with optional reserved capacity; customers report difficulty estimating costs when autoscaling and when using cache/batching features.

Goals & success metrics (Q2 goals)
----------------------------------
Primary goals (deliverables):
1. Launch an "Economics Assistant" recommendation surface in the Console to propose batching + prefix caching + quantization profiles for tenant workloads.
2. Introduce SLO-tiered pricing bundles with explicit cost/SLO tradeoffs and a clear billing simulation tool.
3. Ship server-side adaptive batching thresholds and a fallback route that drops to cheaper-compatible model variants on overload.

Success metrics (target by EOW Q2 2027):
- 20% reduction in average per-token cost for participating tenants (measured net of reserved credits).
- SLO compliance improvement: reduce P99 token latency violations by 50% for opt-in routes.
- 35% of high-volume tenants adopt at least one recommended Economics Assistant suggestion within 30 days of availability.

Scope (in-scope / out-of-scope)
------------------------------
In-scope:
- Console recommendations UI and API surface for suggestions.
- Runtime changes: adaptive batching, model-variant fallback routing, dynamic cache TTLs.
- Pricing bundles: SLO-tiered bundles + billing simulation in Console.
- Metrics, dashboards, and alerting for rollout.

Out-of-scope (this quarter):
- On-prem installer changes for private deployments (will be tracked in eng-private-deployments).
- New model quantization algorithms (research will provide profiles only).

Product Requirements (high-level PRD)
------------------------------------
1) Economics Assistant (Console + API)
- Provide 3 ranked recommendations per tenant route: (a) Batching window adjustment, (b) Prefix/KV cache enablement & TTL, (c) Suggested quantization profile.
- Each recommendation includes estimated monthly cost delta, estimated SLO impact (latency delta at p50/p95/p99), and a confidence score.
- API: /v1/tenants/{tenant_id}/economics-recommendations returns JSON with suggestions.
- Owner: product -> Marina Quintero; eng -> optimizer-service team.

2) SLO-tiered pricing bundles
- Define three bundles: Bronze (cost-first), Silver (balanced), Gold (latency-first).
- Each bundle guarantees a different P99 token latency SLO for a route at a given committed capacity level.
- Bundles must be simulatable in Console using an uploaded workload sample or a sampled 24-hour trace.
- Billing change: new line-item labeling for SLO-bundles (e.g., SLO-BUNDLE:gold:route-123).
- Owner: pricing & revenue ops -> finance-and-legal (product to define tiers).

3) Runtime adaptive controls
- Adaptive batching: runtime must measure request size distribution and dynamically set batching window (min=2ms, max=40ms) to meet latencies for Gold/Silver bundles.
- Fallback routing: when queue depth > threshold (configurable per-tenant), route to compatible quantized variant (e.g., 8-bit) or to a lower-cost region.
- Cache TTLs: support per-tenant route TTLs for prefix cache with automatic eviction on model or prompt template changes.
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime -> kernel-and-scheduling and route-engine subteams.

Design specification (high-level)
--------------------------------
Architecture components involved:
- optimizer-service (new microservice): computes recommendations by synthesizing historical traces, cost model, and perf profiles.
- route-engine (existing): will apply adaptive batching and fallback routing policies at request ingress.
- cost-mapper (billing integration): adds SLO-bundle metadata to invoices and exposes simulation API.

Recommendation algorithm (summary):
- Input: 7-day sampled traffic trace (route, tokens_in, tokens_out, latency percentiles, model_id).
- Steps: 1) compute candidate batching windows and simulate token-latency curves using perf profiles; 2) estimate cache hit rates via prefix overlap heuristics; 3) compute cost delta for quantized model variants using per-token cost coefficients.
- Output: top-3 ranked suggestions with delta estimates and recommended rollout safety gates.

Configuration table (example)
----------------------------
| parameter                     | type      | default | notes                                    |
|------------------------------|-----------|---------|------------------------------------------|
| batching_window_ms           | int       | 8       | adaptive runtime will vary between 2-40 |
| fallback_queue_threshold     | int       | 128     | queue length after which fallback triggers|
| quant_profile_default        | string    | q8_optim | precomputed profile name                  |
| recommendation_confidence    | float pct | 0.75    | minimum confidence to show a suggestion   |

API examples
------------
- Sample response from recommendations API (JSON shown inline):

{"recommendations": [{"type":"batching","value_ms":12,"cost_delta":"-12%","latency_delta":{"p95":"+5ms","p99":"-40ms"},"confidence":0.82},{"type":"cache","value_ttl_s":3600,"cost_delta":"-7%","latency_delta":{"p95":"-2ms"},"confidence":0.68}]}

Pricing and packaging impacts
-----------------------------
- The SLO-tiered bundles introduce a new pricing dimension that combines committed capacity with SLO guarantees.
- Initial price points (draft):
  - Bronze: baseline per-token price (no latency guarantee).
  - Silver: +15% per-token over baseline for P99 <= 450ms at committed capacity.
  - Gold: +40% per-token over baseline for P99 <= 250ms at committed capacity.
- Bundles include an SLA credit schedule tied to SLO violations (credit up to 5% of monthly committed spend for Silver, up to 10% for Gold).
- Billing simulation: allow customers to run a 7-day simulation and view projected monthly spend and expected SLO compliance.

Operational rollout & monitoring playbook
----------------------------------------
1) Staged rollout:
   a) Internal canary: 3 internal tenants with representative workloads (date target: 2027-03-01).
   b) Beta cohort: opt-in customer list (15 customers) for 6 weeks.
   c) General availability: after successful beta (target 2027-05-15).
2) Monitoring and dashboards:
   - New dashboard: "Economics Assistant Adoption" (adoption %, accepted suggestions, estimated savings).
   - SLO dashboards per-bundle: P50/P95/P99 latency, queue lengths, fallback activation count, cache hit ratio.
   - Alerts: page on >3% sustained increase in p99 for Gold routes over 10 minutes or >15% delta between simulated and actual cost.
3) Rollback criteria:
   - If Gold P99 violations increase by >10% for 2 consecutive 1-hour windows in canary, rollback changes and reopen gating.

Release milestones and owners
----------------------------
- Proposal sign-off: 2027-01-15 (product, eng, finance). Owner: Marina Quintero.
- Optimizer-service MVP: 2027-02-28. Owner: optimizer-service lead (Jared Kim).
- Runtime adaptive batching & fallback: 2027-03-20. Owner: route-engine (Ethan Morales).
- Console simulation & UI: 2027-04-10. Owner: frontend (Priya Nair).
- Beta start: 2027-03-25.
- GA: 2027-05-15.

Customer communication and sales enablement
-----------------------------------------
- Publish a "SLO-bundles explained" one-pager for sales and CSMs.
- Training session for GTM: demo of the billing simulator + acceptance criteria.
- FAQ: include guidance for estimating adoption impact, how fallback variants affect model output quality, and how credits are applied.

Open design questions and risks
------------------------------
- Measurement fidelity: simulated latency curves depend on accurate perf profiles; mismatch could lead to degraded customer experience.
- Quality regression risk with quantized fallbacks: must ship automatic quality monitoring and canary evaluation (prompt-set based).
- Contract/legal: bundle SLA language requires legal review for credit terms.

Appendix A: Example rollout checklist (for an opt-in tenant)
---------------------------------------------------------
1. Collect 7-day sample trace from tenant (route, model, tokens).
2. Run Console simulation and present recommended bundle and savings.
3. If tenant accepts: deploy recommendations to a canary route (10% traffic).
4. Monitor p50/p95/p99 and quality evals for 72hrs.
5. Gradually increase to 100% over 72hrs if metrics OK; otherwise rollback.

Appendix B: Contacts and ownership
----------------------------------
- Product lead: Marina Quintero (marina@redwood.ai)
- Optimizer-service: Jared Kim
- Route-engine: Ethan Morales
- Frontend/Console: Priya Nair
- Pricing & Finance: Luis Ortega
- Security & Compliance reviewer: Hannah Strauss

Notes and references
--------------------
- See related PRD: /confluence/product-docs/requirements/predictive-batching-cost-optimizer-prd-2026-03-01 for earlier modeling assumptions.
- Perf profile catalog: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/benchmarking-and-perf-suite/perf-profiles-2026



[Rolling 18M budget + headcount + pricing sensitivity analysis]
Purpose:
This working doc holds a rolling 18-month view combining (1) operating budget by major bucket, (2) a phased headcount plan by function and hire-level costs, and (3) pricing sensitivity tests (3 scenarios) focused on ARR, gross margin and CAC payback. This is an operational model intended for finance + product + GTM alignment ahead of Q2 planning.

Key assumptions (summary):
- Time horizon: rolling 18 months starting 2026-04 (Q2 2026) through 2027-09.
- Currency: USD.
- Revenue drivers: hosted API usage (tokens), Dedicated contracts (committed monthly revenue), and Private deployment licensing.
- Baseline pricing: current list price per 1M tokens = $7.00 (hosted), average Dedicated ARR: $120k/customer/year, private licensing median deal $300k/year.
- Elasticities are segment-specific (see pricing sensitivity section).
- Hiring: average fully-loaded cost per hire depends on level. Assumed blended fully-loaded on-target cost: IC-1: $150k, IC-2: $200k, Sr IC: $280k, Mgr: $340k, Dir+: $450k (includes benefits, hiring overhead, ramp).
- Ramp assumptions: new hire revenue impact begins at 50% productivity month 3, 80% month 6, 100% month 9 for customer-facing roles. Engineering ramp slower for shipped throughput improvements.
- CAC and Sales efficiency: baseline CAC payback = 11 months; this changes under pricing scenarios.

Private sales pipeline has longer sales cycle; assume initial bookings in Q4-2026 under baseline. Customer facing hires spread into Q2/Q3 aligned to expected closed deals. We model hiring slippage (30% risk) separately in sensitivity sheet.

Unit economics and per-hire P&L impact (annualized example)
- Blended revenue per AE (ramped): $600k ARR; baseline AE ramp to quota by month 9.
- Blended gross margin baseline: 65% across product mix.
- Incremental cost of hired engineers primarily in R&D/COGS; for each backend hire we model a 0.5% reduction in per-token COGS over 12 months when combined with optimizer hires due to better batching and caching.

Pricing sensitivity analysis (3 scenarios)
Scenario A - Baseline (current price and packaging):
- Hosted: $7/1M tokens. Growth: organic +20% q/q early then moderating.
- Dedicated: committed ARR closes at baseline probability rates.
- Private deals: slow; conservative recognition schedule.
Result: ARR path matches budget table above; unit economics stable.

Scenario B - Upside (price increase & premium packaging):
- Action: 10% list price increase for hosted, introduce Premium SLA tier (+30% price for 15% of traffic), accelerate Dedicated pricing uplift (average deal size +15%).
- Elasticity assumptions: price elasticity of hosted demand = -0.12 (low elasticity for core API traffic), premium adoption = 15% of customers in 6 months.
- Secondary effects: CAC increases 8% due to more product friction in sign-up.
Impact: +8-11% revenue uplift by Q4-2026, gross margin improves by 200-400bps due to price leverage. CAC payback extends ~1 month.

Scenario C - Promotional / Competitive pressure (price cuts & higher churn):
- Action: 15% temporary discount for 4 months to protect market share vs new lower-cost open model entrants; introduce short-term free-tier expansion for small developers.
- Elasticity assumptions: short-term demand elasticity = 0.45 (usage-sensitive segment expands), enterprise Dedicated renewals unaffected but new deal conversion slows 10%.
- Secondary effects: churn among bargain-seeking customers rises 6% post-promo; retention programs increase S&M costs by 20% for 6 months.
Impact: short-term revenue bump on hosted (+10% hosted revenue during promo), but net ARR and gross margin decays by end of 18 months unless retention investment succeeds; overall EBITDA depressed by 300–500k in first 3 quarters following the promo.

Risk & mitigation notes:
- Hiring slippage risk (30%): model conservative case where hires are pushed 2 quarters; consequence is slower product improvements and delayed COGS reductions. Finance contingency: maintain 12% headroom in op-ex for 6 months.
- Pricing backlash risk: monitor NPX and developer churn weekly; if NPX drops >0.5pt, pause price changes and run segmented promo tests.
- Dedicated conversion risk: pilot a 30-day ramp program for two pilot customers to de-risk Q3 bookings.

Action items (near term):
- Finance to publish the full model (spreadsheet) with toggles for elasticity and hiring slippage (owner: Maya) by 2026-03-05. Linked Confluence: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/FIN/rolling-18m-model
- Product + Eng to estimate realistic COGS reduction per backend hire and optimization workstream (owner: Ben Kline) by 2026-02-28.
- GTM to prepare a price-communication plan and segmented experiments for premium tier (owner: Aisha Raman) by 2026-03-10.

Open questions (for leadership):
1) Tolerance for temporary margin compression to defend share in hosted? (range suggested: tolerate -250bps for up to 3 quarters).
2) Hiring priority if we must cut: preserve infra/SRE vs GTM? Recs: preserve infra + 50% of planned SRE, pause 1 AE.
3) Commitment to Dedicated sales milestones—should we accelerate incentives for early renewals to hit Q4 targets?

Appendix (small excerpt of model logic and formulas):
- Hosted revenue per quarter = sum(customers_i) * usage_i * price_per_1M_tokens / 1M.
- COGS hosted = hosted_token_cost_base * total_tokens + ops_surcharge (hosted_token_cost_base initial = $1.75/1M tokens baseline).
- Gross margin = (Total Rev - COGS) / Total Rev.
- CAC payback months = (Sales + Marketing spend attributable to ACV)/ (monthly recurring revenue from new bookings)

This file is a working artifact; expect multiple updates. For the primary model spreadsheet refer to the linked Confluence page and the finance GitHub model branch.

[Consumption Contract Orchestration Playbook]
summary:
Playbook describing the product design, requirements, rollout, pricing implications, and release notes for the Consumption Contract Orchestration capability — a control plane that codifies per-customer consumption contracts, fidelity tiers, and entitlements and automates enforcement and billing reconciliation across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

content:
Overview:
This playbook defines the scope, product requirements, design constraints, rollout plan, pricing considerations, and release artifacts for the Consumption Contract Orchestration (CCO) initiative. CCO provides a unified contract engine that maps customer entitlements (SLOs, fidelity tiers, capacity commitments, burst allowances) to runtime routing, telemetry tagging, billing hooks, and fallback policies. The goal is to make consumption guarantees auditable, enforceable, and reconcilable across hosted, dedicated and private deployments.

Why this capability:
- Reduce manual contract-translation work between Sales, Legal and Engineering.
- Ensure runtime behavior (fallbacks, throttles, priority shaping) matches negotiated commercial terms.
- Provide deterministic billing and reconciliations for hybrid deployments where enforcement surface differs.
- Enable product experimentation: entitlement-based A/B and canary configurations without bespoke infra changes.

Goals (success metrics):
1) Reduce time-to-turnup for SLA-entitlement customers from signed contract to production enforcement to < 7 business days.
2) Zero customer-facing mismatches between contracted SLOs and observed SLO breaches attributable to configuration drift in 95% of cases.
3) Provide a reconciliation delta < 0.5% between runtime-metered consumption and invoiced consumption for customers with entitlements.
4) Support fidelity tiers and burst crediting for 100% of new Dedicated customer signups in first 6 months after GA.

High-level product scope:
- Contract model language (JSON schema) to express: per-route SLO weights, fidelity tiers, burst credit pools, preemptible capacity allowances, and observability retention levels.
- Orchestration service to compile contracts into runtime routing rules, quota policies, and billing hooks.
- Developer console UI and CLI for preview, validation, and staged activation.
- Integration points: Billing system (reconciliation webhook), Runtime routing API (policy push), Console dashboards (entitlement view), Audit logging (immutable contract events).

Non-goals:
- Not a full legal contract authoring tool (Legal still issues executed master agreements).
- Does not replace low-level per-model execution optimizations (that remains runtime domain).

Requirements (minimum viable):
- RQ-001: Contract Schema - Provide a stable JSON schema v1.0 that expresses: customer_id, contract_id, effective_dates, routes (pattern), slo_targets (p99 latency ms, availability pct), fidelity_tier (enum), burst_pool (tokens), preemptible_percent, metering_tags.
- RQ-002: Validation - Syntactic and semantic validation with helpful error messages surfaced in Console and CLI.
- RQ-003: Compile & Push - Atomic compilation to runtime policies with an idempotent push API and per-deployment target (hosted/dedicated/private).
- RQ-004: Audit log - Every contract change emits an immutable audit event with user, timestamp, diff, and rollout plan id.
- RQ-005: Preview mode - Dry-run simulation that shows expected routing decisions for a supplied traffic sample.
- RQ-006: Billing Hooks - Reconciliation output file (NDJSON) compatible with existing billing ingestion with fields: contract_id, timestamp_bucket, tokens_consumed, fidelity_credit_used, fallback_count.
- RQ-007: Entitlement Mappings UX - Console view that maps commercial line-items to contract fields and highlights gaps.

Design considerations and constraints:
- Backwards compatibility: runtime must accept both CCO-managed policies and legacy per-tenant hand-configured routes during migration; priority: no customer-impacting behavior change during staged activation.
- Deterministic policy ordering: explicit precedence rules documented (contract-level > route-level > global defaults).
- Latency impact: push operations should be ultimately consistent across fleet; runtime must honor last-applied timestamp and support incremental deltas to avoid brief configuration spikes.
- Security: contract documents are sensitive. Encrypt contract storage at rest (KMS) and restrict UI access via RBAC.

Compile & Runtime contract mapping (text table):
| Contract field | Runtime artifact | Notes |
| contract_id | policy_id | 1:1 mapping; used in audit traces |
| routes.pattern | routing_rule | supports glob and regex; prefer prefix match for perf |
| slo_targets.p99_ms | latency_weight | used by adaptive scheduler to shape priority |
| fidelity_tier | model_variant_selector | resolves to allowed model variants and quantization profiles |
| burst_pool.tokens | burst_credit_account | reconciles to metering connector every minute |

Rollout plan (recommended):
1) Phase 0 - Internal dogfood (2 weeks): onboard 1 internal product team, exercise contract lifecycle flows, validate reconciliation hooks.
2) Phase 1 - Beta (4–6 weeks): recruit 3 early-adopter customers (mix of hosted + dedicated) for live traffic trials; provide dedicated SRE support window.
3) Phase 2 - Opt-in GA (8 weeks): open to self-serve for customers with entitlements; add billing reconciliation certification.
4) Phase 3 - Enforced GA (target): default enforcement for new enterprise contracts.

Operational runbook (abridged):
- On contract push failure: rollback using rollout plan id; alert on-call SRE; notify contract owner.
- On reconciliation delta > 1% for any customer: create incident, enumerate diff, pause new activations until manual signoff.
- If policy push causes routing anomalies: revert last policy push and engage the compile-service owner.

Pricing & commercial considerations:
- Entitlement packaging: offer CCO as an included capability for Enterprise tiers; charge an add-on for self-managed Private deployments where we provide orchestration connectors.
- Burst credits accounting: Introduce a fractional credit unit (0.001 credit) to enable fine-grained metering of microbursts; map to billing buckets with hourly aggregation.
- Migration credits: Provide a migration credit pool for the first billing period for early-adopter customers to offset initial reconciliation small deltas.
- Legal hooks: require a short contract amendment template that references CCO policy IDs to create an auditable link between the commercial contract and runtime policy.

Console UX & APIs (developer experience):
- Console views: Contract list, Contract diff viewer, Simulation preview, Entitlement-to-invoice preview.
- CLI: cco validate <file.json>, cco preview <file.json> --sample-traffic sample.ndjson, cco push <file.json> --target=dedicated --staged-rollout=10%.
- API: POST /v1/cco/contracts (returns rollout_plan_id), GET /v1/cco/contracts/{id}/preview, POST /v1/cco/compile/push

Acceptance criteria (product):
- All RQ-* items implemented and tested.
- End-to-end dogfood with at least one Dedicated and one Hosted tenant with simulated and real traffic.
- Billing ingestion successfully reconciles sample NDJSON outputs for 3 billing cycles without manual adjustment.
- Console UX validated by at least 5 customers in beta with NPS >= 8 for contract UX flows.

Compatibility matrix (text):
- Hosted: full support (policy push + billing hooks).
- Dedicated: full support (policy push + billing hooks) for Dedicated clusters running runtime v3.2+.
- Private (on-prem): partial support — CCO provides policy bundle and reconciliation payloads; customer must install local connector (open-source agent) for push and audit ingestion.

Telemetry and observability requirements:
- Emit policy_apply.success and policy_apply.failure metrics with tags: contract_id, target_deployment, user_id.
- Traces: compile -> push -> runtime_apply spans preserved with rollout_plan_id.
- Dashboards: Per-contract SLO attainment, credit burn rate, fallback rate, reconciliation delta.

Security and compliance notes:
- Contract storage: encrypted with customer-key-support for Private deployments.
- Audit retention: 24 months by default; configurable per-contract during commercial negotiation.
- Data residency: allow contract storage region pinning when requested by customer.

Open questions (to resolve prior to GA):
- Q1: How granular should legal amendment linking be (single clause per contract or per route)? Recommendation: per-contract policy IDs with optional route-level clause for high-risk customers.
- Q2: SLA enforcement granularity for mixed-route contracts. Recommendation: allow per-route SLOs but surface an aggregated contract-level SLO in the console and invoices.

Roadmap milestones (quarterly coarse plan):
- Q1 2027: GA for Hosted + Dedicated; billing connectors certified.
- Q2 2027: Private connector release and RBAC console refinements.
- Q3 2027: Advanced fidelity negotiation API and canary-based staged activations.
- Q4 2027: Auto-reconciliation suggestions and billing-exception automation.

Release notes (initial 0.9 beta release):
- Feature: Contract JSON schema v1.0 and validation service.
- Feature: Compile service and idempotent push API (supports prefix-based route matching).
- Feature: Console contract diff viewer and preview mode (sample traffic replay).
- Integration: Billing NDJSON reconciliation schema and ingestion demo.
- Known limitations: Private connector not yet available; reconciliation delta reporting reports hourly buckets (future: minute-level).

Appendix A — Example contract snippet (JSON, trimmed):
{
  "customer_id": "cust-1034",
  "contract_id": "C-2026-451",
  "effective_from": "2027-01-01",
  "routes": [
    {"pattern": "/v1/chat/*", "slo_targets": {"p99_ms": 250, "availability_pct": 99.9}, "fidelity_tier": "standard"}
  ],
  "burst_pool": {"tokens": 100000}
}

Appendix B — Owners and contacts:
- Product owner: Aisha Patel (product)
- Compile service: Marco Ruiz (eng-platform)
- Runtime policy push: Team runtime-policy (eng-serving-runtime)
- Billing integration: Elaine Chen (finance-legal)
- SRE support: Samir Gupta (eng-sre)

Related docs and references:
- Consumption scenario simulator (internal)
- Billing NDJSON schema (internal)
- Runtime policy precedence guide (internal)


[Observability Unification, LLM Quality, and Operator Autonomy Roadmap]
Overview

This roadmap lays out a 15-month program to unify observability signals, introduce automated LLM quality regression detection, and deliver operator autonomy features that reduce time-to-restore and mean time to mitigate (MTTM) for platform incidents. The work focuses on three coordinated pillars:

1) Observability Unification: single telemetry schema, cross-system SLI synthesis, unified trace/span conventions.
2) LLM Quality Monitoring: prompt set-driven regression detection, sample-based semantic diffs, and auto-alerting.
3) Operator Autonomy: safe operator actions, runbook automation, and decision-support UIs.

Goals and guiding principles

- Deliver a single observability contract for platform components by Q2 2027.
- Detect >95% of production LLM quality regressions in top-50 tenants within 30 minutes of occurrence.
- Reduce manual operator interventions for common degradations by 40% within 12 months of rollout.
- Preserve cost visibility and avoid telemetry bloat: new signals must pass a cost/benefit gate.

Success metrics (how we will measure progress)

- Observability coverage: percent of services emitting required fields in the unified schema (target 90% by Q2 2027).
- Regression detection recall/precision on historical labeled regressions (target recall 0.95, precision 0.85).
- Operator effort reduction: median number of manual steps per incident for top-10 runbooks (target -40%).
- SLO compliance: maintain platform token-generation 99.9% availability across regions during migrations.

Timeline and high-level milestones (quarterly)

| Quarter | Milestone | Owner | Acceptance criteria |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Q4 2026 | Program kickoff, schema draft, gating policy | Data + Observability Eng | Schema v0.1 published, gating checklist approved |
| Q1 2027 | Core signal producers adapted (runtime, allocator, kv-cache) | Runtime, Eng-Platform | 50% of services reporting schema fields; sample dashboards|
| Q2 2027 | Cross-SLI synthesis and alerting framework v1 | Observability | SLI joiner service running in staging; first cross-SLI alert generated|
| Q3 2027 | LLM quality eval pipeline (prompt-set hooks + diffs) pilot | Applied ML + Monitoring | Pilot on 10 tenants; automated regression alerts fired and triaged|
| Q4 2027 | Operator autonomy v1: safe-mode runbook automation | Eng-Platform + SRE | 3 runbooks automated with canary and operator override; post-deployment drill completed|
| Q1 2028 | Platform-wide rollout and retrospective | Product + Eng | 90% schema coverage; regression recall/precision goals met; rollout retro published|

Workstreams and owners

- Telemetry Schema and Contract (Owner: Data Observability)
  - Deliverables: schema v1, egress/cost guidelines, migration kit
  - Key fields: request_id, tenant_id, model_variant, input_token_count, output_token_count, latency_ms_p50/p95/p99, kv_cache_hit, batch_size, route_policy

- Cross-SLI Synthesis Engine (Owner: Eng-Platform Observability)
  - Deliverables: SLI joiner service, SLO composer, dashboard templates, alert enrichment pipeline
  - Runtime must support tokenized SLIs (token-cost SLO) and quality-linked SLIs (semantic-fidelity-score)

- LLM Quality Monitoring (Owner: Applied ML + Monitoring)
  - Deliverables: prompt-set manager, ground-truth corpus, semantic-diff model, regression scoring service, labeled-regression dataset
  - Integration points: sampling hooks at inference gateway, synthetic prompt injection for coverage, periodic offline evals

- Operator Autonomy & Runbook Automation (Owner: SRE + Eng-Platform)
  - Deliverables: operator action catalog, safe-mode DSL, automation runner, operator UI with decision playback and rollback buttons
  - Safety primitives: action dry-run, canary scope, feature flag gating, auditable operator approvals

- Dashboard and Alert Migration (Owner: Observability UX)
  - Deliverables: dashboard library, alert-rule translation tool, alert prioritization matrix, oncall training curriculum

Detailed rollout plan: dashboards and alerts

1) Audit & baseline (2 weeks): inventory current dashboards and rules. Produce baseline metrics: duplicate alerts, alert-noise rate, mean time to ack (MTTA).
2) Rule consolidation (4 weeks): map existing rules to the schema and de-duplicate. Apply priority tags: sev0, sev1, sev2.
3) Enrichment and context (6 weeks): wire SLI joiner to include relevant spans and model variant metadata in alert payloads.
4) Phased enablement (rolling 2-week windows): enable new rules for 10% of teams, collect operator feedback, tune thresholds.
5) Global switch (planned maintenance): flip new rules as primary, keep old rules in failover for 30 days.

Example alert rule (Prometheus-style) and enrichment guidance

```
# Alert: cross-tenant-token-latency-spike
expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket[5m])) by (le, tenant_id)) > 1500
for: 3m
labels:
  severity: "sev1"
annotations:
  summary: "P95 token latency > 1500ms for {{ $labels.tenant_id }}"
  runbook: "/confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/platform-operator-resumption-after-region-split-and-traffic-reconverge-2026"
  extra_context: "model_variant={{ $labels.model_variant }}, route_policy={{ $labels.route_policy }}"
```

Enrichment: alerts MUST include tenant_id, model_variant, route_policy, and a top-5 correlated signals block (recent token-burst, kv_cache_hit-rate delta, alloc_evictions).

Migration checklist (service owners)

1. Ensure service emits the unified schema fields. Use the migration kit to validate spans and metrics.
2. Add one sample synthetic prompt to the sampling pipeline (for LLM quality coverage).
3. Enable canary telemetry ingestion in staging; verify dashboards render expected values.
4. Participate in a runbook rehearsal (operator can trigger the automation and observe safe rollback).
5. File a post-migration verification ticket with screenshots and SLI delta comparisons.

Operator autonomy: safety story and allowed actions

- Allowed automated actions (with canary and operator approval):
  - tenant soft-throttle and burst-credit drain
  - model-variant swap to pre-approved fallback (quantized/warm variant)
  - emergency re-route to regional standby (read-only operator consent required)
- Not allowed as automation: schema-change rollbacks, billing-affecting quota resets, long-lived capacity reservation changes

Operator UI expectations

- One-click context bundle: includes correlated traces, recent synthetic prompts and their outputs, token cost delta, recent eval score trend.
- Decision playback: preview of what a model-swap would do (sample inputs routed through fallback variant)
- Audit trail: who triggered what, commands, approvals, and automatic revert timers

Risk register and mitigations

- Risk: telemetry volume growth causing storage/cost blowout.
  - Mitigation: data retention tiers, enforced sampling rates, and a telemetry-cost approval step for new signals.
- Risk: false positive quality alerts causing unnecessary rollbacks.
  - Mitigation: require 2-signal correlation (semantic-diff + user-facing metric drop) before auto-action; operator approval default for first 3 months.
- Risk: operator mistrust due to opaque automation.
  - Mitigation: decision playback, dry-run mode, and post-action explanations surfaced in UI.

Dependencies and cross-team coordination

- Applied ML: provide semantic diff model and labeled regression artifacts.
- Runtime team: emit KV cache and batching signals and support a sampling hook.
- Billing team: expose token cost attribution API for SLO cost-aware dashboards.
- SRE/content: update runbooks to use new field names and decision points.

Acceptance criteria for program completion

- 90% of core platform services emit required schema fields in prod.
- Regression detection pilot demonstrates target recall/precision on a held-out set and live incidents.
- 3 critical runbooks automated with operator override and audited rollbacks.
- Oncall MTTA reduced by 20% and MTTM reduced by 30% for top-10 incident classes linked to LLM regressions.

Retro plan and continuous improvement

- Post-rollout retrospective at 30/90/180 days with cross-team stakeholders. Agenda: telemetry cost vs. signal value, false positive analysis, operator feedback, SLO drift.
- Quarterly evaluation of semantic diff models using new labeled examples curated from customer escalations.

Open questions for leadership and design review

- What threshold of telemetry-level cost increase is acceptable for new signals (proposal: 5% of observability budget per quarter cap)?
- Policy decision: should we permit automatic model-variant swap without operator approval after 6 months of high confidence?
- Runbook ownership: who signs off on the final automation playbooks for customers in Dedicated (suggestion: Eng-Platform + Customer Success joint ownership)?

[Tail Latency Visibility and Mitigation Roadmap — 2027]
Overview:

This roadmap defines our 2027 program to reduce and make predictable the tail latency (p99–p999) observed by customer-facing inference requests across Hosted API, Dedicated, and Private fleets. The goals are visibility, automated mitigation, and controlled rollback/rollback-safe deployments so application owners see repeatable latency behavior while preserving throughput and unit-cost objectives.

Why this matters:
- Tail latency drives user-facing timeouts, degraded UX, and support escalations even when average latency looks fine.
- LLM workloads are bursty and multi-modal (chat vs. batch embedding), causing transient queuing and cache miss amplification.
- Reducing p99/p999 variance improves SLAs and reduces over-provisioning.

Scope and services in-scope:
- Router layer: inference-router (traffic classification and hint propagation)
- Serving runtime components: batcher-service, kv-prefix-cache, host-kernel-runner, continuous-batcher
- Orchestration: capacity-shedder, pool-autoscaler, hybrid-burst-controller
- Observability: tokenized-sli-collector, request-trace-indexer, runtime-metrics-pipeline

High-level objectives (OKRs):
1) Reduce median-to-p99 delta for standard generation route (seq_len <= 1024) by 35% by end of 2027 Q2.
2) Establish p99.9 visibility and automated mitigations for top-3 incident classes by Q3.
3) Create an SLO guardrail that keeps p99 under 350ms for 90% of requests in the Hosted tier; surface violations as an operational incident.
4) Integrate latency-aware routing into traffic-shepherd with canary rollouts.

Metrics and SLOs (concrete):
- SLOs (service-level):
  - inference-router: p99 < 100ms (control plane), p999 < 250ms (control plane)
  - batcher-service: p95 < 80ms, p99 < 300ms, p999 as alert signal (>1200ms)
  - end-to-end generation (hosted-api default-gen): p50 < 60ms, p95 < 150ms, p99 < 350ms
- Operational metrics to track: queue-length-percentiles, kv-cache-miss-rate, batch-size-distribution, continuous-batcher-latency, evicted-kv-prefixes-per-minute, CPU-steal-per-GPU, kernel-preemption-count
- Error budget policy: p99 > SLO for 6 hours triggers a severity-2 review; 24h continuous violation escalates to severity-1.

Phases and milestones (timeline):
- Phase 0 — Baseline & instrumentation (Q4 2026 — Q1 2027):
  - Deliverables: p99/p999 dashboards, request-level traces indexed by request-id, per-tenant latency histograms (24h rollup).
  - Owners: observability-team (dashboards), eng-platform (data schema), eng-serving-runtime (trace hooks).
  - Acceptance: available dashboards with historical 90-day retention; synthetic-runbook can reproduce a p99 spike in staging.

- Phase 1 — Classify and prioritize incident classes (Q1 2027):
  - Action: run two-week high-resolution trace capture across fleet, identify top-3 contributing patterns (e.g., cold kernel load, kv-prefix-cache thundering, oversized batches).
  - Output: incident-class playbooks and SLIs per class.

- Phase 2 — Automated mitigations and fast-fallbacks (Q2 2027):
  - Features: adaptive-batching-safety, kv-prefix-prefetch heuristics, kernel-eager-warmup, route-fallback-to-compact-model on elevated p99.
  - Acceptance: mitigations reduce simulated engineering-induced p99 spikes by >=50% in canary.

- Phase 3 — Latency-aware routing & rollout integration (Q3 2027):
  - Deliverables: traffic-shepherd policy extension to consider tokenized-cost and tail-latency risk score; rollout hooks to auto-fallback if p99 regression > 10% post-deploy.

- Phase 4 — Stabilization, cost tuning, and runbook codification (Q4 2027):
  - Deliverables: finalized runbooks, automated incident playbook triggers, run-rate cost impact report, cross-team training.

Key features to implement (detailed):
1) Request-level trace enrichment
   - Add stable request_id and route_hints at ingress and propagate across routers, batchers, kernels.
   - Ensure traces include: model_variant_id, quantization_profile, batch_size, origin_region, tenant_priority, kv-prefix-cache-hit.
   - Storage: high-sample-rate (10% of requests) stored for 7 days; aggregated histograms for 90 days.

2) Tail-aware batching policy
   - Implement continuous-batcher thresholding that publishes a "latency-risk" score per batch.
   - Policy: if latency-risk > 0.7 then prioritize smaller batches for affected tenants for next 30s; revert after risk decays.

3) KV prefix prefetching & admission control
   - Heuristic prefetch for top-10 prefixes per tenant based on 5min sliding window.
   - When prefetch budget is exhausted, apply admission-control to low-priority background requests.

4) Kernel warmup + preemption safety
   - Maintain a small pool (3%) of pre-warmed kernels per GPU type for top models.
   - Introduce kernel-soft-preemption that allows long-running kernels to checkpoint KV cache and yield to high-priority work.

Dashboards and alerts (what to build):
- New dashboard "Tail Latency Observatory" (owner: observability-team) containing:
  - Per-route p50/p95/p99/p999; stacked by model_variant and region.
  - Queue length percentiles and batch-size distribution heatmap.
  - Top contributing traces and a link to the trace viewer query.
- Alerting rules (examples):
  - alert: TailLatencyDegradation
    severity: P2
    condition: route_p99 > 1.2 * SLO for 30m AND queue_length_p95 > baseline
    runbook: runbooks/tail-latency-detection-and-mitigation
  - alert: KernelStorm
    severity: P1
    condition: kernel-preemption-count > 50/min OR prewarmed-kernel-pool-utilization < 20%
    runbook: runbooks/kernel-warmup-and-preemption

Runbooks and playbooks (links and summary):
- runbooks/tail-latency-detection-and-mitigation — step-by-step triage: identify route, isolate tenant, compare batch size distributions, check kv-cache-misses, apply adaptive-batching mitigation, optionally scale dedicated pool.
- runbooks/kernel-warmup-and-preemption — how to inspect kernel metrics, force warmups, tune preemption thresholds, and roll back preemption parameters.

Rollout plan and gating criteria:
- Canary cadence: start with 5% traffic in staging -> 1% in production (low-risk tenants) -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%.
- Gate criteria for increasing traffic: all canary p99 <= baseline*1.05 for 30m and no P1/P2 incidents.
- Auto-fallback safety: if p99 > baseline*1.1 for 15m, traffic-shepherd will route new traffic to previous variant and mark variant for rollback.

Ownership and responsibilities:
- Program owner: Avery Lin (eng-platform) — overall roadmap coordination and stakeholder updates.
- Observability team: dashboards, SLI collection, alerting rules.
- Eng-serving-runtime: implement batcher, kernel warmup changes, trace hooks.
- Eng-sre: oncall-runbooks, incident escalation, and capacity planning adjustments.
- Product: define customer-impact thresholds and public SLA language.

Dependencies and risks:
- Dependencies: tokenized-sli-collector upstream changes, pool-autoscaler API for soft-shed, billing team for cost reports.
- Risks: mitigations could increase per-token cost; prewarming increases baseline GPU occupancy; complexity in heuristics may create maintenance overhead.
- Mitigations for risks: run A/B cost experiments and document quantization/cost tradeoffs in the Optimize playbook.

Cross-team communication and training:
- Host two brown-bag sessions (engineering + product + support) during Phase 2 to walk through dashboards and runbooks.
- Publish a short "tail-latency FAQ" for support and sales describing expected behaviors and SLO semantics.

Success criteria (end of 2027):
- Measured reduction: median-to-p99 delta improved by >=35% for default generation route.
- SLO maturity: p99 SLO established and enforced with automated rollback for new variants.
- Operational readiness: runbooks cover top-3 incident classes and are exercised in one game-day.

Appendix: example CLI diagnostics and queries
- Request histogram (example):
  - curl -sS https://telemetry.internal/api/histograms?route=default-gen&window=1h | jq '.p99'
- Prefetch diagnostics (example):
  - kubectl logs deploy/kv-prefetch -c prefetch | grep "prefetch-error" | tail -n 50

Related pages:
- /confluence/eng-platform/runbooks/tail-latency-detection-and-mitigation
- /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/gpu-interference-detection-and-mitigation-playbook-2026

Questions and next steps:
- Decision to prioritize prewarming budget vs. admission control to be made by 2027-01-15 at the platform roadmap sync.
- Action: Observability-team to deliver initial dashboards and a synthetic workload by 2026-12-20.

notes:
Snapshot: Global trading desk (equities + options) exploring Dedicated capacity for inference. Goal: embed LLM features into trader workflow (real-time assistant), market data retrieval via embeddings, and fast reranking for signal prioritization.

Firmographics / constraints:
- Regulated finance firm, strict residency + audit needs. prefer US/UK data residency for trading data.
- Treasury requires net-30 billing + invoice format; procurement demands SLA clauses tied to penalties.

Technical targets and requirements (from SE workshops):
- Workload mix: 60% trading assistant (chat), 30% embedding search (historical market data), 10% reranking (signals).
- Latency SLO: P99 tail target for assistant < 60ms; ideal P90 ~ 20-30ms during market hours. Procurement pushing for 99.95% availability.
- Throughput: peak bursts up to ~1,200 TPS (small queries during open-market spikes), steady-state 200-400 QPS.
- Avg tokens per assistant call: 60-120 tokens (prompt + short completion). Reranking calls smaller (~30 tokens). Embeddings batch sizes mix 1-8 vectors.
- Model preference: want an LLM compatible with low-latency variant (quantized H100/A100-optimized) and an embeddings model with deterministic cost profile. Open to Redwood-curated model variants.

Reserved capacity / sizing discussion notes (working assumptions):
- Candidate hardware: H100-80GB or equivalent; aiming to commit 8 GPUs initially for Dedicated pool in US-East.
- Unit economics assumptions used in internal model:
  * Baseline GPU cost (list) assumed $11,000/GPU/month (vendor blended).
  * Slotting & infra overhead ~20% on top of raw GPU cost.
  * Estimated average utilization 55% (conservative) to 75% (optimistic) after batching and KV caching.
  * Effective tokens/sec per GPU (in production mix): ~6k-12k tokens/sec depending on model/sequence length.
  * Avg tokens/request ~ 90 -> implies ~66-133 reqs/sec worth per GPU under batch-friendly patterns.
- Commit scenarios modeled: 8 GPUs / 16 GPUs / 32 GPUs. Modeled monthly cost, expected utilization uplift from Redwood Optimize, and projected unit cost per 1M tokens.
- Example unit-econ excerpt (illustrative numbers from model):
  * 8 GPU commit, 55% util -> blended cost ~ $110k/month -> ~ $0.38 per 1k tokens -> $380 per 1M tokens.
  * 16 GPU commit, 70% util -> blended cost ~ $200k/month -> ~ $0.22 per 1k tokens -> $220 per 1M tokens.
  * 32 GPU commit, 75% util -> blended cost ~ $380k/month -> ~ $0.12 per 1k tokens -> $120 per 1M tokens.
- Notes: numbers are sensitive to tails/peak-hours; caching and routing to cheaper model variants reduces marginal cost. We stressed model switch fallbacks for degraded capacity scenarios.

SLA / commercial negotiation points:
- Procurement wants explicit P99 latency SLOs with financial penalties; Redwood must propose measurement windows and realistic SLOs for 99th percentile vs 99.9th.
- Requested: on-call escalation matrix, quarterly SLA review, audit rights, and detailed incident playbook.
- Pricing asks: discount tiers for multi-quarter commits + flexible bursting to hosted pool during unplanned peaks. They want a defined overage rate and ability to trade commit level at 6mo intervals.

POC plan & milestones:
- Phase 1 (2 weeks): small sandbox on Dedicated 2-GPU pool to validate latency profile and average tokens/sec; run synthetic market bursts.
- Phase 2 (4-6 weeks): expanded POC on 8-GPU cluster with real ingestion of historical trade data (anonymized) and compare tail latencies with Redwood Optimize suggestions (batching + caching).
- Phase 3 (8-12 weeks): pilot across one trading desk with canary routing, canary SLA, and runbook for fallbacks to hosted API if Dedicated pool saturates.

Decision criteria / risks:
- Will sign if Redwood can show: predictable P99 latency during market hours, unit cost per 1M tokens < $200 at committed volumes, and contract terms that satisfy procurement (billing + SLO language).
- Major risk: real-world utilization higher than modeled during market events -> needing additional GPUs or unacceptable tails. Procurement also wants data-residency proofs and SOC2 attestation.

Quote / paraphrase from CTO: "We need predictable cost per trade at scale — if you can show the math and the guarantees, we'll move fast."

Short-term next steps (CRM action items):
- AE to deliver detailed sizing spreadsheet with 3 commit scenarios and per-token economics by 2026-03-15.
- SE to run 48-hr synthetic spike test on 4-GPU sandbox and upload results (linked_fireflies).
- Schedule procurement + legal call to review SLA language week of 2026-03-22.

Stubs/links: pricing deck (drive), security questionnaire (drive), Fireflies recordings (ff_2026-02-18, ff_2026-03-02).

[SIEM customer contract and connector checklist]
Purpose and context:
This doc is a lightweight customer-facing contract + internal checklist for SIEM export integrations (Splunk HEC, Datadog logs, Azure Sentinel/Event Hub). It captures customer requirements we need to sign off on, the connector feature contract (schema + delivery guarantees), RBAC and audit implications, and an acceptance test checklist for pre-prod handoff.

Quick note: this is a working draft — expect TODOs and open questions. The aim is to have a single-page contract a sales/CS lead can hand a customer during onboarding, plus a dev checklist for the connector engineer.

1) High-level customer contract (one-paragraph summary to include in onboarding emails)
- Redwood will deliver a continuous export of production audit and activity logs related to the customer tenancy to the customer’s designated SIEM endpoint(s). Exports follow the "Connector Field Contract v1" schema (field set + schema_version header) and include the following event classes: auth events, admin activity, inference requests (metadata only), model rollouts and deploys, RBAC changes, and evidence generation events. Delivery modes supported: Splunk HEC (HTTPS with token), Datadog Logs (HTTP/S or TCP with API key), Azure Event Hub/Log Analytics (SAS or Managed Identity).

2) Required customer inputs (what CS asks the customer before we start)
- Primary SIEM type: Splunk / Datadog / Sentinel
- Endpoint details: HEC URL or Datadog intake URL or Event Hub namespace + hub name
- Auth mechanism: token (HEC/Datadog) or SAS + AAD/MI for Azure
- TLS requirements: TLS1.2+ enforcement, client cert if required
- Retention requirements: min retention (days), PII retention exemptions
- Allowed IP ranges for push (if customer restricts ingestion)
- Field mapping expectations: whether customer expects our canonical schema or a custom field map (we prefer canonical)
- Throughput expectations (events/sec, peak burst) and SLO for ingest latency (e.g., <= 30s for low-latency monitors)
- Contact points and on-call window for connector troubleshooting

3) Connector Field Contract v1 (canonical fields we will always send)
- schema_version: string (e.g., "v1.0") // top-level header in each payload
- event_id: string (uuid)
- timestamp: iso8601 string UTC
- tenant_id: string (redwood tenancy id)
- product_area: string (e.g., "hosted-api" | "dedicated" | "private")
- event_type: string (auth | admin | inference_request | model_deploy | rbac_change | evidence_generated | system_alert)
- actor: string (email or service principal)
- actor_role: string (RBAC v2 role at time of event)
- resource: string (resource id or name)
- resource_type: string (route | model | deployment | organization | project)
- outcome: string (success | failure | partial)
- details: string (freeform short description)
- metadata: JSON-string (optional freeform map for connector-specific fields)

Notes:
- For Splunk HEC we will send JSON events in the standard HEC format with the above as the "event" object plus fields.hec_index when provided.
- For Datadog we will map event_type to "ddsource" and include all canonical fields as attributes.
- For Sentinel via Event Hub we will wrap events as newline-delimited JSON with schema_version and tenant_id in each record.

4) Required vs optional fields and PII guidance
- Required fields: schema_version, event_id, timestamp, tenant_id, event_type, actor (anonymize on request), outcome.
- Optional: metadata, resource_type, actor_role (if RBAC v2 not yet enabled for a tenant we will send "unknown").
- PII: actor by default is human-readable email; if the customer requests PII minimization we will hash the actor (sha256) and provide a mapping artifact under strict contract (stored in Redwood vault and shared via secure transfer). Must be agreed in contract addendum.

5) RBAC v2 mapping considerations
- Redwood's RBAC v2 introduces role scoping by project and route. For SIEM consumers we emit actor_role as the effective role at the time of the event, plus metadata.role_scope = "project:<id>" if applicable.
- When customers request mapping to their internal role names, we must agree on a mapping table; do not attempt to translate without explicit mapping. Add mapping to "linked_artifacts" in onboarding ticket.

6) Delivery guarantees and latency SLOs (what Redwood commits to)
- Best-effort, at-least-once delivery for HEC/Datadog Event APIs. We'll include sequence ids and retry metadata in the event for idempotency reconciliation.
- For Event Hubs (Sentinel) use checkpointing on our side; duplicates can occur.
- SLO targets (negotiable): 99% of events delivered within 30s; 99.9% delivered within 5m for standard export. For strong SLAs (Dedicated/Private) we can tighten with reserved bandwidth.

7) Acceptance tests (Dev -> CS handoff checklist)
- [ ] Schema conformance: run connector against sample events and validate against JSON schema (unit tests exist in repo).
- [ ] End-to-end flow: send 1k synthetic events across 10 event_types and confirm arrival in SIEM index/hub.
- [ ] Latency test: measure median and p95 end-to-end latency for a 1-minute 50rps burst.
- [ ] RBAC labels: create RBAC v2 changes and confirm actor_role and role_scope present in resulting events.
- [ ] PII mode: confirm actor is hashed when PII minimization is requested.
- [ ] Failure modes: simulate SIEM auth failure and confirm connector backoff and alerting triggers.
- [ ] Backpressure and rate-limiting: verify connector respects customer-specified max QPS and graceful drop strategy documented in incident playbook.

8) Customer-facing onboarding steps (to include in the email template)
- Step 1: Customer provides endpoint details + auth token/SAS + allowed IPs
- Step 2: Redwood provisions connector config and shares a pre-prod test token
- Step 3: Customer runs a short ingest test (we provide curl examples) and shares logs/acknowledgements
- Step 4: Redwood runs 10-minute load test and shares raw results + sample events
- Step 5: Customer signs acceptance or opens issues (we have 5 business days SLA to resolve pre-prod issues)

9) Sample curl / payload snippets (quick samples for CS)
- Splunk HEC: curl -k -H 'Authorization: Splunk <HEC_TOKEN>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"event":{ "schema_version":"v1.0","event_id":"...","timestamp":"2026-02-15T12:00:00Z","tenant_id":"t-123","event_type":"inference_request","actor":"svc:frontend","outcome":"success","metadata":"{"tokens":34}"}}' https://siem-customer:8088/services/collector/event

- Datadog: POST to https://http-intake.logs.datadoghq.com/v1/input/<APIKEY> with JSON body being the canonical event. Include ddsource instead of event_type if requested by customer.

- Sentinel/Event Hub: send newline-delimited JSON to Event Hub namespace; ensure schema_version and tenant_id per line.

10) Troubleshooting notes (quick internal runbook bullets)
- If events not arriving: check network (IP allowlist), token validity, TLS handshake errors. Most common fail: customer IP restriction and wrong HEC port.
- If duplicate events observed: confirm connector is emitting at-least-once; advise dedupe by event_id on SIEM side.
- If fields missing: check schema_version mismatch; connector releases may add fields only in newer schema_version. Ask CS to confirm schema agreed.
- If latency > SLO: measure queue backlog on connector host; check for GC pauses, CPU contention, or downstream throttling from SIEM.

11) Operational and security controls (short)
- Secrets: tokens stored in KMS and rotated every 90 days by default. Customer can request shorter rotation windows.
- Encryption: TLS1.2+ enforced. For on-prem/private deployments customer can supply client certs; we will support mutual TLS where required.
- Audit trail: every config change to connector will produce an internal audit log event (rbac_change) that is included in exports. This satisfies evidence automation requirements for many auditors.

12) Open questions / TODOs
- Do we want to include raw request payloads for inference_request events in production exports? (privacy/cost tradeoff). TODO: propose opt-in flag for payload_trim_level: none | metadata_only | full_truncated.
- Should we support Syslog (UDP) for legacy SIEMs? Current priority is HEC/HTTP-based endpoints. TODO: product review.
- Add standardized sample dashboards and saved-searches per SIEM (Splunk SPL, Datadog query, KQL) — owner: Marco.

13) Acceptance sign-off (place to capture customer signoff in ticket)
- Customer name: __
- SIEM type: __
- Endpoint provided: __
- Agreed schema version: v1.0
- PII mode: default | minimized | hashed
- CS rep: __
- Date: __

Appendix: quick KQL / SPL examples (one-liners)
- Splunk (find failed auths): index="redwood_customer" event_type=auth outcome=failure | stats count by actor
- Datadog (failed model deploy events): @event_type: "model_deploy" AND @outcome:"failure" | count()
- Sentinel (KQL for admin changes): RedwoodLogs | where event_type == "rbac_change" | summarize count() by actor, tostring(metadata.role_scope)

End of draft.

Notes-to-self: attach the JSON Schema file from repo before final; check with legal about hashed actor mapping addendum. Follow up with Solutions Engineering for prebuilt dashboards and add to playbook.

[Security Data Bridge — Export Requirements and Connector Checklist]
Purpose:
This document captures a pragmatic, checklist-driven spec for exporting Redwood security and audit telemetry to customer SIEMs (Splunk, Datadog, Microsoft Sentinel) and to partner observability platforms. It focuses on customer requirements, connector-level design, RBAC v2 implications, audit log schema, evidence automation hooks, and operational constraints (throttling, redaction, retention).

Context and constraints (summary):
- Target consumers: customer security/IR teams and our SOC/Trust teams validating ingestion.
- Support model: hosted-managed connectors (Redwood-managed forwarders) and customer-managed forwarding (customer-owned HEC/collector endpoints).
- Security posture: Data must be transferable without exposing secrets; default behavior is to strip or redact PII unless explicit customer opt-in exists.
- SLAs: Best-effort delivery for non-enterprise; guaranteed ingest for Dedicated/Private customers under contractual SLAs.

1) Customer intake matrix (minimal required fields)
For each customer onboarding to export, collect the following:
- Customer SIEM type (Splunk, Datadog, Sentinel, other)
- Destination endpoint (URL), preferred protocol (HEC/HTTP/Syslog/CEF), TLS requirements
- Authentication method: token/HEC key, mTLS, Azure Event Hubs/Managed Identity, API key rotation window
- Allowed event categories: auth, admin-audit, model-inference, billing, alerting, compliance-evidence
- Redaction profile (none, default, strict) and PII policy document link
- Retention & sampling policy (retain full audit for N days / sample inference logs at X%)
- Contact(s) and escalation list (emails + paging)
- Required proofs of ingestion and evidence automation hooks (see section 6)

2) High-level connector modes
- Push-mode (Redwood-managed): Redwood sends batched events to customer endpoint. Use for customers that provide stable endpoints and trust Redwood-managed outbound traffic.
- Pull-mode (customer-managed collectors): Customer pulls from a signed S3/GCS location (short-lived URL) or subscribes to Event Hubs. Use when outbound to customer is not allowed.
- Hybrid (stream + archive): Near-real-time forwarding for alerts + batched archival export for full evidence bundles.

3) Connector spec (v0.3) - fields and behavior (this is a single-file spec used by engineering and ops)
- Protocols supported: HTTP/JSON POST, Splunk HEC, Datadog Events API, Azure Log Ingestion (Data Collector API / Event Hubs), Syslog (RFC5424) for legacy stacks.
- Batch size: default 512 events or 1 MB per batch, whichever first.
- Retry/backoff: Exponential backoff with jitter. Retries up to 5 attempts over 30 minutes before marking events as failed and writing to quarantine.
- Failure handling: store failed batches in encrypted, short-lived blob store (7 days) for re-delivery or customer pull.
- Authentication: token header (Authorization: Bearer <token>) or HEC token header (Authorization: Splunk <token>) or mTLS. Support token rotation by accepting previous token for grace period of 24 hours.
- Idempotency: include "redwood_event_id" and "ingest_sequence" in each event; dest should tolerate duplicates.
- Throttling: honor 429 with Retry-After; if missing, backoff using policy. Track observed RPS and drop lower-priority events (inference traces) when saturated.

4) Event shape and minimal audit schema (recommended canonical fields)
We push a canonical JSON envelope to simplify downstream correlation. Minimal required fields:
- timestamp: ISO-8601 UTC string
- event_type: one of [auth, admin, api_call, inference, model_load, deployment, alert, billing, evidence]
- redwood_event_id: UUIDv4 string (unique per event)
- request_id: customer-visible request id (if available)
- actor: short struct flattened as actor_type and actor_id (e.g., actor_type=user, actor_id=alice@example.com OR actor_type=svc, actor_id=svc-infer-42)
- resource: resource_type and resource_id (e.g., model, deployment, route)
- outcome: success | failure | partial
- outcome_reason: short message (optional)
- details: free-form message or compact JSON string with non-sensitive fields
- severity: numeric or string mapped to SIEM locale (default mapping: info=3, notice=4, warning=5, error=7, critical=9)
- tenant_id: customer id (for multi-tenant customers using single endpoint)
- rb_role_change: optional: when RBAC v2 role changes occur include role_name, change_type (grant/revoke), actor_id
- audit_version: "v1"

Sample event (as JSON string inside content):
{
  "timestamp": "2025-02-01T15:12:32Z",
  "event_type": "admin",
  "redwood_event_id": "b3f2c1d0-9c6a-4f2a-8d2e-1234567890ab",
  "request_id": "req_0b12f...",
  "actor_type": "user",
  "actor_id": "security@acme-corp.com",
  "resource_type": "rbac_role",
  "resource_id": "role-readonly-123",
  "outcome": "success",
  "details": "Granted role to user via UI",
  "severity": "notice",
  "tenant_id": "acct-9876",
  "audit_version": "v1"
}

5) Field mapping guidance for common SIEMs
- Splunk HEC: send the entire JSON envelope into the HEC _raw field and set index, source, sourcetype headers. Add Splunk metadata: event_time=timestamp, host=redwood.redwood-inference.com, sourcetype=redwood:audit:v1. Recommend compressed gzip POST when payload >1MB.
- Datadog: use Logs API with attributes tagging. Map tenant_id to dd.source and add dd.service=redwood-inference. Include redwood_event_id as dd.trace_id to tie logs to traces in Datadog APM if applicable.
- Sentinel (Log Analytics / Data Collector API): map top-level keys to custom fields; include "TenantId_s" and "EventType_s" suffix conventions for Kusto. Support batching into JSON array payloads up to Azure limits (30 MB).

6) Evidence automation and audit trace attachments
- Evidence bundles: Some compliance customers require the ability to request evidence for a specific audit window or request_id. The connector should support producing an evidence bundle containing: the primary events, associated inference inputs (if allowed by contract), model version fingerprints, and signed integrity manifest (SHA256).
- Automation API: provide a signed, short-lived download link to a zipped evidence bundle when requested via Support API. Logged actions (who requested evidence) must themselves be emitted as audit events.
- Data minimization: by default redact raw model inputs from exported bundles unless customer checks the explicit opt-in checkbox during onboarding and signs the required data processing addendum.

7) RBAC v2 considerations
- Role-change events must include before/after snapshots when possible. For changes via API or UI, include granularity: permissions_added:[], permissions_removed:[], scope_changes:[] fields.
- Export access control: require a dedicated export role (export-siem) that is mapped to service principal used by the connector. This role must be documented in RBAC policies and limited to read-only access to audit logs and delivery configuration.

8) Privacy, redaction, and allowed PII patterns
- Default-redaction list: email addresses, full user ids, input text longer than 256 chars, client IPs (unless requested), tokens. Replace with pseudonyms: user_email -> user_pseudonym (hash: sha256(lowercase(email)) truncated to 12 chars).
- Redaction strategy: deterministic hashing for correlation plus field-level suppression for sensitive content. Provide an option for tokenization (token vault) for customers with strict retention needs.

9) Operational runbook (SRE + SOC playbook snippets)
- On 429/slow responses: scale to smaller batch sizes and increase flush frequency for realtime events.
- On auth failures: rotate and re-deploy token; alert customer contact; point to mitigation page.
- On data mismatch complaints: support retrieving raw batch from quarantine and provide signed integrity manifest.
- Monitor metrics: outbound success rate, avg latency, 99th percentile per-destination latency, drop-rate, and quarantine size. Emit these metrics into Redwood observability with dashboards per-customer.

10) Testing checklist before go-live
- Connectivity test (TLS handshake and cert validation)
- Auth test (token acceptance and rotation grace period)
- Throughput/latency test at expected peak load + 30% headroom
- Redaction verification (sample set of events containing PII)
- Evidence bundle generation + signed manifest validation
- Duplicate suppression/idempotency test
- End-to-end ingestion sample event validated by customer SIEM team (provide test token and sample event)

11) Example configurations and snippets
- Splunk HEC POST sample headers:
  Authorization: Splunk <HEC_TOKEN>
  X-Splunk-Request-Id: <redwood_event_id>
  Content-Type: application/json

- Datadog example: send event with tags: ["tenant:acct-9876", "env:prod", "source:redwood"] and include request_id as attribute.

12) Open questions and action items
- Should we standardize on a single canonical envelope field naming for all destinations to reduce transform logic in connectors? (ops + eng to decide)
- Confirm which customers will require raw-model-input export (legal + product).
- Run a security review of token rotation and whether we should support customer-provided KMS-wrapped tokens for HEC keys.

Appendix: quick-reference mapping
- redwood_event_id -> unique id for deduplication
- tenant_id -> customer account id
- actor_type/actor_id -> who performed the action
- resource_type/resource_id -> object acted on
- details -> non-sensitive contextual info
- audit_version -> schema version for parsing

Contact and escalation: Priya Menon (security), Ethan Zhao (platform eng), Laura Kim (customer success).
